articleBody:
A few years into my practice, I began to feel deeply unsettled. Every day I would come home from my stressful job in downtown San Francisco, collapse on the sofa, and sigh. One day, as I released my daily sigh, a part of me spoke up and said, ‘I just want the space and time to feel my feelings!’

I sighed again and listened more deeply. I noticed that the voice was coming from my body. My body was asking to be fully known and felt as this deeply soft, sensitive receiver of every experience unfolding in each moment of my life. I had, up until then, paid it very little attention. All of a sudden, I could see the subtle violence behind this turning my back on my embodied experience.

On the next sigh, I invited the body to tell me what it needed next. And, in that moment, it sighed again. I turned towards the sighing, softened, and began to bring awareness to the breath.

I kept watching my breathing. The longer I attended to the breath, the more the body revealed a deep reservoir of pent-up emotions. I sat and opened to the sensations as best I could, humbling myself to them and allowing them to move through me. Later that evening, reflecting on what had happened, it occurred to me that the intention to bring awareness to my breath was the key to dropping more deeply into my direct, embodied experience.

Up until then, I had been meditating on the breath so that I could get away from my busy mind and escape the pain and stress of my day-to-day life. Now, I knew that awareness of the breath was not about getting away from anything. On the contrary, it was inviting me to lean in closer to the raw sensations of being alive.

## Breath as Bridge

Since you started reading this, have you noticed that you’re breathing? Probably not. The breath is so intimate to our moment-by-moment experience, but many of us go through our entire lives hardly ever noticing it. Or perhaps we only notice it when it doesn’t feel comfortable, like when we’ve got a cold, suffer with asthma, or feel anxious. For every human being and most animals, the breath is here from the day we are born until the day we die. We’ve been breathing all along, and the breath is always with us, connecting us to all of life, whether we are conscious of it or not.

Just like the breath, awareness is also always with us, a fundamental part of our experience of being alive. Breath awareness is a practice of applying just enough effort to allow two things that are always here to come together: we invite awareness to find the breath, and the breath to arise in awareness. Once they merge, we can deepen into a felt experience of the breath.

Take a moment to notice your breath. How does it feel just now? As you read on, see if you can maintain a gentle awareness of the breathing body and notice the effect this has.

The science behind how we breathe is incredible. We have evolved so that, as soon as we leave the womb, our automatic drive to breathe kicks in. And it doesn’t stop, not even for a moment, until the day we die. Of course, there are exceptions to this, like for those who suffer a life-threatening event where the breath stops. But, for the majority of people, there are no conscious or unconscious moments of our lives when we are not breathing. And we don’t even have to think about it. It just happens as a function of our autonomic nervous system.

Our breathing is mostly controlled by the movements of the central diaphragm, located just below the lungs. This large muscle receives automatic signals from the brain to move downward and outward each time we breathe. Its movement expands the ribcage, drawing air into the lungs and delivering the vital oxygen our cells need to survive and stay healthy. In exchange, the cells give back carbon dioxide, a byproduct of cellular respiration. Once the diaphragm returns to its resting position, air flows back out of the lungs, taking with it the carbon dioxide, which is toxic to us, but vital to plants for survival. All this happens in one breath, and we breathe in and out on average 22,000 times a day and millions of times over a lifetime.

Breathing is a central part of what it means to be alive. To take it for granted is to take life for granted.

The breath connects us with everything around us, like a bridge we can choose to cross at any time. We are intimately connected to the air, the earth, animals, plants, and each other, an inseparable part of everything in the universe. Breathing is a central part of what it means to be alive. To take it for granted is to take life for granted. To begin to get interested in the breath is to begin to get interested in life. What does it *feel* like to be alive? What is our direct, moment-by-moment embodied experience *actually* like?

## Practice: Three deep breaths

This is a practice that can be done anywhere, anytime, and is particularly helpful during transitions, like when you arrive in a new place. It can also be helpful whenever you feel alone or isolated, stressed out or frustrated, or in any other activated state.

Begin by extending the exhale, pulling the belly in and up, and emptying the lungs completely. Then allow the body to take a naturally deep inhalation and exhalation. Repeat three times.

Feel the expansion and contraction of the ribcage as you breathe in and out – cool air as it comes and warm air as it goes, and any sensations that follow. Feel the breath deep in the belly, the internal organs swelling and receding with each breath.

Feel the texture, depth, and duration of the breath. Can you follow it for as long as it lasts? How deeply can you sense the breathing body? As the breath comes in, see if you can sense it from deep inside to all the way out on the edges of the skin. As the breath goes out, feel the body soften.

Remember that this experience is universal to all human beings and many animals. Remember that the air you are breathing is an inseparable part of the universe and has been circulating the earth for longer than you’ve been alive. Remember that the carbon dioxide you breathe out will support some plant, somewhere, someday. Remember that you are alive and deeply connected to all things. Notice any effect these three deep breaths have on your mind and body.

♦

From [The Radical Embrace: A Meditator’s Guide to Embodying Love](https://www.windhorsepublications.com/product/radical-embrace/?srsltid=AYCX9vKymNgoi6cPuigXTsMo4feYuROzwXWJscB3S2w40iEsqdFubqae), © 2026 by Singhashri Gazmuri. Reprinted with permission from Windhorse Publications.

articleBody:
# Injured Ukrainian soldiers learn to use their new limbs | Psyche Videos

https://www.youtube.com/embed/N0T7NCuN4GA

### Far from home, Ukrainian soldiers relearn to inhabit their bodies

It’s estimated that as many as 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers and civilians have lost a limb since Russia began its full-scale invasion in 2022. At the Protez Foundation in Oakdale, Minnesota, such patients are fitted with state-of-the-art prosthetics free of charge and are taught how to use their new limbs. However, as the stirring short documentary Liminal captures, the process is far more than just physical.

For the film, the director Brennan Vance profiled a group of Ukrainian soldiers who, injured on the front lines, came to Minnesota to recover far from the brutal war that had defined their lives for years. Yet, despite their life-altering injuries, most were still eager to continue fighting, especially as the US commitment to the cause seemed to be waning. With the encouraging guidance of Yakov Gradinar, the Ukrainian-American chief medical officer at the Protez Foundation, the young men learned not only how to be in their bodies once again, but also how to inhabit the world. Poignant and inspiring, Vance’s documentary is both a unique window into the ongoing conflict and a powerful portrait of what it means to suffer a profound loss and yet still find a way forward.

Director: Brennan Vance

Producers: Norah Shapiro, Brennan Vance

title: Heith & Tarawangsawelas ~ Duori
subtitle: What comes after Jon Hassell’s Fourth World?
feedText: In 1980, Hassell and Brian Eno’s Fourth World, Vol. 1: Possible Musics imagined a musical geography in which traditions from different cultures merged with advanced electronic techniques, with Hassell’s electronically treated trumpet sounding at times like an instrument of indeterminate origin. articleBody:
What comes after Jon Hassell’s Fourth World? In 1980, Hassell and Brian Eno’s *Fourth World, Vol. 1: Possible Musics* imagined a musical geography in which traditions from different cultures merged with advanced electronic techniques, with Hassell’s electronically treated trumpet sounding at times like an instrument of indeterminate origin. For Italian producer **Heith**and Sundanese musician**Teguh Permana**, who records as**Tarawangsawelas**, the answer is a Fifth World, a post-apocalyptic continuation of Hassell’s vision in which what was once futuristic has become archaic, and musical traditions are no longer confined to their geographical origins.

Recorded over several years between Indonesia and Europe, *Duori* takes its name from an invented word combining the Italian *dentro* (inside) and *fuori* (outside), suggesting a space between worlds rather than one belonging exclusively to either. In his 1996 essay on the formation of Sundanese linguistic identity, Japanese scholar [Mikihiro Moriyama](https://kyoto-seas.org/pdf/34/1/340108.pdf) observes that, before Dutch colonial intervention, the people of West Java moved between languages according to circumstance, being sometimes Sundanese, sometimes Javanese, sometimes Malay. The Dutch encouraged a more rigid consciousness of linguistic and cultural difference, creating what Moriyama, borrowing from Mikhail Bakhtin, calls a state of “polyglossia”. There is something of a reversal of this process in *Duori*, where different musical languages coexist without being confined to their supposed places of origin. Heith’s electronics encounter Permana’s tarawangsa, the bowed string instrument associated with Sundanese ritual music, but it is Heith himself who plays the bonang on four tracks, while Luigi Monteanni’s saxophone and flutes introduce yet another voice.

Yet this exchange is not simply a matter of transplanting traditional sounds into a contemporary setting. As Permana explained in an interview with [Glamcult](https://www.glamcult.com/articles/in-conversation-with-heith-and-tarawangsawelas/), “I don’t think it removes the ritual context, because in the end it creates another kind of ritual itself.” Rather than treating Sundanese ritual music as an inherited form to be preserved or dismantled, *Duori* allows its spiritual and communal functions to acquire new meanings through collaboration. The musicians’ different approaches to time are equally revealing: the organic, cyclical repetition of tarawangsa encounters electronic composition’s more flexible structures, without either necessarily imposing its logic on the other.

The music moves freely between ritualistic repetition, electronic abstraction and moments of unexpected exuberance. Monteanni’s saxophone is particularly prominent on “Sangkakala Malaikat (Bandung Version)”, its expressive lines threading through bowed strings and electronic textures, at times recalling the otherworldly sonorities of Hassell’s trumpet. Not everything develops into a fully fledged composition. Some tracks are closer to sketches, brief excursions more concerned with atmosphere than musical development. “Pasar Setan” (Devil’s Market), barely two minutes long, is one such miniature, its title invoking the supernatural marketplace said to appear to travellers lost in the mountains of Java. On “Pragmatisme di Lembah Pegunungan” (Pragmatism in the Mountain Valley), an opening bordering on industrial noise gives way to sounds suggesting communal life, allowing the surrounding environment to enter the music. The recordings themselves carry traces of their circumstances, having travelled through portable recorders, deteriorating media and files exchanged across continents, their imperfections becoming part of the compositions rather than blemishes to be removed.

“Dua Jadi Hiji”, Sundanese for “two become one”, could almost serve as the album’s manifesto, although the music resists such a tidy interpretation. Its voices include a Ma’ Brakka funeral chant recorded by Heith in Sulawesi, subsequently combined with tarawangsa recordings from Bandung, Monteanni’s flutes and spoken words by Permana. What emerges is less a fusion of traditions than an encounter between different places, practices and memories, their original contexts remaining audible even as they acquire new meanings.

The linguistic playfulness extends to the track titles, which wander between Indonesian, Italian and English, sometimes taking the form of neologisms or improbable constructions. “Someone Took Off The Taste From My Cigarettes Overnight” sounds like an absurdist joke, although it refers to the belief that cigarettes offered to spirits lose their flavour when the offering is accepted. Even the closing “Chlorophyll Plantet” seems to inhabit a world of its own, with Permana’s voice taking on the character of an unidentified animal.

For all its invocations of ritual, mythology and spiritual communication, *Duori* rarely takes itself too seriously. Its Fifth World is populated by accidents, jokes, unfamiliar voices and the accumulated traces of a friendship that has developed across continents. Yet the album’s post-apocalyptic premise also raises a question about the language of musical progress. As Egyptian producer Abadir argued in an [interview](https://acloserlisten.com/2026/09/18/abadir-the-primitivist/) about his EP *The Primitivist*, electronic music’s enduring fascination with futurism has become a form of nostalgia, with novelty too often measured against Western ideas of technological advancement. “It became a habit to link newness to the future,” he observed. Heith and Permana approach the question from another direction. Rather than rejecting the futuristic imagination, they make the distinction between past and future increasingly difficult to sustain. Where colonial scholarship once sought to identify and preserve supposedly pure linguistic traditions, *Duori* finds pleasure in their coexistence and transformation. Perhaps the most convincing thing about its imaginary Fifth World is that none of its musical languages needs to belong to the past, or to the future, to have something new to say. ( **Gianmarco Del Re** )

title: Laurie Spiegel’s cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth
subtitle: Earlier this month, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft traveled beyond 25.902 billion km from Earth, a distance light would travel in 24 hours.
feedText: # Laurie Spiegel's cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth - CDM Create Digital Music MusicMusic techTech ## Laurie Spiegel’s cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth Peter Kirn - November 26, 2026 Add comment Earlier this month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft traveled beyond 25.902 billion km from Earth, a distance light would travel in 24 hours. Now is a great time to listen to Laurie Spiegel’s contribution to that record — a dizzying sonic model of Kepler’s Harmonice Mundi. An Earth day is essentially meaningless now that Voyager 1 is far from its home planet, but suffice to say the spacecraft is now, in our scale, really far away. Now is a great time to listen to Laurie Spiegel’s contribution to that record — a dizzying sonic model of Kepler’s Harmonice Mundi. An Earth day is essentially meaningless now that Voyager 1 is far from its home planet, but suffice to say the spacecraft is now, in our scale, really far away. It’s a reminder that this whole project was an interstellar equivalent of tossing a bottle into the ocean, with no real chance of ever passing into another star system, let alone being found. So the project, in the words of Carl Sagan at the time, “says something very hopeful about life on this planet.” It’s a reflection on Earth’s life as much as the near-void around. Voyager’s Golden Record would seem a little anachronistic to young humans now if they were to find it. It comes with instructions and a handy accessory pack including a needle and cartridge — we are literally talking a phonograph record here, albeit one printed on copper. Laurie Spiegel’s own composition, then, is both the least-mentioned detail of the record, and perhaps the most forward thinking. I actually wonder if it was fully appreciated by Sagan’s committee at the time; I understand just an excerpt made it on the record. And maybe the reason it doesn’t get mentioned in NASA’s music section is that a lot of 1970s ears didn’t really consider this music. And yet — give it a listen. Kepler’s Harmony of the Worlds is a hypnotic, sonic expression of geometry. (The re-release is sold out as physical, in case you had a spacecraft you wanted to glue it to, but is available as digital download.) It’s an exquisite piece of code and composition. The Expanding Universe by Laurie Spiegel The music collection is compelling — maybe more creative in its non-Western choices. (Kudos to Carl Sagan for the breadth of ideas here, though; that kind of spirit is something we could use more now!) The sound choices, from humpback whale song to a kiss, are to me the most fun to listen back on, a 1970s sound portrait of humanity. And that’s ultimately the thought experiment, asking us to consider our place on a cosmic scale. It’s not the Total Perspective Vortex — more like a reflection on an Earth perspective. (You’ve had since 1979; too late. See, maybe if they’d done what the ISS did in the movie, they wouldn’t have had this catastrophe.) articleBody:
As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).

As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.

Slated for release in January, *[The Book of the Human Body](https://www.taschen.com/en/books/classics/09603/the-book-of-the-human-body/)* delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.

Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”

Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, *Fabrica*, published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.

Pre-order your copy on [Bookshop](https://bookshop.org/a/96/9783754402474).

articleBody:
The [campaign to secure land for the Uganda Buddhist Centre](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-seeks-to-save-wetland-build-africas-first-dedicated-retreat-center/) (UBC) has passed $1 million, putting it halfway to its $2 million goal, organizers announced this week. Another $750,000 is needed to complete the land purchase by [the December 15 deadline](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-campaign-secures-land-deposit-sets-new-december-deadline/).

“What we do in the next three weeks decides whether this land is protected forever,” campaign organizer Leslie Booker wrote in the announcement.

### The story so far

Lion’s Roar [first reported on the campaign](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-seeks-to-save-wetland-build-africas-first-dedicated-retreat-center/) in August, as UBC marked its 20th anniversary. Founded in 2005 by Bhante Buddharakkhita, UBC was the first Buddhist center in Uganda and the first in Africa established by an African monk. Its campus in Bulega-Garuga, near Entebbe, includes the Buddhist Peace School, the African Buddhist High School, and a medical center serving the surrounding community.

The campaign aims to buy 13 acres of wetland next to the campus, on the shores of Lake Nalubaale (Lake Victoria), the source of the Nile. Bhante Buddharakkhita plans to build what organizers describe as the first retreat center on the African continent dedicated solely to sharing the dhamma, and to protect the wetland permanently. If the land isn’t secured, it could be sold for a resort or a military base. Organizers warn that either would threaten food and water security for nearby schools, an orphanage, and surrounding villages.

In September, [we reported](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-campaign-secures-land-deposit-sets-new-december-deadline/) that supporters had paid the $875,000 deposit needed to hold the land, and that the seller had extended the deadline for the remaining balance to December 15.

### “ Halfway home “

The $1.75 million asking price makes up most of the campaign’s $2 million goal. The rest covers surveys and unexpected costs. With $1 million raised, the $750,000 still needed by December 15 would complete the purchase itself.

Booker credited the campaign’s community for the milestone, saying every dollar came “from people like you,” through gifts large and small and through supporters sharing the campaign with others. Organizers are asking for “gratitude gifts” over the Thanksgiving week, whether it’s a donor’s first gift or their fifth. They’re also asking supporters to share the campaign with friends.

### A new film

The campaign has also released a short film, *Find Friends: Bhante Buddharakkhita and the Uganda Buddhist Centre*. It tells the story of UBC, Bhante Buddharakkhita’s vision for the land, and why protecting it matters. The film features Bhante Buddharakkhita and Booker.

“If you’ve ever tried to explain what Bhante means to you and couldn’t find the words, this film does it for you,” Booker wrote.

### How to help

Donations can be made through the campaign’s [Chuffed page](https://chuffed.org/project/201770-expanding-bhante-buddharakkhitas-uganda-buddhist-centre). Gifts are tax-deductible in the US. Donor-advised fund grants and employer matching gifts are also accepted. Supporters can also start a fundraising team with their sangha or friends through the same page.

Release: datasette-charts 0.4a0

The new datasette-charts plugin has its own plugin hook to allow other plugins to define new chart types, but I hadn't actually used it for anything yet. I had Claude Opus 5.5 build an experimental plugins just to try out the hook and it came up with a bunch of friction points in the design. This release addresses those, which should make building additional chart plugins a whole lot more ergonomic.

I've also added a website for the plugin, at charts.datasette.io. The new website includes a tutorial for plugin authors, and a gallery showing all of the core charts and annotations, each one linking to an interactive demo on Datasette Lite.

body:
# 1909 Chinese provincial elections - Wikipedia

Jump to contentFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopediaFirst Chinese provincial elections

Elections were held in 21 of Qing China's 22 provinces, excepting Xinjiang. Non-provinces are marked in white.

The Qing dynasty held its first set of provincial assembly elections from February to June 1909. Following a lengthy period of political turmoil which included the failure of the 1898 Hundred Days' Reform and the 1899–1901 Boxer Rebellion, the constitutionalist movement gained approval from the imperial court and Empress Dowager Cixi. Seeing local self-governance as a first step towards constitutionalism, in 1907, the Qing Government approved the creation of provincial assemblies. The following year, an indirect election system was outlined to fill these assemblies. They were held in 21 of the country's 22 provinces; Xinjiang elections were postponed due to low rates of literacy in Chinese. Suffrage and candidacy were limited to a small population of wealthy men, most of whom were members of the scholar-gentry. Public attitudes towards the elections were generally apathetic, and corruption, fraud, and vote buying were common across the country. Turnout greatly varied between provinces and regions, but was generally low.

The elected provincial assemblies were composed largely of constitutionalists, who were often divided between progressive and conservative wings. Some assemblymen were clandestine members of the revolutionary organization Tongmenghui. The assemblies agitated for a variety of economic and political reforms, which brought them into conflict with the provincial governors, who held veto power over the bodies. The assemblies participated in parliamentary elections, electing half of the members of the National Assembly. Before another set of elections could be held, the Qing dynasty collapsed in the 1911 Revolution and the Republic of China was founded. The first provincial elections under the new government were held in 1912.

### Background

Further information: Late Qing reformsConstitutionalist leader Liang Qichao, c.1905

Since the Song dynasty (960–1279), scholars were appointed to positions in the imperial Chinese bureaucracy through the imperial examination system.[1] This system was carried through to the late Qing dynasty, although it had come under increasing intellectual opposition during the late 19th century as corrupt and ineffective. As it entered the 20th century, the Qing empire was in social and political turmoil, facing a series of defeats by the Western powers. Despite the repression of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898, the constitutionalist movement continued to advocate for the creation of a constitutional government in lieu of Qing absolutism. The writer Liang Qichao emerged as the movement's most influential leader.[2][3][4]

articleBody:
# Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Back to Articles

## Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Published November 27, 2026Update on GitHub Upvote 17

David CorvoysierdacorvoJingya HuangJingyaSayak Paulsayakpaul

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

A seal dreams of warm sand. Generated entirely on Trainium3.

### Two goals

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

### How it works

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:

[{"name":"dream","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, shallow depth of field. A plump seal ... is fast asleep on warm golden sand under palm trees ...","seed":3},{"name":"nap","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... a plump grey seal is fast asleep on a small ice floe ...","seed":1,"to":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":9}},{"name":"iceberg","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... the whole iceberg slowly rolls over ... and washes over the seal. ..."},{"name":"shake","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... It slowly shakes its head and body ... and flops down on its belly on the floe, ...","from":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":25}}]

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:

- from: the shot starts from the last frames of an earlier shot. Starting from the earlier shot's last frame keeps a subject's look across a cut; starting from its last 25 frames (1 s) also continues the motion.
- to: the shot ends on the first frames of a later shot, so that it leads into it.
A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

The seal film's shot chain. iceberg, the payoff, is made first; nap ends on its first 9 frames and shake starts from its last 25, so the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same.

On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

The fox film: a walk in the snow, made "straight ahead": each shot continues the one before.The goat film: two trimmed shots, and a caption drawn over the payoff.

### Running on Trainium3

Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no plan to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.

Five days later:

10-second clip with soundNeuronCoresWall timeOn the NeuronCoresvs. first attemptFirst attempt, 960×54445 min 20 s45 s1×Optimized, 2048×1024 (~4× more pixels)3222 to 23 s15 s14×

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.

TP-4 × SP-8: 32 cores on one clip. The weights split 4 ways, one band of every layer per core; the video tokens split 8 ways, one stretch of the clip per chip.

# Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Back to Articles

## Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Published November 27, 2026Update on GitHub Upvote 17

David CorvoysierdacorvoJingya HuangJingyaSayak Paulsayakpaul

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

A seal dreams of warm sand. Generated entirely on Trainium3.

### Two goals

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

### How it works

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:

[{"name":"dream","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, shallow depth of field. A plump seal ... is fast asleep on warm golden sand under palm trees ...","seed":3},{"name":"nap","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... a plump grey seal is fast asleep on a small ice floe ...","seed":1,"to":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":9}},{"name":"iceberg","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... the whole iceberg slowly rolls over ... and washes over the seal. ..."},{"name":"shake","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... It slowly shakes its head and body ... and flops down on its belly on the floe, ...","from":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":25}}]

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:

- from: the shot starts from the last frames of an earlier shot. Starting from the earlier shot's last frame keeps a subject's look across a cut; starting from its last 25 frames (1 s) also continues the motion.
- to: the shot ends on the first frames of a later shot, so that it leads into it.
A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

The seal film's shot chain. iceberg, the payoff, is made first; nap ends on its first 9 frames and shake starts from its last 25, so the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same.

On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

The fox film: a walk in the snow, made "straight ahead": each shot continues the one before.The goat film: two trimmed shots, and a caption drawn over the payoff.

articleBody:
[Quill Kukla](https://www.quillrkukla.xyz/), who recently resigned from their position at as professor of philosophy at [Georgetown University](https://philosophy.georgetown.edu/), has accepted a position as Chair of Social Philosophy of Science and Language at [Leibniz University Hannover](https://www.philos.uni-hannover.de/en/) (LUH).

Professor Kukla works across a wide range of areas, including philosophy of place, philosophy of geography, ethics, applied philosophy of science, philosophy of language, epistemology, disability studies,, philosophy of health and medicine, and aesthetics. Their recent books include *Sex Beyond ‘Yes!’: Pleasure and Agency for Everyone* (2025) and *City Living: How Urban Spaces and Urban Dwellers Make One Another* (2021). You can learn more about their work [↗ quillrkukla.xyz](https://www.quillrkukla.xyz/research).

At LUH, Kukla will be working on their ERC-funded project, *TERRAINS: Territory, Agency, and Inhabiting Space*, the details of which (including open positions) can be found [↗ quillrkukla.xyz](https://www.quillrkukla.xyz/terrains).

In addition to their new position as Chair in Social Philosophy of Science and Language, at LUH Kukla is also a Humboldt Visiting Researcher as well as an affiliate of the [SOCRATES Centre for Advanced Studies](https://www.socrates.uni-hannover.de/en/).

## Folk Psychology as Mental Simulation

Folk psychology is the capacity to understand and interact with other agents. Until recently, it was commonly held in both philosophy and cognitive science that folk psychology is mainly underwritten by mindreading —i.e., the ability to represent what an agent thinks , feels , and wants , and to interpret and anticipate their behavior in light of those mental state attributions (Stich and Ravenscroft 1994). [ 1 ] For example, when we see that a student is walking up and down the department hallway, we infer that they are trying to find a certain room and do not know where that room is. On this basis, we stop them to offer assistance in locating the room.

This widespread assumption also shaped the Simulation Theory (ST), which was traditionally conceived of as a theory of mindreading (Davies and Stone 1998). Common sense has it that, in many circumstances, we arrive at representing others’ mental states by taking their perspective. For example, we understand the student’s behavior by putting ourselves in their shoes, imagining what we would think or want in that situation. ST takes this common-sense idea seriously and develops it into a fully-fledged theory. At the core of the theory, we find the thesis that mental simulation plays a central role in mindreading: We typically arrive at representing others’ mental states by simulating these states in our own mind and, on this basis, form predictions about, or explain, their behavior. The basic idea of ST is therefore that if the resources our own brain uses to guide our own behavior can be modified to work as representations of other people’s mental states, then we have no need to store general information about what makes people tick: We just do the ticking for them. Accordingly, ST challenges the Theory-Theory of mindreading (TT), the view that a tacit psychological theory underlies the ability to represent and reason about others’ mental states.

In this entry, we will discuss the debate between TT and ST. We will also discuss an outside challenge to this rivalry. Mindreading is no doubt an important skill in our folk psychological toolkit, as it enables us to navigate complex social interactions involving, e.g., irony, sarcasm, pretense, deception, and manipulation (Currie 2002; Leslie 1994; Nichols and Stich 2003). However, advocates of Pluralistic Folk Psychology maintain that mindreading, including simulation-based mindreading, has been overemphasized in the study of folk psychology. Folk psychology is, on this view, much broader than simply attributing mental states and explaining and predicting behavior. Proponents of Pluralistic Folk Psychology propose that behavioral scripts, stereotypes, and norms play a much larger role in our social interactions than mental state attribution, and that our interactions are often aimed at shaping or regulating others’ thoughts and behavior rather than explaining and predicting them (Andrews, Spaulding, and Westra 2021).

We will start by considering what mental simulation is (Section 1) and its cognitive architecture (Section 2). We will then explore its role in mindreading (Section 3) and in a broader, more pluralistic folk psychology (Section 4).
