on television

How Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC split coverage of fouls in television chyrons

One particularly powerful right-wing WNBA narrative — which arguably ties both implicit racism and transphobia together — is about fouls.

From the moment Clark entered the league, conservatives have pushed a story that other players are purposely targeting her on the court, often suggesting it’s because she is white. While Clark has faced real physicality — and calls for better officiating were widespread — the narrative of racialized persecution was pure political spin.

Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner

The Republicans cite, as evidence, the fact that “Clark has been hip-checked, poked in the eye, and struck in the throat during games.” It was an almost verbatim echo of Fox News, who spent months repeating those exact words across more than 200 articles fretting about the need to “protect” Clark.

That fixation on “protecting” Clark easily merged with another familiar right-wing narrative. By casting the WNBA as a hostile environment in need of cultural rescue, commentators tapped into the exact same “protect women and children” playbook long weaponized against trans women.

### This coverage matters

It’s tempting to dismiss this coverage as drivel. But unfortunately, it matters.

Fox News

Fox News anchors a media pipeline connecting prolific right-wing blogs and fringe online content farms directly to Republican politicians, including Donald Trump, who fawned over Cunningham’s looks and castigated the league to loud boos at rallies in the lead-up to the 2026 midterms.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ cable coverage of the WNBA. Two videos of Trump talking about the WNBA are pulled out.

As their own host Jesse Watters openly said on air, Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. They are exploiting world-class athletes as lucrative ragebait. And it’s working, at least as a business strategy: in August 2026, Fox’s OutKick hit a record 13 million visitors.

Three Fox News clips are pulled out: The Five on a WNBA coach’s “Trans kids belong” T-shirt aimed at Sophie Cunningham, The Big Weekend Show on WNBA Finals ratings amid national anthem drama, and Joe Concha on Cunningham’s post-election message going viral.

The issue isn’t that women’s basketball is being made political — sports are, and have always been, political. The danger is how quickly manufactured panic hardens into policy: Even as the 2026 midterms signaled a broader pushback against anti-trans rhetoric, voters in several states, including my home state of Washington, passed measures restricting transgender students from participating on sports teams that align with their gender identity.

We can’t let the WNBA be weaponized as a Trojan horse for anti-trans politics, or bigotry of any kind. The version of the league peddled by conservative media, the “ragebait W,” is unrecognizable to anyone actually watching the games. So let’s change the channel.

As Roxane Gay argued, the WNBA must match its players’ progressive courage — welcoming trans women while fiercely shielding its athletes from “bad-faith attacks, death threats, harassment, and other racial animus.”

The background switches like a TV changing channels and now shows roughly 40 examples of other outlets’ coverage of the WNBA. Four clips are pulled out: Gabby Williams in an interview, CBS Evening News on the WNBA and players reaching a historic deal, CNN on average WNBA salaries that could rise to over $1 million, and Layshia Clarendon speaking to Andscape.

The W is built different. Inclusivity is in its DNA: from the community in the stands, to beloved non-binary and Black-coded mascots, to the players' relentless push for equity on and off the court. And the basketball is electric. In this pivotal moment of the league’s growth, we need to see the outrage machine for what it is and push back, lest we all get played.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of other outlets’ coverage of the WNBA. Four game clips are pulled out: the Seattle Storm’s in-arena show with its mascot, a moment from a Storm game, and three-pointers from Gabby Williams and Angel Reese.

articleBody:
As I noted in my [last essay](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/technology-as-a-search-problem), I increasingly think that the process of creating new technologies is usefully thought of as a search process — the would-be inventor must sift through a huge mass of possibilities and pluck out from within it the specific arrangement of phenomena, parts, and components that actually performs some useful function. This is done by way of collecting and applying information about which arrangements work and which don’t, information which the inventor can use to narrow down what would otherwise be an outrageously enormous and intractable search process. When an inventor is trying to bring some new technology into the world, gathering and applying information to narrow down the space of possibilities is the primary thing that they’re doing.

But while this is useful as a high-level description, it doesn’t tell us much about what, specifically, inventors are actually doing when they’re trying to invent something. A search process implies a search *algorithm* — some method, or methods, that inventors are using to find working designs amidst the vast sea of potential ones. Our previous explorations of the technological search process have used random generation of possible technologies, but of course actual inventors aren’t combining elements randomly in the hopes of stumbling across something that works. To understand the nature of technological progress, it would be useful to have a sense of what algorithm our would-be inventors are using when creating some new technology, and whether some other algorithm might work better.

It’s probably not feasible to figure out the exact algorithm at work (at least, not feasible for me), since that would basically mean understanding the still-mysterious workings of the human brain. But enough histories of inventions have been written that we can draw some tentative conclusions about what sort of algorithm inventors are using.

In particular, if we look at a large number of invention case studies, we see that the first milestone is almost always the same: the would-be inventor creates some *technological concept*, a basic idea of the arrangement of components and phenomena that will create the desired effect.

This idea goes by different names. In patent law it’s referred to as the “[inventive concept](https://www.dlapiper.com/en/insights/publications/intellectual-property-news/2022/ipt-news-q3-2020/divergent-theories-of-the-inventive-concept-in-patent-eligible-subject-matter).” Thomas Edison called it the “base principle,” as did economist Brian Arthur. Soviet inventor and creator of the TRIZ method of invention Genrich Altshuller called it the “solution concept.” Engineer and professor of engineering Walter Vincenti referred to it as the “operational principle.” But regardless of what we call it, creating the technological concept is virtually always one of the very first steps when creating some new technology: once the concept is in hand, the technological search problem becomes considerably easier.

#### Technological concepts

Read any history of invention, and you’ll almost always find the creation of the technological concept behind it as a critical early step. The maser, for instance, began its life when physicist Charles Townes stitched the concept together while he was [sitting on a park bench](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/the-age-of-the-amplifier):

> Sitting in the park, Townes took an envelope from his pocket, and worked through how such a device might work. By feeding a stream of appropriately stimulated molecules into a resonator (a cavity that would reflect electromagnetic radiation of the appropriate wavelength), any electromagnetic radiation generated within the resonator would bounce back and forth, gaining energy each time it passed through the molecules as more and more photons were generated. The device would amplify any incoming signal as an electromagnetic wave passed through the population inversion molecules. And because the resonator would reflect the wave back and forth through the molecules (a form of feedback), it could also act as an oscillator — a generator of electromagnetic signals. Power would only be limited by how quickly molecules carried energy into the resonator.

Likewise, Chester Carlson assembled the concept for what would become the Xerox machine by [trawling through the scientific literature](https://calteches.library.caltech.edu/4142/1/Copies.pdf) to find phenomena that could be used to copy the contents of a document:

> Using finely divided powders to make visible images of electrostatic charges was an old idea in physics; it had first been done in 1777, when George Christoph Lichtenberg, a German professor, noticed that house dust adhered to an electrostatically charged piece of amber in a distinctive arrangement, which later became known as a “Lichtenberg figure.” Carlson knew about Lichtenberg figures, and Selenyi’s work reminded him of them. Suddenly, he saw that he might be able to make copies by employing a similar phenomenon in combination with photoconductivity. Instead of trying to use light to generate an electric current in a sheet of paper placed on top of a photoconductor, as he had done in his kitchen experiments, he would use light to remove electrostatic charges from the nonimage areas of a uniformly ionized photoconductor. Then he would make the pattern visible by dusting it with powder, and transfer the powder to a sheet of untreated paper.

And Paul Lauterbur came up with the concept for MRI when thinking through how the phenomenon of [nuclear magnetic resonance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_magnetic_resonance) (NMR) might be used to [extract information from living tissue](https://direct.mit.edu/books/book/3425/Paul-Lauterbur-and-the-Invention-of-MRI):

> If you could find a way to localize the NMR signals to specific places in a patient without using harmful invasive procedures, well, that would be a different matter altogether. If physicians could do that, they could look into any part of the body remotely to see what the problem was, and the patient would be unaffected by the analysis. “I believed that NMR relaxation time measurements on tissue specimens were unlikely to contribute much to the rich variety of information available from optical microscopy. All of this information about the tissues was apparently there, however, within the living organism. Was there any way that one could tell exactly which location an NMR signal was coming from within a complex object?” That same evening he figured it out. He had taken a dinner break with Don Vickers, a friend and company officer, at a fast-food place. “On the second bite of a Big Boy hamburger,” just as he was explaining to Don that the physics of NMR precluded imaging, in midsentence, he found the principle of MRI. “I realized that inhomogeneous magnetic fields labeled signals according to their spatial coordinates, and made a leap of faith to the conclusion that the information could be recovered in the form of images.” He sketched the general idea to Don. “Heck, you could make pictures with this thing!”

We see the same thing if we look at [Frank Whittle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Whittle)’s invention of the jet engine, or [Kary Mullis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kary_Mullis)’s invention of PCR, or [James Watt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt)’s invention of the separate condenser for the steam engine; in each case, the first step was the technological concept.

Technological concepts have different origins. Sometimes, like with Townes and Carlson, a concept is the product of working backward from a desired goal and gets stitched together piece by piece. Other times, they seem to appear suddenly in an inventor’s mind, such as with [Tesla and his AC induction motor](https://teslasciencecenter.org/pivotalmoments/alternating-current/):

> As I uttered these inspiring words the idea came like a flash of lightning and in an instant the truth was revealed. I drew with a stick on the sand the diagrams shown six years later in my address before the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, and my companion understood them perfectly. The images I saw were wonderfully sharp and clear and had the solidity of metal and stone, so much so that I told him: “See my motor here; watch me reverse it.” I cannot begin to describe my emotions. Pygmalion seeing his statue come to life could not have been more deeply moved.

Sometimes concepts are the result of thinking by analogy, applying some existing technology or concept to a new domain. The idea for the [Greenfield blood clot filter](https://www.inventionandtech.com/content/clot-stopper-0), for instance, was adapted from a similar filter used in oil wells, which itself was adapted from a filter to prevent people from siphoning gas out of cars:

> Greenfield took his dilemma to Garman Kimmell. Kimmell, a prolific inventor, ran a company that made valves and other machinery for oil and gas wells and pipes, but he also dabbled in medical devices. As Greenfield recalls, upon hearing about pulmonary embolism, Kimmell told him, “That sounds a lot like the problem we have in the oil field with sludge.”
> In oil pipelines, sludge and debris are trapped by a cone-shaped filter. The geometry of the cone, Kimmell explained, allows oil to continue flowing around its edges while concentrating the sludge in the center, whereas a flat screen, with sludge spread across it, could completely clog the pipeline. Kimmell and Greenfield decided that the conical-filter idea was worth a try in blood vessels.

Sometimes concepts are the immediate, obvious implication of some newly discovered phenomenon or material. When [William Perkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Perkin) accidentally created a mysterious purple chemical when trying to synthesize quinine, he immediately saw that it might be useful as a dye. Similarly, when learning about electromagnetic waves, [Guglielmo Marconi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guglielmo_Marconi) immediately saw that they might be used for communication. And the discovery of X-rays by [Roentgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6ntgen) immediately prompted people to use them for medical imaging.

A concept will often be sufficiently obvious that it will be “in the air,” and the would-be inventor will inherit it rather than come up with it themselves. The concept of the incandescent lamp is sufficiently obvious once you know that running electric current through a resistor will make it glow that it was well established decades before Edison worked on the problem. Likewise, the basic concept of a heavier-than-air flying machine was in place for [nearly a century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cayley) before the Wrights mounted their attempt.

Different concepts might pin down the combinations and arrangements of the elements of an invention to different degrees. Some might be rather abstract, and some might be quite specific, though they almost never pin it down so completely that no subsequent empirical searching is required. The transistor, for instance, started with what was barely a concept at all — merely the idea that some sort of solid-state phenomenon could be used to construct an electronic amplifier — and it took years of studying solid materials and how they behaved before the specific phenomena that made it possible were uncovered. The concept of the pendulum clock, by contrast — using the (nearly) constant-time swing of a pendulum as the oscillator in a clock — pinned the specifics of the invention much more tightly. Often a concept lies somewhere in the middle, providing a general idea of how an invention should work but leaving significant blank spaces in how it will be implemented. Edison, for instance, started his hunt for a practical electric lamp with the high-level concept of using electric current to heat a filament to the point of incandescence, but there were many specifics that needed to be worked out. Edison’s first implementation used a platinum filament (chosen for its resistance to oxidation) connected to a temperature regulator, specifically because he wanted to avoid dealing with vacuums. Only later did Edison modify this arrangement to eliminate the temperature regulator and use a carbon filament in a [high-vacuum bulb](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/the-surprisingly-long-life-of-the).

More generally, while having a starting technological concept doesn’t eliminate further technological search, it does considerably narrow it. Each phenomenon selected has specific triggering conditions: to get incandescence you need some way of heating your object; to get a population inversion you need the right sort of energy combined with the right sort of material. When Edison was creating his lamp he had a huge number of possibilities to sift through — different ways to prevent the filament from burning up, different materials that might be used as a filament, different bulb atmospheres — but it was massively reduced compared to a blind search through the entirety of technology space. Similarly, any existing technology that’s used as a component can be implemented in a variety of ways, but the range of possible variation is constrained by what’s needed to make that technology work. This kind of refinement is different than needing to make a discovery of a new phenomenon, wholesale. When Frank Whittle was working on his jet engine, he needed to build new, better compressors that were far more efficient than existing ones. But he wasn’t inventing a new type of compressor working on some novel principle: Whittle’s compressor worked more or less like existing compressors did and had a very similar arrangement of elements.

We can see the effects of this search space reduction using [a PTOP (Phenomena Triggered by Objects with Properties) model](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/technology-as-a-search-problem) — a model of technology inspired by Brian Arthur’s work, where different sorts of objects, with different sorts of properties, are placed in specific arrangements to trigger various phenomena, which then modify the objects in various ways. We’ll use the simple, linear PTOP model that we looked at previously. In this model, the goal is to create an object with the highest-level triggered property (P4), by placing the right objects with the right sizes in the right order. Even with this very simple implementation — 10 object types, 10 size values, and five objects that must be chosen correctly — there are 1 billion possible options. Guessing the entire technology at once randomly requires an expected 1 billion guesses, and even randomly guessing one step at a time still requires roughly 1,300 expected guesses.

But let’s say we have a technological concept guiding our search, telling us roughly how the technology we’re searching for will work. This hypothetical concept pins down the final phenomena exactly (we know the two object types and sizes that we need), but everything else is only narrowed a bit: we know the first and third objects’ types but not their sizes, and we know that objects 1 and 2 need to be equal in size. We can see that this basic concept provides a great deal of information, significantly reducing the expected number of trials required.

This level one search is so simple that it only barely resembles the search for a real technology (even very simple technologies in the modern age have more components and potential states), but we could conduct the same exercise with a larger and more complicated PTOP model and get the same results. A concept encodes knowledge about the world and how it works, and that knowledge narrows down the range of possibilities that must be considered when building a working technology. It may not fill in the blanks completely: the would-be inventor might have no initial idea how some step in his imagined process will work. Paul Lauterbur, for instance, had to make a “leap of faith” that there would be some way to recover the magnetic field strengths of individual coordinates to turn it into pictures. And Bell’s concept for the telephone was to use a varying electric current to carry voice along a wire, but he didn’t know how to produce that current and only stumbled across a method for doing so by accident. But a concept nevertheless makes the search process far easier, bringing it from “impossible” to “tractable.”

#### Concepts and information

Technological concepts are, obviously, a product of our knowledge: knowledge of existing phenomena (such as the particle physics Townes used to create the concept for the maser), knowledge of existing technological elements (such as the knowledge of compressors and turbines Whittle used when creating the jet engine), and so on. This knowledge might be virtually certain, such as Edison’s knowledge of carbon’s melting point, or it might be only probable, such as the bet that there was a second histamine receptor that could be blocked by an appropriate molecule for [ulcer treatment](https://www.acs.org/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/cimetidinetagamet.html).

The knowledge that a would-be inventor has available to him acts as a sort of “palette” that he can draw from when coming up with ideas, and different inventors with different stocks of knowledge might proceed down different paths; historian Reese Jenkins notes that “[a]ny creative technologist possesses a mental set of stock solutions from which he draws in addressing problems,” (gorman and carlson 1990). Thomas Edison, for instance, repeatedly used mechanisms that he was familiar with in his inventions: Edison’s first kinetoscope used the same sort of rotating cylinder he had used in his phonograph. Likewise, in the race to build the first laser, every team attempting to build one was working off the same high-level concept but implemented it in different ways depending on their existing information endowment: the glass experts at American Optical pursued a glass laser, the gas experts at Bell Labs pursued a gas laser, ruby expert Theodore Maiman pursued a ruby laser, and so on. The more knowledge a would-be inventor has, the more possible options they have available to them, and the greater the chance they can come up with a workable concept: in the 1931 book “Industrial Creativity,” which surveyed 710 inventors on the characteristics that make for a successful inventor, “knowledge and memory” was the third most frequent characteristic noted.

When [we looked](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/information-and-technological-evolution) at Brian Arthur’s technological evolution simulation, we noted that the key thing that made it possible to generate complex circuits randomly was *modularity* — combining simple elements into chunks, then making that chunk an element that could be directly manipulated and combined with other elements. Our knowledge of the world also has this basic structure: we can mentally manipulate things — concepts such as compressors, or motors, or resonant cavities — that are themselves arrangements of many individual elements, making it possible to orchestrate the arrangement of a large number of elements simultaneously.

Related to this ability to manipulate chunked information, some evidence suggests that strong mental visualization ability is an important characteristic for coming up with promising technological concepts. Inventors such as the Wright Brothers and Samuel Morse have been described as having exceptional mental visualization ability, and other notable inventors, such as Elmer Sperry, Oliver Evans, and Elihu Thomson, all described picturing a working invention in their minds before trying to build anything. Thomson stated that he “regard[ed] the imaginative faculty as chief in value to the inventor,” and that he never began a piece of work “in which I could not in my mind follow the whole thing through to an apparently satisfactory conclusion.” In “Industrial Creativity,” “imagination” was the second most frequently mentioned characteristic of successful inventors, losing out only to “perseverance.”

With mental visualization, together with the use of visual aids such as drawings, the inventor can to some extent “test” the workability of a concept, modifying it as necessary or discarding it for a new one without having to take the time and effort to build something in the real world. The Wright Brothers, for instance, initially considered a series of gears and shafts as a way to control their aircraft, but were able to foresee that its performance would be poor, and discarded it in favor of their famous wing-warping system without ever having built it. We can think of visualization as another way of processing a large number of elements at once. “A picture is worth a thousand words” is a saying for a reason: an image contains a huge number of relationships between different objects displayed that, thanks to our extensive neural machinery devoted to vision, we can process simultaneously and rapidly.

#### What makes a good technological concept?

We can think of a technological concept as a region in technology space that’s promising to search. A good concept is one that both has a high probability of containing a working technology and has what we might think of as an easily traversable “technological landscape” — ideally, we’d like a region that, from a given starting point (a first attempt to build a working invention), we can improve the performance of the technology rapidly in as few iterations as possible, and that allows us to reach a very high level of performance without getting trapped in local optima.

There’s probably much to be explored about what sort of technological concepts will have these sorts of characteristics, but we can venture a few guesses. One key characteristic is that we’d like our technological landscape to give us information on how we should traverse it. Specifically, if you think of “technology space” as compressed down to a 2D plane, with the third dimension, height, representing a technology’s performance, we’d like to know the *slope* of the landscape, so we can walk uphill: make adjustments that will yield higher and higher performance. This, of course, is how machine learning works: gradient descent via backpropagation calculates the slope of the loss landscape and then walks downhill by changing the model parameters to move in the direction of lowest loss.

This sort of technological landscape doesn’t necessarily exist automatically. In “Inventive Minds,” a book about the nature of technological creativity, Harvard professor David Perkins talks about the concept of technological “Klondike spaces”: spaces that give little to no information on the direction to proceed:

> Suppose you were searching for gold in the Alaskan Klondike at the end of the nineteenth century. The governing principle of your search would have to be, “Gold is where you find it.” You would look here, there, everywhere you could. You would be persistent, try different areas, and hope for the big strike. You would know a good deal about how to look, of course. You would know what kinds of rocks might bear ore. You would have a sharp eye out for the glint of gold in river gravel. You would search upstream from sites that showed some traces, in hopes of finding the mother lode. Despite this savvy, however, you would still find that most of your time was spent in searching rather than in systematically homing in on a find.
> Your search for gold is, of course, a special case of problem-solving. You are searching in the physical space of the Klondike, shifting from one position to another, exhausting dead ends, seeking new and promising terrain. Indeed, it’s useful to generalize the characteristics of this “Klondike Space,” because many other problem situations not so geological and geographical in nature have essentially the same logical topography. Many problem spaces, that is, involve punctuate targets with sharply defined boundaries (see Figure 13.1A), like a needle in a haystack or a few large nuggets or a hominid bone in a stratum. In such circumstances, it is difficult to move systematically toward a target. Rather, you find yourself casting about a lot. [My emphasis]

“Klondike spaces” are spaces where modifying a technology — making some part bigger or smaller, or faster or slower — doesn’t give obvious clues as to the direction of improvement. There are, broadly, two reasons this might occur. One is that a landscape might be highly *uncorrelated* — the performance of one technological option might have little relationship to adjacent options, so figuring out the local slope by making a small tweak and observing the change in performance doesn’t tell us much about which direction to head generally. When Edison was first hunting for a workable carbon filament, he found himself in this sort of landscape — he didn’t know which sort of carbon would work best, and just testing a material and seeing how long it lasted didn’t tell him much about the results he’d get from other materials, so he simply tested every type of carbon he had available to him until he found an option that was good enough.

The other reason that modifications might be uninformative is if the landscape is *flat*, and all nearby areas have the same performance. Consider, for instance, a string of Christmas lights where bulbs are connected in series, and every bulb needs to be working for the string to light up. If you plug the string in and it doesn’t turn on, you know that at least one bulb is burned out, but you don’t know which one, and testing one bulb doesn’t tell you anything about other bulbs or give hints as to which of them might be burned out.

An example of this sort of failure is Shockley’s first attempt to build a field-effect transistor in 1945; his theory of semiconductor behavior suggested a field-effect device should work, but extensive experiments with slightly different variations produced an effect “at least 1500 times smaller than predicted,” and he was forced to shelve the idea.

However, inventors are not simply at the mercy of these sorts of technological Klondike spaces; in practice it seems to be nearly always possible, with the proper knowledge, to determine a direction to proceed. This comes down to how we create concepts: a concept is based on some orchestration of phenomena whose behavior and triggering conditions are, to some extent, known; the individual workings of a technology can thus (in theory) be probed and experimented with to see whether the individual phenomena are behaving as expected, and give ideas as to the sort of modifications that are needed. Shockley’s failure to build a field-effect device suggested something was wrong with the existing theory of semiconductor behavior, which could then be tested and explored. Thanks in part to Shockley’s failure, it was eventually discovered that electrons trapped on the surface of a semiconductor (so-called “surface states”) were blocking the predicted field effect, a phenomenon that was then exploited to build the first point-contact transistor.

Similarly, Edison’s initial search for a carbon filament simply tested [every carbon material](https://edison.rutgers.edu/life-of-edison/biographical-essays/lighting/the-carbon-filament-lamp) that happened to be available, but careful examination of the materials tested suggested that materials that consisted of [many parallel fibers](https://patents.google.com/patent/US251540) performed the best — Edison later stated that paper was useless as a filament material because under a microscope it looked like “a bunch of sticks thrown together.” This initial search was followed then by a second, more thorough search that was focused specifically on fibrous carbon materials, leading to the bamboo filament.

This, I think, is one of the key things that technological concepts, and the knowledge that underlies them, do for the technological search process: they mean that the would-be inventor is never trapped in a Klondike space, and with the proper information and experiments can nearly always figure out a promising search direction.

We can similarly make some tentative conclusions about the sorts of technological concepts that might be improved upon rapidly, in as few iterations as possible. Something that has been demonstrated repeatedly is that the more modular the design of a technology is, the easier it is to improve rapidly. [McNerney et al. 2011](https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.1017298108), for instance, used simulations to show that technologies with a greater degree of connectivity between components — the more the performance of one element was a function of other elements — had shallower learning curves and a slower rate of improvement compared to technologies with less connectivity.

But the most thorough demonstration of this effect I’m aware of is Stuart Kauffman’s [NK model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NK_model), developed to model fitness landscapes in evolution. In the NK model there are two parameters: N, which is the number of genes in some genome, and K, which is how much each gene’s fitness contribution depends on other genes. When K is 0, every gene contributes to fitness independently; if genes can have either a “good version” with a value of 1 and a “bad version” with a value of 0, overall fitness is just the sum of every gene’s value. But if K is 1, then the fitness of each gene depends on the value of one other gene; if K is 2 it depends on two other genes, and so on.

Via Opus 5.5

Increasing K increases the ruggedness of the fitness landscape. When K is 0, the landscape is smooth, there’s a single peak of maximum fitness, and it’s easy for evolution to walk up the hill to reach it. When K is very high, the landscape becomes, according to Kauffman, like “the surface of the moon,” there are a huge number of local optima, and finding the peak becomes very slow. From “At Home in the Universe”:

> As the density of interconnections increases, changing a single gene (or bit in the program) will have effects that ripple throughout the system. It will be difficult indeed for it to smoothly evolve, with slight changes in the genome making correspondingly slight changes in fitness. So putting the effects together, as K increases, the heights of the peaks decrease, their numbers increase, and evolving over the landscape becomes more difficult.

We can demonstrate these same benefits of modularity with a PTOP model. The technology below is made up of 25 objects, arranged in five modules; each group of objects triggers its own series of phenomena, which modifies a different property in the final, output object. The goal of the technology is to maximize the product of all five output phenomena, which is achieved by dialing in the proper size for each object.

This implementation of the technology is highly modular; there’s little connectivity between the various objects/phenomena, and finding the maximum possible performance is relatively quick. This is the equivalent of a very low value of K in Kauffman’s NK model.

We can increase “K” by changing the nature of phenomena. In the model below, phenomena have a 40% chance to depend on the properties of multiple input objects, not just one, and these extra connections can be between any predecessor object, including ones in different modules. This makes it harder to find the best possible design, because hill-climbs now get stuck on local peaks. And the greater the degree of connectivity, the smaller the chance that the best design gets found. While in the unconnected version you could dial in each object’s size independently (smoothly climbing up the single peak), that doesn’t work when you start adding connections: you can’t simply dial in the optimum value at one spot and then move on to the next one.

So modularity doesn’t just make it easier to find working arrangements in technology space — it makes improving the performance of a technology far faster and easier.

#### What sort of algorithm should we use to find concepts?

Creating the concept is only the first milestone in the technological search process, and it’s my impression that it’s not a particularly binding step — if it was, I think we’d see a lot more inventions that could have been invented far earlier than we do. But it would nevertheless be useful if we could create technological concepts that reliably contained workable technologies capable of a high degree of performance. How might we go about this?

There have been various suggestions for these sorts of “invention algorithms.” One such algorithm has been suggested by Ed Boyden, neuroscientist and co-inventor of expansion microscopy and optogenetics. Boyden calls his method the “[tiling tree](https://conversationswithtyler.com/episodes/ed-boyden/)”: break the problem down into the elements that it needs to contain and think of every possible way of doing each of them:

> With optogenetics, my co-inventor Karl Deisseroth and I — when we were both students, we just started going through all the laws of physics. How would you control the brain? Well, there’s only so many kinds of energy. There’s mechanical force. There’s magnetism. There’s light. The list is pretty short, actually. You can actually try to write down every possible way of doing it. I call this method the tiling tree method, where you try to take this base of possibilities and break it down into parts.
> If you draw it properly, it looks like a tree diagram. Here’s this base of possibilities split into two parts, and each of those splits into more parts, and eventually it covers a page. It looks like a tree, and then the leaves of the tree — the bottom nodes — are ideas you could actually test by doing a literature search or doing an experiment. A lot of our projects, actually, at some point or another involve this kind of can-we-think-of-every-possible-idea approach.

Boyden points to Fritz Zwicky, a 20th-century astronomer, as the originator of this concept, who dubbed it “morphological analysis.” [Here,](https://www.swemorph.com/pdf/amg-4-1-2015.pdf) for instance, is a chart showing a partial morphological analysis of different sorts of telescopes you might build:

In Zwicky’s version, the result is a “morphological box” — a multidimensional box where each axis is one category of variation the technology could have. So in the example above, you could have “unmanned, balloon-mounted neutrino detectors,” or “moon-based gamma ray telescopes that send telemetrics back to earth.” The goal of this sort of algorithm is to systematically list the different possibilities, letting you come up with concepts that you otherwise might have missed.

But the most developed method I’m aware of for coming up with technological concepts is called “TRIZ.” TRIZ, which is an acronym for “Theory of Inventive Problem Solving” in Russian, was created by Soviet engineer Genrich Altshuller in the second half of the 20th century. In the 1940s, Altshuller was in the Soviet Army working as an “invention inspector” and was tasked with helping inventors prepare patent applications and solve various problems related to invention. Having no good method for helping inventors with their problems, Altshuller eventually created one.

I would classify TRIZ as a sort of industrial improvement system, like Lean or Six Sigma or scientific management, with all that the designation implies. Having spent a lot of time studying industrial improvement systems, I think that they’re almost always based around some core insight or insights that are correct and useful. But they tend to put too little emphasis on building the intellectual foundations around these insights, and the insight tends to get applied in a “when you have a hammer everything looks like a nail” sort of fashion; practitioners are quick to take the insight out of its original domain and try to apply it as broadly as possible. Literature on industrial improvement systems tends to have “salesman energy,” implying the ability to solve all your problems with one weird trick. It’s often targeted at managers or other nontechnical people (and thus written in a less-than-rigorous way), and is often extolled by a sort of cadre of consultant-types that collects around the system, selling books and courses and offering cringey-sounding certifications. (So just as you can be a [black belt](https://www.asq.org/cert/six-sigma-black-belt) in Six Sigma, you can earn the title of [TRIZ Master](https://aitriz.org/articles/802-master-s-certification/).) In my experience there’s often value in extracting the actual valuable information embedded within industrial improvement systems from the consultant slop that accretes around them — my book “[The Origins of Efficiency](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1953953522)” is in some ways one big exercise in doing this — and I suspect TRIZ is similar.

TRIZ is, essentially, based around the idea of technological search. Altshuller breaks new inventions down into five categories, based on how difficult the search process is for coming up with the idea for them. Level 1 inventions require simply small variations of an existing idea and can be discovered easily after a few trials. Level 2 inventions are slightly more complex and might require 10 to 100 different ideas before an engineer discovers a workable concept. At level 5, the most complex, the unaided inventor might require 10 to 100,000 trials, or perhaps might never discover a workable concept, because it requires a fundamentally new phenomenon that the inventor isn’t aware of. The greater the level of invention, the greater the knowledge needed to find a good concept.

The basic thesis of TRIZ is that by default people do not search for concepts very efficiently; they try different arrangements of elements based on their own experience or simply try and combine ideas by pure trial and error in the hopes they might work. This sort of search process might work for the simplest level 1 and level 2 inventions, but it’s inappropriate for the more transformative inventions of the higher levels. TRIZ is in large part devoted to getting people to think in new ways to come up with more promising concepts, sort of in the tradition of brainstorming or [Oblique Strategies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oblique_Strategies). Altshuller notes Zwicky’s morphological analysis as a way to generate new concepts that’s better than people’s default methods, but thinks it’s insufficient in part for combinatorial explosion reasons: the more axes of possibility you add, the more possible options you must consider, and the number of variants quickly gets enormous. An invention with merely mid-level difficulties, Altshuller notes, might have millions of possible variations to consider.

Instead of enumerating all possible concepts, TRIZ focuses on using tools to come up with better concepts. The heart of this is what’s known as a “technical contradiction.” Per Altshuller, the fundamental difficulty in coming up with a good technological concept is conflicting requirements: increasing performance along one axis might require raising some value, while increasing it along another axis might require lowering it. For an airplane, getting it into the air is aided by decreasing the weight, but making it strong enough to withstand the forces subjected to it is aided by increasing the weight. In Altshuller’s view, the creation of a new invention fundamentally requires some way of overcoming this contradiction, so you don’t have to sacrifice one measure of performance for another.

To overcome these technical contradictions, TRIZ provides several tools, chief of which is its list of 40 principles: a list of heuristics for how to rearrange the elements of a concept to eliminate the technical contradiction. Principles are things like “segmentation — divide an object into independent parts,” “prior counteraction — preload countertension to an object to compensate for excessive and undesirable stress,” and “asymmetry — replace symmetrical forms with asymmetrical forms.” These principles are, supposedly, based on analysis of tens of thousands of patents to determine what technical contradictions are encountered in practice and what methods can be used to overcome them. There’s an involved algorithm for applying these principles called ARIZ, but in essence a would-be inventor first imagines the most perfect, ideal version of an invention, a North Star to navigate by. He then determines the technical contradiction at work preventing him from achieving the ideal version of the invention and consults a “contradiction matrix,” which states which principles might be applied to resolve it. Properly applied, this results in the generation of a better concept that pushes an invention toward its ideal state.

I don’t necessarily think TRIZ holds the key to understanding the nature of invention; like with any industrial improvement system, I think it’s probably a mix of valuable ideas, exaggerated benefits, and consultant drivel. But I suspect there’s some promising work that could be done by analyzing the various elements of TRIZ — the ARIZ algorithm, the contradiction matrix, the list of principles, and so on — to try and understand more about the nature of technology space and how it might be searched effectively.

For instance, many TRIZ principles suggest pushing some particular parameter higher or lower: making air more reactive (principle 38) or less reactive (principle 39), changing the degree of feedback (principle 23), amplifying a harmful factor (principle 22), and so on. (In fact, principle 35 is just a bunch of parameters you might try changing.) This reminded me of a bit from Richard Hamming’s “[The Art of Doing Science and Engineering](https://stripe.press/book/the-art-of-doing-science-and-engineering),” where he notes that in high-dimensional spaces, almost all the mass of an object is concentrated near the surface, which suggests that for any given design of an object the optimal design will have some particular parameter pushed as far as it can go.

Similarly, one of the steps in one version of the ARIZ algorithm is applying the “size time cost” heuristic — imagining the invention with size, time, and cost pushed either toward zero (as small as possible, a process as fast as possible, or a cost as cheap as possible) or toward infinity, and imagining what the solution looks like under these modified constraints. This is a specific example of a more general idea, expressed in Judea Pearl’s [book on problem-solving heuristics](https://mat.uab.cat/~alseda/MasterOpt/Judea_Pearl-Heuristics_Intelligent_Search_Strategies_for_Computer_Problem_Solving.pdf), that search heuristics are often developed by thinking of ways to solve simplified versions of the problem (such as problems with various constraints eliminated or added).

#### Conclusion

The first milestone in creating some new technology is the creation of the technological concept: some basic idea of what arrangements of phenomena and objects will, together, create a working technology. This doesn’t eliminate the search problem — many of the most famous inventors, such as the Wright Brothers and Thomas Edison, faced most of their difficulties once the concept was in place. But the concept transforms what would be an impossibly difficult search problem into one that’s far more tractable.

articleBody:
Everyone asks themselves the same thing: what’s in it for me?

David Ogilvy spent his whole career answering that question. People call him the father of advertising, and for good reason. He wrote iconic campaigns for Rolls-Royce, Dove, and Hathaway shirts, and his book, Ogilvy on Advertising, is still in print forty years later.

Yet at 38, he was an unemployed college dropout.

He didn’t learn persuasion in a classroom or even a boardroom. He learned it on doorsteps in Scotland, selling stoves.

In this episode of Outliers, I break down seven timeless lessons from Ogilvy that you can use in your next email, sales pitch, presentation, or anytime you’re trying to convince someone. You’ll learn how to:

- Put a clear, unique benefit in your opening line
- Write to one person in plain English—without jargon or fluff
- Replace empty adjectives with specific facts that build trust
- Create curiosity that pulls people into your message
- Repeat what works and edit your drafts until they land

The true test of persuasion isn’t whether people admire your words. It’s what they do after reading them.

articleBody:
## Nari Ward builds a ship for a port

For the second Public Art [Abu Dhabi](https://www.designboom.com/tag/art-and-architecture-in-abu-dhabi/) Biennial, Jamaican-American[artist](https://www.designboom.com/tag/immersive-installations/) [Nari Ward](https://www.designboom.com/tag/nari-ward/)has created a giant, land-bound vessel, titled Ground Break Duty, that looks out onto the historical [Mina Zayed port](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-the-united-arab-emirates/), or MiZa for short. Measuring 30 × 30 meters and sitting atop an 18-square-meter copper platform, the skeleton of this purple barge, tipped at an angle, recalls the *‘dhow’*, or a traditional wooden sailing vessel that carries heavy goods around the Gulf and Indian Ocean. **Speaking with designboom, Nari Ward** shares his material choices, the significance of the form, and advice for emerging artists.

portrait of Nari Ward with Ground Break Duty in Abu Dhabi | all images by Lance Gerber, courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi unless stated otherwise

## Art and Fish in Mina Zayed

*‘I think for me the important part is a kind of acknowledgement of the importance of these structures, in the history of the country and in terms of the progress and growth of the country.’* says Ward, referring to the connection between his dhow created for the [biennnial](https://www.visitpaad.ae/en), the ships docked in the port just beyond the exhibition, and Mina Zayed’s historic wooden dhows, which fishermen still use today. ‘I think there’s also the sense that you’re looking at something that’s been poetically changed. It’s a boat, which references water, but it’s built out of rebar, which is about architecture, stability and the land. So, thinking about this kind of shift in expectation: how do you get somebody to think differently about their experiences and their relationship to history? For me, that’s an important part of the possibility of this project.’

Ward’s Ground Break Duty is a new commission for the event and one of eleven pieces in Mina Zayed area, with the Biennial itself consisting of twenty-two works in total. Covering four sites in Abu Dhabi – Souq Al Mina, Mina Zayed (MiZa), Hidd Al Saadiyat Promenade, and the park between Zayed National Museum and Louvre Abu Dhabi – the pieces each speak to this edition’s thematic title, Home: A Glossary for a Communal Sense of Place.

measuring 30 × 30 meters atop an 18-square-meter copper platform, the purple barge, tipped at an angle, recalls the ‘dhow’

a dhow i *s* a traditional wooden sailing vessel that carries heavy goods around the Gulf and Indian Ocean

## From the US to Abu Dhabi

Ward describes himself as *‘an artist who reacts to site conditions.’* Born in Jamaica, the artist moved to the United States at twelve and went on to study and practice in New York City. An exhibition at the onset of his career, Amazing Grace (1993), in a former firehouse in Harlem, featured a large-scale collage of strollers that he found in the surrounding city streets. In his subsequent works, he similarly creates sculptures and compositions from found objects to speak to the environment around him, African American history, and political movements in the US.

In Abu Dhabi, Ward applies a similar line of logic. *‘There are ideas within the work that I could never have thought of in my studio. I really needed to react to the space,’* he says of working in and with MiZa’s history as a port. ‘So that’s been exciting, that growth and discovery as an artist. And it’s also about being in a whole other culture than I’m normally accustomed to. For me as a person, that really nourishes me creatively, but also socially. So, I’m excited to engage with all of it.’

Ward describes himself as ‘an artist who reacts to site conditions’

born in Jamaica, the artist moved to the United States at twelve and went on to study and practice in New York City

he creates sculptures and compositions from found objects to speak to the environment around him

## Creating a modern-day dhow

Ground Break Duty, which is on view during the Biennial from November 15, 2026 to February 15, 2027, is constructed from rebar and fishing nets, which give the boat its deep purple color. *‘The boats are very important historically for the development of the country,’* says Ward, who was given this location near the water by the Biennial’s curatorial team. ‘The dhows were used to bring in commerce and goods, but they were also a use of the water for trade and for moving different materials, especially in the early history of the country. So, they’re kind of like the bones of the country for me, and I wanted to do something with that.’

Additionally, the choice of a patinated copper base plays into the title of the work. *‘That’s the “Groundbreak” part,’* he says before elaborating on his choice. ‘The title, for me, is a dual title. Then there’s the “Duty” part, which is more the dialogue with the boat. So, what I was thinking about is the idea of “groundbreak” as a new beginning, like breaking ground. But when you talk about electricity, grounding is also about safety. And “duty” is something that deals with responsibility, honor, and commitment, but it’s also about tax, something maybe not as sought after. So, I like the conflation of both of those things in the title.’

Ground Break Duty is on view during the Biennial from November 15, 2026 to February 15, 2027

the sculpture is constructed from rebar and fishing nets, which give the boat its deep purple color

## Ward’s advice for emerging artists

Over his decades-long career, Nari Ward has been able to expand his site-specific approach to places spanning the globe. When asked about the advice he’d pass along to emerging artists, he recommends that they *‘take risks.’* Although risks can be frightening, he cites this experience in Abu Dhabi as an example of putting this advice into practice: *‘being on site and being in a different culture is always about being open to this idea of risk, and seeing what things can evolve in your own creative adventure.’*

articleBody:
When people talk about India’s economy, they almost always compare it negatively with China’s, it has not industrialized as fast, its bureaucracy is still maddening, its cities are still choked with traffic and smog. All true. But if you step back one of the greatest stories of the twenty-first century is unfolding: India, like China before it, is on the move.

India reached a GDP per capita of $10,039 in 2025, (PPP constant 2021 international dollars), nearly five times its 1990 level. India now has the same GDP per capita China had in late 2009! India has lagged behind China but by only about 15 years, approximately the time difference between Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 economic opening and India’s 1991 dismantling of the License Raj–a blink in historical time.

Moreover, India is now growing faster than China. At 6% per-capita growth, living standards double every twelve years. Another decade and a half of this and India is a $20,000-per-capita middle-income country, looking more like today’s Brazil or Mexico than the India of Mother Theresa.

Indeed, India’s growth has already greatly reduced the worst forms of poverty, as China’s growth did previously. Extreme poverty in India fell from 47.5 percent in 1993—and 27.1 percent as recently as 2011—all the way down to [2.6 percent in 2023](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.DDAY?locations=IN)(using the World Bank’s extreme poverty line, $3.00 a day in 2021 PPP). Hundreds of millions of people climbed out of destitution in a single generation.

Visiting India, you can see the transformation in daily life. In 2000, four in ten Indians lacked electricity and nearly three-quarters practiced open defecation. By 2024, electricity reached 99.9 percent and open defecation had collapsed from 73.2 percent to 6.7 percent. Infant mortality has fallen 72 percent since 1990, from 84.4 to 23.3 deaths per 1,000 live births, while life expectancy has climbed nearly fourteen years to 72.2 (compared to 79 in the US).

India still has enormous work ahead—it needs [freer labor](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/india-has-more-restrictive-labor-law-than-germany.html) and [land markets](https://the1991project.com/writing/papers/reforming-land-laws-west-bengal), [cleaner air](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/magazine/pollution-in-india-harms-health-and-wealth-says-economist-alex-tabarrok), [faster courts](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2017/04/twisted-tale-rent-control-maximum-city.html) and [more state capacity](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2024/06/accelerating-indias-development-2.html). Of course. That is what being a rising middle-income country looks like; China in 2009 had plenty of problems too.

India’s rise is part of a larger trend: the end of the big-and-poor correlation. For most of modern history, rich countries were relatively small, and when you pictured extreme poverty, you pictured a nation with a lot of people. Many observers, notably Paul Ehrlich, mistook that correlation for causation and panicked about a “population bomb.” But big and poor wasn’t causal—it was a historical contingency that a handful of smaller nations adopted capitalism first. It didn’t have to be that way, and today we are returning to historical normality: a world where gaps in GDP per capita no longer overwhelm *capita*, and big countries are rich countries too.

Today, none of the world’s nine largest countries are classified as low-income by the World Bank. Only Ethiopia—tenth on the list—remains in the World Bank’s low-income tier, and even Ethiopia has more than tripled its income per person since 1990. Increasingly, poverty is concentrated in smaller, fragile, and conflict-ridden states.

The era of big and poor is over.

India has lagged behind China but by only about 15 years, approximately the time difference between Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 economic opening and India’s 1991 dismantling of the License…

title: We need to understand “health care costs” better
subtitle: A doctor speaks with her patient in the waiting room.
feedText: To just toss a hot take into the permitting reform discourse, one thing that I think we see in these debates is that there is way too much non-park federally owned land in the American West, and that creates some very confusing exchanges about activities happening on “public lands.” It’s good to have parks. articleBody:
To just toss a hot take into the permitting reform discourse, one thing that I think we see in these debates is that there is way too much non-park federally owned land in the American West, and that creates some very confusing exchanges about activities happening on “public lands.” It’s good to have parks. And obviously there’s lots of otherwise useful infrastructure that you wouldn’t want to put in a park. But if you look at the [federal land portfolio](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R42346.html?), it’s 12.5 percent run by the National Park Service and then 14 percent run by the Fish and Wildlife Service. A majority of the land, though, is run by either the U.S. Forest Service or else the Bureau of Land Management, and that land is *designed* for economic exploitation — logging, mining, ranching, and so forth — in a way that just somewhat arbitrarily excludes uses like housing development.

I think we should have more real parks and more real wildlife preservation and then more privately owned land that’s put to its highest and best use by market forces. A lot of what passes for “public land” preservation is in practice a kind of subsidy-masquerading-as-conservation to favored industries involved in natural resource extraction.

**Peter: I’m just retired from the tech industry, and need something to do after I finish Slow Boring in the morning. You’ve mentioned in the past that you thought there was not enough analytical work on policy related questions. There have also been examples of someone with a computer providing valuable data to the world, for example during Covid. So, what’s your list of topics that you wish someone would get to the bottom of?**

To pick just one example, because it’s a big topic and it’s been on my mind recently, the whole policy community has a very poor grasp of what exactly is going on with health care costs.

articleBody:
## New Exhibition Celebrates the Cultural Landscapes of Indigenous Peoples in Latin America

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/i-follow-rivers-denver-art-museum/)

Latin America’s contemporary borders reflect the region’s colonial history, marked by a shared past with colonizers. But these maps fail to represent the Indigenous peoples who call this region home, each with a distinct cultural landscape. *I Follow Rivers: Indigenous Worlds in Latin America*, a new exhibition at [Denver Art Museum,](https://www.denverartmuseum.org/) shines a light on these diverse and rich artistic traditions.

The show features over 100 works from more than 50 modern and contemporary Latin American artists. As such, the artworks on display range from early 20th-century pieces to art recently commissioned for this particular exhibition. This choice sends the message that Indigenous art in Latin America evolves and experiments like any other art scene. Above all, it seeks common threads while spotlighting the striking differences among regional neighbors.

The works that make up * I Follow Rivers* span several media, from the more traditional painting and sculpture to innovations in video, sound, and installation. The questions the creatives behind the artworks ask are even more varied, including the necessity of linking their practice to Indigenous identity; which customs should change and which should be safeguarded; and how they navigate resilience and history from a present-day perspective.

Among the artists featured in the exhibition are Claudia Alarcón, a Wichí artist from the Salta region of Argentina; Denilson Baniwa, a Baniwa visual artist from the Brazilian Amazon; Edgar Calel, Maya-Kaqchikel artist and poet based in Guatemala; Seba Calfuqueo, a Chilean-born Mapuche trans artist who works on installations and performance; and the late Martín Chambi, one of the first major Indigenous Latin American photographers.

“Working across a variety of media and engaging in dialogues that challenge conventional distinctions between modern and contemporary art, the artists gathered here reveal the complexity and diversity of Indigenous experiences and visual cultures,” says Raphael Fonseca, Curator-at-Large for Modern and Contemporary Latin American Art at the Denver Art Museum. “Like a river, these artists, their images and the very idea of belonging remain in constant transformation.”

*I Follow Rivers: Indigenous Worlds in Latin America* is on view through July 27, 2027, at the Denver Art Museum. To plan your visit and buy tickets, visit the [Denver Art Museum website](https://www.denverartmuseum.org/). To stay up to date with this art institution, follow the [Denver Art Museum on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/denverartmuseum/?hl=es).

title: Dresden - BSW-Parteitag lehnt scharfe Abgrenzung zur AfD ab - 30 Mitglieder erklären Austritt
subtitle: Der Bundesparteitag des BSW hat eine scharfe Abgrenzung zur AfD abgelehnt.
feedText: Eine Mehrheit der rund 600 Delegierten stimmte in Dresden gegen einen Antrag mehrerer BSW-Gründungsmitglieder. Diese hatten gefordert, mit der AfD in keiner Weise zusammenzuarbeiten.
articleBody:
# Dresden - BSW-Parteitag lehnt scharfe Abgrenzung zur AfD ab - 30 Mitglieder erklären Austritt

Die BSW-Vorsitzenden Amira Mohamed Ali und Fabio De Masi bei der Abstimmung auf dem Parteitag. (dpa / Katharina Kausche)Der Ko-Bundesvorsitzende De Masi und die Parteigründerin Wagenknecht hatten dagegen vor der Abstimmung für den sogenannten "Magdeburger Weg" geworben. Damit ist der Kurs des BSW in Sachsen-Anhalt gemeint, das in Sachfragen mit der AfD zusammenarbeitet, eine engere Kooperation aber ausschließt. De Masi sagte, wenn das BSW in inhaltliche Debatten kommen wolle, um die Unzufriedenheit im Land abzubauen, dann müsse man auch mit dieser Partei parlamentarische Absprachen führen.Nach dem Parteitagsvotum gaben 30 Mitglieder ihren Austritt bekannt. In einer gemeinsamen Erklärung hieß es, der Gründungskonsens des BSW habe darin bestanden, eine soziale und friedenspolitische Alternative auch gegen die AfD aufzubauen. Fast die Hälfte der Unterzeichner kommt aus dem Landesverband Nordrhein-Westfalen. Auch der sächsische Landtagsabgeordnete Rudolph, der BSW-Mitbegründer und bayerische Ko-Landesvorsitzende Ernst sowie der sächsische Landtagsabgeordnete Rudolph kündigten ihren Austritt an.Diese Nachricht wurde am 28.11.2026 im Programm Deutschlandfunk gesendet.

## Sallust's Theorem

- Download
- Prints
👇 Get new sketches each week

The surprising benefit of a common enemy

Sallust’s Theorem is that fear of an external enemy promotes internal social unity.

Perhaps more pertinent is the other side of Sallust’s Theorem: the absence or removal of an external enemy leads to internal moral decay and conflict.

Sallust, or more fully Gaius Sallustius Crispus, was a Roman historian and politician around the time of Julius Caesar. Remarkably, several of his works have remained intact to be read over 2000 years later.

Sallust describes unity in the face of common enemies and decline in their absence at several points in the history of Rome’s Republic. His strongest example is the fear of Carthage.

Here’s Sallust in his work The War with Jugurtha, chapter 41 (Latin terms included):

“…before the destruction of Carthage the people and senate of Rome together governed the republic peacefully and with moderation. There was no strife among the citizens either for glory or for power; fear of the enemy (metus hostilis) preserved the good morals of the state.

But when the minds of the people were relieved of that dread (formido), wantonness and arrogance naturally arose, vices which are fostered by prosperity. Thus the peace for which they had longed in time of adversity, after they had gained it proved to be more cruel and bitter than adversity itself.

For the nobles began to abuse their position (dignitas) and the people their liberty (libertas), and every man for himself robbed, pillaged and plundered. Thus the community was split into two parties, and between those the state (res publica) was torn to pieces.” (quoted from Neal Wood, see below)

Sallust sees Rome’s rise and decline as a psychological progression from liberty through glory and ambition to avarice (greed).

You may remember Carthage from the Colosseum scene in the film Gladiator, where Maximus is forced to represent the Carthaginians in Rome’s great victory at the “Battle of Carthage.” It doesn’t go to plan.

Tim Marshall introduced me to Sallust’s Theorem in his fascinating and relevant book Prisoners of Geography. He summarises Sallust’s idea in terms of alliances: “alliances are only strong with the fear of a common enemy.”

In some ways, Sallust’s Theorem is about the danger of getting what we want. We may resent a demanding boss, a fierce local rival, a struggle to build ourselves up from nothing, or a powerful business competitor, yet find that they gave us purpose and brought out the best in us as a group. We can miss them when they’re gone.

I believe the term Sallust’s Theorem was introduced by Neal Wood in Wood, N. (1995). Sallust’s Theorem: A Comment on “Fear” in Western Political Thought. History of Political Thought, 16(2), 174–189.

# Juso-Bundeskongress: Die Jungen verzweifeln an der SPD

- Startseite
- Politik
## Die Jungen verzweifeln an der SPD

Stand: 28.11.2026, 16:48 Uhr

Von: Christine Dankbar

Kommentare

Uns auf Google folgenDer Bundesvorsitzende der Jungsozialisten (Jusos), Philipp Türmer spricht beim Juso-Bundeskongress zu den Delegierten. © Bernd Thissen/dpa

Rund sechs Wochen vor dem SPD-Parteitag hat der Juso-Kongress vor allem atmosphärische Bedeutung. Das Führungsvakuum der Partei macht sich bemerkbar.

Bochum – Die SPD ist unter die Fünf-Prozent-Hürde gerutscht. Nicht bei den Landtagswahlen in diesem Jahr, da ist sie meist mit einem blauen Auge davongekommen. Es geht um die Kompetenz der Partei, die Anliegen junger Menschen zu vertreten. Laut einer Umfrage von Infratest dimap in diesen November vertrauen darauf gerade mal noch drei Prozent der 18- bis 34-Jährigen in Deutschland.

Viel mehr scheinen es an diesem Wochenende auch in Bochum nicht zu sein. Hier trifft sich der Bundeskongress der Jusos. In der SPD-Nachwuchsorganisation darf Mitglied werden, wer zwischen 14 und 35 Jahre alt ist. Doch über 30 scheint hier in der RuhrCongress-Halle kaum jemand zu sein. Der Vorsitzende Philipp Türmer, der im Januar 31 wird, scheint zu den Älteren hier zu gehören. Er merkt es selbst und macht am Mikrofon auf der Bühne auch einen Witz dazu.

### Die Jusos verzweifeln an ihrer Partei

Rund sechs Wochen vor dem Parteitag der SPD hat der Juso-Kongress vor allem atmosphärische Bedeutung. Nach dem Rücktritt von Bärbel Bas befindet sich die Partei in einem Zwischenstadium. Im Januar soll der gesamte Bundesvorstand neu gewählt werden. Wer antritt, ist noch immer weitgehend unklar. Klar ist allerdings, dass die Jusos an ihrer Partei verzweifeln. Und drei Tage lang mehr oder weniger an der sozialdemokratischen Realität vorbeidiskutieren. Doch dazu später.

Am Samstagnachmittag ist Hubertus Heil nach Bochum gekommen. Er ist bisher der Einzige, der seine Kandidatur für den Parteivorsitz angekündigt hat. Große Beifallsstürme hat er damit nicht ausgelöst, aber er scheint deutlich beliebter zu sein als der derzeitige Parteichef Lars Klingbeil. Jeder ist derzeit beliebter als Klingbeil, was einer der Gründe ist, warum sich der Finanzminister und Vizekanzler bisher noch nicht zu einer möglichen Kandidatur geäußert hat.

### Gespaltene Stimmung nach Heils Rede vor den Jusos

Auch Manuela Schwesig nicht, die am Nachmittag für eine Videobotschaft zugeschaltet ist. Sie ist wegen einer Operation nicht angereist. „Meine Galle muss raus und das dringend“, sagt sie lächelnd im Video und dankt den Jusos für ihr Engagement. Dann kommt Hubertus Heil an die Reihe. Für sein persönliches Erscheinen gibt es immerhin freundlichen Applaus. Wie viele Sympathien er sich für seine Kandidatur erwirbt, ist nach dem anderthalbstündigen Austausch schwer zu sagen. Heil kämpft wacker und er ist Profi genug, sich auch kritischen Fragen souverän zu stellen. Da hat er seinem Konkurrenten Klingbeil etwas voraus, der schon mal dünnhäutig auf Vorhaltungen reagiert.

Heil erläutert in seiner Rede, warum er sich entschlossen hat, anzutreten und er bringt darin gleich eine Kritik an der Parteiführung unter. Die sei nach der Wahl in Sachsen-Anhalt viel zu schnell zur Tagesordnung übergangen, weil man zufrieden gewesen sei, dass das Ergebnis für die SPD dort stabil geblieben ist. „Und das, obwohl sich zum ersten Mal seit 1945 die Rechten anschicken, in einem Bundesland die Macht zu übernehmen.“ Die SPD müsse wieder erkennbarer werden: „Es reicht nicht, Regierungspartei zu sein, wir müssen wieder stärker in der Gesellschaft verankert werden.“ Konkreter wird es an diesem Nachmittag nicht.

Die Stimmung im Saal hinterher ist gespalten. Ein Delegierter spricht am Mikrofon von nichtssagenden Antworten des Kandidaten und erntet Applaus von einem Teil der Zuhörenden. Da steht Hubertus Heil schon im Foyer und macht Fotos mit den Jugendlichen, die ihn darum bitten.

### Schweitzer verkörpert das aktuelle Dilemma der SPD

Das aktuelle Dilemma der SPD hatte am Vortag der neue Bundesarbeitsminister Alexander Schweitzer verkörpert. Er musste in Bochum seinen Rentengesetzentwurf verteidigen, mit dem er am Freitag die Union irritiert hatte. Auch beim Parteinachwuchs in Bochum gab es keinen Beifall dafür. Eine Delegierte sprach sogar von „neoliberaler Scheiße“. Im näheren Gespräch mit einzelnen Delegierten waren die Äußerungen differenzierter. Es ist nicht so, dass die Parteijugend die Zwänge der Spitzenpolitker:innen in Berlin nicht sieht.

Der Juso-Vorsitzende Philipp Tümer vermied es, konkret zu Schweitzers Vorstoß Stellung zu nehmen. Deutliche Worte hatte er dagegen für den abwesenden Lars Klingbeil. Dieser sei, „Stand jetzt“ der Parteivorsitzende der SPD, so Türmer. Klingbeils Grundsatzrede bei der Bertelsmann-Stiftung im März habe den Tenor gehabt, dass in Deutschland mehr gearbeitet werden müsse. „Was ist das denn für ein Narrativ?“, fragte Türmer. Das Land kranke nicht daran, dass seine Menschen nicht fleißig genug sind. „Das Problem ist, dass durch Arbeit nicht genug hängen bleibt. Das Problem ist, dass man nur durch Erben reich wird“, so Türmer. „Wir fangen doch nicht an, die Geschichten der CDU zu erzählen.“

### Kaum Streit bei den Jusos – man ist sich einig im Klassenkampf

Dass die Jusos absolut nicht einverstanden mit dem Mittekurs der Partei sind, zeigte auch der Leitantrag „Mut statt Mitte“. „Deutschland ist ein Ungleichland“, heißt es darin. Das Land befinde sich in einer „tiefen, demokratiegefährdenden Krise der Ungleichheit“. Das individuelle Aufstiegsversprechen sei für die meisten Menschen eine Farce, heißt es in dem Antrag weiter, „aber die Erzählungen vom Individualismus haben den Zusammenhalt innerhalb der Klasse nahezu zum Erliegen gebracht.“ Diese Fehler habe die Sozialdemokratie mitzuverantworten, obwohl sie es besser wissen müsste, so der Antrag weiter. Starke Worte, die auf dem Kongress unumstritten waren. Das fiel am meisten auf: Untereinander gestritten wurde kaum. Der Leitantrag ging glatt durch. Man ist sich einig im Klassenkampf.

Sehr viel pragmatischer zeigen sich die Jusos dagegen, wenn man einzeln mit ihnen spricht. Oder es zumindest versucht. Außer der Berliner Delegation gab es keinen Kommentar zu den gerade laufenden Koalitionsverhandlungen von Rot-Grün-Rot. Dabei müsste der Plan der Vergesellschaftung von Wohnungsbauunternehmen doch auf ungeteilte Zustimmung stoßen, oder? „Wir warten jetzt erst einmal ab, was dabei herauskommt“, sagte eine Delegierte vorsichtig. Wenn es darauf ankommt, macht auch schon mal Realpolitik.

**STUTTGART. „Vielfalt stärken – Zukunft gestalten“ lautete das Motto des Jahreskongresses Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026, zu dem am 26./27. November in der IHK Region Stuttgart rund 400 Ausbilder:innen, Schulleitungen und Lehrkräfte zusammenkamen.**

Dr. Christoph Franz, Dr. Benny Pock, Andrea Bosch, Dr. Jens Brandenburg und Andreas Deuschle beim Jahreskongress Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026. (Foto © Laurenz Bostedt für Klett MEX)

Mit **Andreas Deuschle, Staatssekretär im Ministerium für Kultus Baden-Württemberg**, wurde heute der Jahreskongress Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026 in Stuttgart eröffnet. Deuschle vertrat Kultusminister Andreas Jung, der in diesem Jahr erstmals die Schirmherrschaft des Kongresses übernommen hat. Jung bezeichnete die berufliche Bildung kürzlich in einem Interview als „Flaggschiff“, „Aushängeschild“ und eine Basis des wirtschaftlichen Erfolges seines Bundeslandes. Entsprechend wurde auf die duale Ausbildung im Koalitionsvertrag von BÜNDNIS 90/DIE GRÜNEN und CDU ein besonderer Schwerpunkt gesetzt. Im Begrüßungsgespräch mit der stellvertretenden Hauptgeschäftsführerin der IHK Region Stuttgart, Andrea Bosch, ging es darum, wie das Kultusministerium dieses Vorhaben gemeinsam mit dem Wirtschaftsministerium in Schulen und Betrieben mit Leben füllen will. Deuschle betonte dabei, dass es gelte, „gemeinsam Perspektiven zu schaffen“.

**Austausch über Zuständigkeiten hinweg**

Dass diese politische Zielsetzung nur gemeinsam gelingen kann, spiegelte das Teilnehmerfeld des jakobb 2026 wider: Als Plattform für die berufliche Bildung versammelt der Kongress einmal im Jahr alle Schlüsselakteure an einem Ort. Von der Berufsschullehrkraft bis zur Personalleitung mittelständischer und globaler Unternehmen nutzten die Entscheidungsträger den Austausch in Stuttgart, um Weichen für die Ausbildung von morgen zu stellen.

**Dr. Christoph Franz**, Vorsitzender des Berufsschullehrerverbands Baden-Württemberg (BLV), und Mitveranstalter des jakobb, zum Konzept: „ Wir erleben täglich, unter welchem Druck die berufliche Bildung steht: Fachkräftemangel, Transformation der Wirtschaft, Digitalisierung und KI, Integration und zunehmend heterogene Klassen. Diese Aufgaben kann niemand allein lösen. Der jakobb bringt Lehrkräfte, Schulleitungen, Wirtschaft, Verwaltung und Wissenschaft an einen Tisch. Genau diesen Austausch über Zuständigkeiten hinweg brauchen wir jetzt. Gleichzeitig zeigt der jakobb, was die beruflichen Schulen in Baden-Württemberg leisten. Sie sind kein Plan B, sondern ein Erfolgsmodell und das Rückgrat der Fachkräftesicherung im Land.“

Der jakobb bringt die Akteure der beruflichen Bildung miteinander ins Gespräch. (Foto © Laurenz Bostedt für Klett MEX)

**Raus aus dem Tagungsraum, rein in die Praxis**

title: The Pain in You and the God in You: Carl Jung on the Relationship Between Psychological Suffering and Creativity
subtitle: When AI first began colonizing language — which is still our best instrument for bridging the abyss between us, a container for thought and feeling…
feedText: It returned a ledger of cliches in rhymed couplets. Getting the form wrong — Whitman did not rhyme — seemed like an easy correction by a line of code.
