articleBody:
When AI first began colonizing language — which is still our best instrument for bridging the abyss between us, a container for thought and feeling that shapes the contents — I asked chatGPT to compose a poem about a solar eclipse in the style of Walt Whitman. It returned a ledger of cliches in rhymed couplets. Getting the form wrong — Whitman did not rhyme — seemed like an easy correction by a line of code. Getting poetry itself wrong was the interesting question, the question that gets at the heart of why we make poems (or paintings or novels or songs) — a question fundamentally about what it means to be human.

I asked an elder poet friend why she thought chatGPT rang hollow where Whitman could compact infinities of feeling in a single image, could unseat the soul in a word.

She paused, then said: “Because AI hasn’t suffered.”

On the one hand, this echoes [a dangerous myth](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/09/14/elizabeth-barrett-browning-art-suffering/): the archetype of the tortured genius handed down to us by the Romantics, who, cornered in their time and place, in a century of bloody revolutions, deadly epidemics, and punitive Puritanical norms, must have needed to believe that their suffering — those lives of poverty and privation, those ill-fated exercises in projection mistaken for love, all those premature deaths — was a fair price to pay for such creative volcanicity.

On the other hand, this is reality: Art is the music we make from the bewildered cry of being alive — sometimes a cry of exultant astonishment, but often a cry of devastation at the collision between our wishes and the will of the world. Every artist’s art is their coping mechanism for what they are living through — the longings, the heartbreaks, the triumphs, the wars within and without. It is these painful convolutions of the psyche — which used to be termed *neurosis* at the dawn of modern psychotherapy, and which we may simply call suffering — that reveal us to ourselves, and it is out of these revelations that we create anything capable of touching other lives, that contact we call art.

Our power and our freedom lie in learning to neither negate our suffering nor romanticize it but to harness its catalytic power as a current passing through us to jolt us alive, then passing on and down into the ground of being.

Carl Jung

No one has refuted the myth of the tortured genius without negating the fact and fertility of suffering more pointedly than [Carl Jung](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/carl-jung/) (July 26, 1875–June 6, 1961), who [thought deeply about the nature of creativity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/04/09/carl-jung-creativity/).

In 1943, a scholar of Kierkegaard asked Jung’s opinion of the relationship between “psychological problems” and creative genius. With an eye to Kierkegaard’s gift for [letting his anxiety fuel rather than hinder his creativity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/06/19/kierkegaard-on-anxiety-and-creativity/), Jung declares him a “whole” person and not “a jangling hither and dither of displeasing fragmentary souls,” and writes:

> True creative genius does not let itself be spoilt by analysis, but is freed from the impediments and distortions of a neurosis. Neurosis does not produce art. It is uncreative and inimical to life. It is failure and bungling. But the moderns mistake morbidity for creative birth — part of the general lunacy of our time.
> It is, of course, an unanswerable question what an artist would have created if he had not been neurotic. Nietzsche’s syphilitic infection undoubtedly exerted a strongly neuroticizing influence on his life. But one could imagine a sound Nietzsche possessed of creative power without hypertension — something like Goethe. He would have written much the same as he did, but less strident, less shrill — i.e., less German — more restrained, more responsible, more reasonable and reverent.

Art from [An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days](https://almanacofbirds.org), also available as a [stand-alone print](https://www.society6.com/a/products/bird-divinations-summer-red-bird-about-almanacofbirdsorg_print) and as [stationery cards](https://www.society6.com/a/products/bird-divinations-summer-red-bird-about-almanacofbirdsorg_cards?curator=brainpicker).

A century before Alain de Botton offered his [assuring perspective on the importance of breakdowns](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/13/alain-de-botton-normalcy-breakdown/), Jung weighs what makes suffering generative or degenerative:

> Neurosis is a justified doubt in oneself and continually poses the ultimate question of trust in [man](https://www.themarginalian.org/pronoun/) and in God. Doubt is creative if it is answered by deeds, and so is neurosis if it exonerates itself as having been a phase — a crisis which is pathological only when chronic. Neurosis is a protracted crisis degenerated into a habit, the daily catastrophe ready for use.

Jung considers the advice he would have given Kierkegaard about how to orient to his suffering, which was the raw material of his philosophical writings:

> It doesn’t matter what you say, but what it says in you. To it you must address your answers. God is straightaway with you and is the voice within you. You have to have it out with that voice.

Couple with a forgotten young poet’s [extraordinary letter to Emily Dickinson about how to bear your suffering](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/08/11/anne-reeve-aldrich-emily-dickinson/), then revisit Kierkegaard himself on [the value of despair](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/06/10/kierkegaard-despair/).

Art from [An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days](https://almanacofbirds.org), also available as a [stand-alone print](https://society6.com/product/bird-divinations-chestnut-sided-wood-warbler-about-almanacofbirdsorg_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [stationery cards](https://society6.com/product/bird-divinations-chestnut-sided-wood-warbler-about-almanacofbirdsorg_cards?curator=brainpicker).

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

title: How a Thanksgiving Crisis Inspired the Invention of Swanson’s TV Dinner (1953)
subtitle: “Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food…
feedText: “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. articleBody:
“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” [writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne](https://www.nytimes.com/1976/11/22/archives/westchester-weekly-what-taste-means-to-one-man-in-the-kitchen.html?eafs_enabled=false). “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a [letter of objection](https://www.nytimes.com/1977/01/12/archives/westchester-weekly-letters.html) from one Rosalie Levine of Lakewood, California.

“I live alone, I must control my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV dinner’s price “cannot possibly be bettered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready dinner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to prepare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up afterward.” While none of these advantages were accidental, the oft-told story of the concept’s emergence begins with a corporate crisis.

“In 1953, someone at Swanson colossally miscalculated the level of the American appetite for Thanksgiving turkey, leaving the company with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” [as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/tray-bon-96872641/). “Inspired by the trays of pre-prepared food served on airlines,” Swanson salesman Gerry Thomas set the machinery in motion to package the unwanted meat with gravy and sides like cornbread and sweet potatoes, ready for stocking in America’s frozen-food aisles.

The following year, Swanson sold ten million such “TV dinners,” a name attributed to both the shape of the boxes and the form of entertainment families tended to enjoy while eating the meals within. “In 1950, only 9 percent of U.S. households had television sets — but by 1955, the number had risen to more than 64 percent, and by 1960, to more than 87 percent,” writes Kovie Biakolo in [a more recent Smithsonian piece](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/brief-history-tv-dinner-180976039/). (Among the Smithsonian Institution’s holdings, incidentally, is [an original Swanson TV dinner tray](https://www.si.edu/object/swanson-tv-dinner-tray%3Anmah_741033).) Another breakthrough came with the introduction of microwave-safe trays, bringing total preparation time under ten minutes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Americans rekindled their love affair with frozen meals, “spending nearly 50 percent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”

Where holiday and commercial lore intersect, the details tend to get complicated. Swanson’s TV dinner did have its precedents: the core technology for quick-freezing packaged foods was invented over a century ago by entrepreneur Clarence Birdseye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remembers as “little cryogenic miracles”), and in the late 1940s, different companies planned or attempted to bring frozen meals to market under brands like Strato-Plates, FridgiDinners, and One-Eyed Eskimo. None of those names tapped into the technology transforming not just American mass culture, but also the American way of life. In the fifties, associations with television (and, indeed, with air travel) carried a kind of sophistication they certainly don’t have today. Perhaps Craig Claiborne would be pleased that Americans never quite accepted microwaved TV dinners as a substitute for the Thanksgiving meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is another matter entirely.

subtitle: French architecture studio PCA-Stream has completed Centre Pompidou Francilien in Massy, a storage and exhibition space fronted by a gridded timber…

articleBody:
French architecture studio PCA-Stream has completed Centre Pompidou Francilien in Massy, a storage and [exhibition](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/exhibitions) space fronted by a gridded timber deck and external [stair](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/staircases/) that echo the high-tech character of the iconic original [Centre Pompidou](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/centre-pompidou/) in Paris.

Officially named Centre Pompidou Francilien Fabrique de l'Art (Art Factory), the 30,000-square-metre building is the first Centre Pompidou annexe in Île-de-France. It is scheduled to open to the public in spring 2027.

### Photographs

Previous

Next

### Photographs

Close

Overlooking a small lake, the building will house over 150,000 pieces from the Centre Pompidou's reserve collections made visible to the public through temporary exhibition spaces, alongside private conservation and restoration areas.

It was built around a nine-metre cubic grid described by the studio as "a giant [Sol LeWitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_LeWitt)" artwork, which creates open, flexible spaces for both storage and exhibitions.

The grid is fronted by an open timber frame and traversed via an external staircase dubbed "the caterpillar", nodding to the glass-tube escalators at the original Pompidou Centre in Beaubourg, Paris.

"The brief posed a paradoxical question: how do you display what normally remains invisible?" [PCA-Stream](https://pca-stream.com/en/) founder Philippe Chiambretta told Dezeen.

"What truly constitutes the spirit of Beaubourg is not its image but its principle: large, flexible floor plates, made possible by great constructive rationality, which leave the institution free to reinvent its uses over time. That is the heritage we wanted to carry into Massy," he added.

"The caterpillar, by contrast, is a gesture in the literal sense: a wink, a homage. The great timber stair that climbs the facade quotes the escalator on the outside of the Paris building, like a label of the Beaubourg spirit."

Across the grid is a shifting gradient of openness, which moves from the more enclosed storage and restoration areas in the centre and eastern half of the building, where the facade is finished with curved metal louvres that control the entry of natural light.

The open timber stair on the western side of the centre connects a cafe and book store on the ground floor to the exhibitions level in the centre of the building and a rooftop terrace above.

"Beaubourg had pioneered the idea of a museum open to the city, with its piazza and its urban, accessible ambience. In Massy, we transposed this generosity of spirit into a different setting, no longer the dense urban fabric of Paris but a landscape of park, lake and trees," said Chiambretta.

"Visitors never enter the vault, but they experience the whole building as a sequence that leads them from the water up to the canopy," he added.

[Read: Diller Scofidio + Renfro transforms London hangar into V&A East Storehouse](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/05/28/diller-scofidio-renfro-va-east-storehouse/)

Behind the timber grid, the rest of the centre's exterior has been finished with precast concrete panels, while inside the exhibition spaces sit beneath ceilings covered in black steel rigging.

Several museums in Europe have recently explored combining storage and display, giving visitors varying degrees of access behind-the-scenes. In London, [Diller Scofidio + Renfro designed the V&A East Storehouse,](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/05/28/diller-scofidio-renfro-va-east-storehouse/) while in 2021, [MVRDV completed the Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen](https://www.dezeen.com/2021/11/08/depot-boijmans-van-beuningen-rotterdam-mvrdv/).

The [Centre Pompidou is currently closed for five years as part of a renovation project](https://www.dezeen.com/2024/06/21/centre-pompidou-2030-renovation-moreau-kusunoki-frida-escobedo/) being led by French studio Moreau Kusunoki Architectes and Mexican practice Frida Escobedo Studio.

articleBody:
The great Danish philosopher and religious writer Søren Kierkegaard was born at the beginning of the 19th century and died at age 42, suddenly, on the street one day. He was educated at the University of Copenhagen, where he later completed theological seminary to prepare for the Danish Lutheran priesthood, but—being perhaps too stubborn and uncertain of himself—he never ordained and never held a pulpit, though he remained a passionate Christian throughout his life and is considered one of the great Christian theologians. Kierkegaard was certainly an extreme and unusual person: a brilliant thinker and writer whose opinions were often as obscure as they were vehement. Internally fixated, he was equally a social person; he spent long hours each day roaming the streets of Copenhagen, stopping to chat with passersby about anything and everything, a practice he called “people-bathing.”

The central event of Kierkegaard’s life was his strange, brief engagement to Regine Olsen in 1840. Kierkegaard was apparently deeply in love with this attractive young woman, but as soon as they became engaged, he realized that an ordinary life of marriage and household would be impossible for him, and he would do her a great disservice by attempting it. So he broke off the engagement. Regine was devastated, and the more Kierkegaard demurred the more she wanted him. Eventually he attempted to dissuade her by pretending to be a terrible cad who was playing philosophically and experimentally with her affections (which he actually believed), but this did not work either. Eventually he had to move to Berlin to escape the emotional entanglement and the public ridicule all this brought on him. His profound reflections about this love affair—which for him involved the questions of what love actually is or isn’t, what a person is or isn’t, and what commitment, eternity, and religious faith are—never left off and may well have been the source of his creativity and the genesis of his ideas. He wrote about the affair in his work *Repetition*, which is a sort of novel about the complex and philosophical therapeutic relationship between a psychologist and a young man in love (whose circumstances are more or less identical to those of Kierkegaard).

During the decade that followed this event, Kierkegaard published an astonishing number of nearly unclassifiable works, many under pseudonyms—spanning philosophy, psychology, aesthetics, literary criticism, devotional works, fictions. No one seems to have a handle on exactly what his point of view was, because he was against systematic thinking (his works are full of passion and range all over the place) and because of the pseudonyms. Kierkegaard never straightforwardly stated his positions, so it’s unclear to what extent the pseudonymous works represent his own point of view and to what extent they espouse ideas he wanted to satirize. This is not surprising: He wrote his doctoral thesis on the use of irony in the Socratic dialogues, so irony—getting at meaning by not saying what you mean and possibly meaning many things at once, or not meaning what you mean or meaning what you do not mean—was central to his literary impulse.

To the extent his ideas can be characterized, we could say he emphasized the complexity of subjectivity, the awesome responsibility of every individual to their eternal inner nature, and the need for each person to become free of social norms and the tyranny of the crowd so as to find the true path for themselves. I have often thought of Kierkegaard as the ultimate Protestant—one who could accept no religious authority other than his own private and not-communicable relationship to himself and to God: an inherently terrifying and lonely path.

The titles of two of his greatest books tell the story: *Sickness unto Death*, and *Fear and Trembling*. Some call Kierkegaard a Christian existentialist, forerunner to 20th-century existentialist philosophers like Martin Heidegger and Jean-Paul Sartre.

Kierkegaard also wrote a book titled *Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing*. The title summarizes the book. The theme comes from Jesus’s well-known teaching from the Sermon on the Mount, “Blessed are the pure of heart for they shall see God,” and from a lesser-known passage in James that reads, “If someone lacks wisdom let him pray... but in faith, not like a double-minded man.”

Humans are meant to go beyond the temporal, to touch the eternal, to “see God,” and the only way they can do this is by singleness of mind and heart—by willing one thing and one thing only.

Kierkegaard, in his usual fulsome manner, writes that ordinary temporal life is inherently partial and fragmented. People follow ghosts within and without, and have no firmness or integrity, and whether they are conscious of this or not, they suffer because of it. Humans are meant to go beyond the temporal, to touch the eternal, to “see God,” and the only way they can do this is by singleness of mind and heart—by willing one thing and one thing only. The only way to will one thing is to will the Good, because willing anything else will always be “double-minded.” Any priority, any wish or desire other than spiritual single-mindedness will dim one’s inner light, so that willing one thing with a pure heart is in fact the only possible way for a human to live—although most people don’t see this, and so don’t live it, and their lives are therefore sadly deficient. Even the one who desires to will one thing will have trouble, because self-deception and blindness are so pervasive and so sneaky. In *Purity of Heart*, Kierkegaard details in intricate and sophisticated arguments the many ways we justify and cover our many-mindedness, including by writing books and preaching from the pulpit about willing one thing. Though Kierkegaard’s elaborate and often tortured subjectivity (his writing often seems to me to be the flailing about of arms in many directions, or, perhaps, the wringing of hands) and his Christian faith are of course completely different from Soto Zen founder [Dogen](https://tricycle.org/author/eiheidogenzenji/)’s mood and perspective, Dogen’s concept of continuous practice does seem very close to the idea that “purity of heart is willing one thing.” What’s daunting in both cases is the power of the conviction that human life must always be religious life, and that the only possible religious life is a completely committed one, in which everything is subsumed under the category of truth, purity, or goodness—continuous practice—with nothing whatsoever left out.

“Purity of heart” is also a Buddhist idea. One of the greatest Buddhist classics of all time, a 5th-century handbook of practice according to the Theravada tradition, is called *Visuddhimagga* ( *Path of Purification* ). While in Zen, purity means fullness of view, and defilement means limited view, in [Theravada Buddhism](https://tricycle.org/buddhism-theravada/) the concepts of purity and defilement are more conventional. I quote below a talk by the contemporary Western Theravadin master Thanissaro Bhikkhu titled “Purity of Heart.”

## Purity of Heart

During my first weeks with my teacher, Ajaan Fuang, I began to realize that he had psychic powers. He never made a show of them, but I gradually sensed that he could read my mind and anticipate future events. I became intrigued: What else did he know? How did he know it? He must have detected where my thoughts were going, for one evening he gently headed me off: “You know,” he said, “the whole aim of our practice is purity of heart. Everything else is just games.”

That one phrase—purity of heart—more than intrigued me. It reverberated deep down inside. Although I was extremely disillusioned with Christianity, I still valued Kierkegaard’s dictum: Purity of heart is to will one thing. I didn’t agree with Kierkegaard as to what that “one thing” was, but I did agree that purity of heart is the most important treasure of life. And here Ajaan Fuang was offering to teach me how to develop it. That’s one of the reasons why I stayed with him until he died.

His basic definition of purity of heart was simple enough: a happiness that will never harm anyone. But a happiness like that is hard to find, for ordinary happiness requires that we eat. As the first of the Novice’s Questions says: “What is one? All beings subsist on food.” This is how the Buddha introduced the topic of causality to young people: The primary causal relationship isn’t something gentle like light reflecting off mirrors, or jewels illuminating jewels. It’s feeding. Our bodies need physical food for their well-being. Our minds need the food of pleasant sensory contacts, intentions, and consciousness itself in order to function. If you ever want proof that [interconnectedness](https://tricycle.org/buddhism-dharma/#dependent-origination) isn’t always something to celebrate, just contemplate how the beings of the world feed on one another, physically and emotionally. Interbeing is inter-eating. As Ajaan Suwat, my second teacher, once said, “If there were a god who could arrange that by my eating I could make everyone in the world full, I’d bow down to that god.” But that’s not how eating works.

Ordinarily, even well-intentioned people may not see eating as harmful. We’re so compelled to eat that we blind ourselves to its larger impact. Our first pleasure, after the terror of being born, was getting to feed. We did it with our eyes closed, and most people keep their eyes closed to the impact of their feeding throughout life.

But when you go to a quiet, secluded place and start examining your life, you begin to see what an enormous issue it is just to keep the body and mind well fed. On the one hand, you see the suffering you create for others simply in your need to feed. On the other, you see something even more dismaying: the emotions that arise within you when you don’t feel that your body and mind are getting enough to eat. You realize that as long as your source of physical or mental food is unreliable, *you’re* unreliable, too. You see why even good people can reach a point where they’re capable of murder, deceit, adultery, or theft. Being born with a body means that we’re born with a huge bundle of needs that compels and can overwhelm our minds.

Fortunately, we human beings have the potential to civilize our eating habits by learning to wean ourselves from our passion for the junk food of sights, sounds, smells, etc., and look instead for good food within. When we learn to appreciate the joy that comes from generosity, honor, compassion, and trust, we see that it’s much more fulfilling than the pleasure that comes simply from grabbing what we can for ourselves. We realize that our happiness can’t be independent of the happiness of others. We can give one another our belongings, our time, our love, our selves, and see it not as a loss but as a mutual gain.

When we learn to appreciate the joy that comes from generosity, honor, compassion, and trust, we see that it’s much more fulfilling than the pleasure that comes simply from grabbing what we can for ourselves.

Unfortunately, these qualities of the heart are conditional, for they depend on a tender web of beliefs and feelings—belief in justice and the basic goodness of human nature, feelings of trust and affection. When that web breaks, as it so easily can, the heart can turn vicious. We see this in divorce, broken families, and society at large. When the security of our food source—the basis of our mental and material well-being—gets threatened, the finer qualities of the mind can vanish. People who believe in kindness can suddenly seek revenge. Those who espouse nonviolence can suddenly call for war. And those who rule by divisiveness—by making a mockery of compassion, prudence, and our common humanity—find a willing following for their law-of-the-jungle agenda.

This is why compassion based only on belief or feeling is not enough to guarantee our behavior—and why the practice of training the mind to reach an unconditioned happiness is not a selfish thing. If you value compassion and trust, it’s an imperative, for only an unconditioned happiness can guarantee the purity of your behavior. Independent of space and time, it’s beyond alteration. No one can threaten its food source, for it has no need to feed. When you’ve had even just a glimpse of this happiness, your belief in goodness becomes unshakable. That way other people can totally trust you, and you can genuinely trust yourself. You lack for nothing.

Purity of heart is to know this one thing.

♦

*From* [The Great Road](https://www.shambhala.com/the-great-road.html?srsltid=AU7gw4VGaQ8zSFlWq536-xpNrpNxeOhEwCAF-tvOG-4L9T06T8YAhbmT) *© 2026 by Norman Fischer. Reprinted in arrangement with Shambhala Publications, Inc. Boulder, CO.*

title: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth
subtitle: On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern.

articleBody:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate [rose 144% from 2007 to 2020](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls [increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10900-019-00678-x).

As the teenagers brainstormed, [Jasmin Brooks Stephens](https://psychology.berkeley.edu/people/jasmin-brooks-stephens), a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s [Jabali Youth Advocacy](https://www.hcnkids.org/jabali-youth-advocacy) organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

The ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she said. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”

## A pathway to hope in the face of racism

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, [suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt57150/2025-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf). Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she said.

It’s easy to talk about [structural racism](https://news.berkeley.edu/2025/08/14/watch-berkeley-scholar-explain-structural-racism/) as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the [Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together [worsened suicide risk for Black young adults](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2025-01327-001).

Brooks Stephens’s work is informed by both her research and her own experience of how race can shape young people’s sense of self. “I became aware very early on that Black children are often navigating expectations about who they are supposed to be before they have even had the opportunity to figure out who they are for themselves,” she said. “That has stayed with me—the importance of creating space for Black young people to define themselves, recognize their strengths, and imagine who they want to become.” At the same time, she saw how the stigma surrounding mental health could make it harder for Black youth and families to seek support, even as racism and other chronic stressors were impacting their well-being.

When she took an African American psychology class as an undergraduate at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, with Enrique Neblett, a renowned scholar of race and health who became her mentor, Brooks Stephens saw the connection between those experiences—and found her passion. “I realized that there was an entire field devoted to understanding how racism affects mental health and how Black children come to understand themselves and their racial identity,” she said.

Later, during her doctoral research at the University of Houston, Brooks Stephens worked with Rheeda Walker, an expert on suicide science and African American adult mental health research. Brooks Stephens noticed that there was very limited discussion about building upstream resilience in suicide prevention research—an approach that focuses on child well-being and happiness before the development of a mental health crisis.

“We’re studying why people choose to end their life without understanding what makes people want to live,” she said. For Brooks Stephens, that realization opened up a different way of thinking about suicide prevention, one that made room for the strengths that were often absent from traditional models, such as racial identity, spirituality, family connection, belonging, or hope.

## Focusing on strengths to prevent suicide

Brooks Stephens knows she can’t single-handedly eliminate the racial traumas faced by young Black people. Nor can she end other factors that lead to higher suicide rates in her community, such as systemic injustice or poverty. Instead, she’s focusing on where she can make a difference through her research.

“While I may not be able to eradicate racism, I can help build programs that change how Black young people see themselves and their futures—programs that help them feel grounded in their identity and able to imagine a life that feels worth living,” she said.

*Brooks Stephens and her colleagues identified six positive factors that reduce suicidality among Black youth (courtesy of Jasmin Brooks Stephens).*

As a first step, this year she and her colleagues created the [Black Youth Thriving Framework for Suicide Prevention](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2027-42684-001). It’s based on a literature review that identified six protective factors that can reduce suicidality among Black youth, including family support, community ties, and self-acceptance. “What we’re working to identify now are the strategies that can help cultivate those strengths in young people’s lives,” Brooks Stephens said.

Already, in a [study from 2023](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00957984211037440), she and her colleagues showed that Black young adults with stronger feelings of self-acceptance are less vulnerable to depression and suicide. Likewise, she has identified [mindfulness and meditation as potential tools](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12671-023-02180-x) for Black Americans in their early 20s to buffer the impulsivity that is often associated with suicide risk.

This approach is a radical departure from the status quo. Right now, resources for preventing suicide orbit around moments of crisis, Brooks Stephens said. When a child shows signs of depression or arrives at a hospital following a suicide attempt, that’s when an intervention is often provided. Brooks Stephens wants to develop research-backed ways to prevent a child from ever getting to that troubling point in the first place.

And, increasingly, she is asking Black young people themselves to help determine what those approaches should look like. Brooks Stephens said that the four teens with whom she worked this summer were not simply research participants; they were collaborators in imagining what suicide prevention could become.

“It’s very uplifting for me because I’m bringing underserved voices into our research and I’m designing solutions,” she said. “And those solutions are how we make kids want to live and love themselves. That’s it. It’s loving themselves, loving their life. That’s what I’m helping them discover.”

This article was originally published on [Berkeley News](https://news.berkeley.edu). Read the [original article](https://news.berkeley.edu/2026/10/07/as-the-suicide-rate-grows-among-black-youth-heres-where-a-berkeley-researcher-sees-reason-for-hope/).

title: Feeling at home in a new country makes you a stranger in the old
subtitle: A five-month stay in Berlin has become nearly nine years, my sense of self and home changed by a peculiar arithmetic - by Iuri Portalegre Read on Psyche
feedText:

title: Nicola Di Croce ~ Attuning To / Resonating with (Aomori)
subtitle: Birdsong and flowing water are familiar staples of field recording, and both feature in Nicola Di Croce’s Attuning To / Resonating With (Aomori).
feedText: But they are only part of a more complex sonic ecosystem encompassing fishing communities, nuclear facilities and wind farms. articleBody:
Birdsong and flowing water are familiar staples of field recording, and both feature in **Nicola Di Croce** ’s *Attuning To / Resonating With (Aomori)*. But they are only part of a more complex sonic ecosystem encompassing fishing communities, nuclear facilities and wind farms. Recorded in Japan’s Aomori Prefecture in June 2023, the album grew out of an installation presented at the Aomori Contemporary Art Center, exploring the relationship between energy production, landscape and the more-than-human world.

There is something reminiscent of Derek Jarman’s garden at Prospect Cottage in Dungeness, where flowers flourish on shingle beneath the looming presence of a nuclear power station. Nature and industry are not presented as opposing forces so much as uneasy neighbours, sharing an environment shaped by human intervention.

“Dialogue I” opens with a muted thump and low rumble, followed by a bell, birdsong and maritime sounds underpinned by a persistent hum. Industrial noises gradually assert themselves, rising and receding without ever entirely overwhelming their surroundings. Once noticed, however, these sounds become difficult to ignore. As Greg Hainge observes in *Noise Matters*, noise has a peculiar capacity to impose itself upon our attention. Di Croce neither celebrates nor suppresses it, instead allowing its textures to become part of the landscape’s acoustic identity.

“Dialogue II” follows a more pronounced narrative arc. It opens with bell chimes that mimic those of London’s Big Ben, a strangely familiar sound in this Japanese setting that introduces another, almost globalised dimension of disorientation. Barking dogs give way to maritime activity and crashing waves, before an increasingly unruly chorus of birds creates a strangely disorientating environment. Natural sounds become almost mechanical, while industrial noises occasionally seem to tune into the creatures around them. The accumulation of competing frequencies reaches an oppressive intensity before receding into the sound of the sea. A semblance of calm returns, although it proves temporary.

The distinction between natural and artificial sounds becomes increasingly difficult to maintain. Indeed, one of the album’s most intriguing qualities is the way it challenges our instinctive tendency to associate nature with tranquillity and industry with disturbance. Here, birdsong can be unsettling, while the steady vibrations of machinery acquire an unexpected familiarity.

In conversation, Di Croce explained that some workers at Aomori’s nuclear facilities regarded energy as essentially silent, despite the considerable noise generated by the equipment inside. Local residents, meanwhile, frequently associated the sound of energy with ocean waves, a constant presence intimately connected with their everyday lives. Such contrasting perceptions are central to his approach.

For Di Croce, listening is not simply a means of documenting an environment but a practice of *attunement*, requiring patience and a willingness to engage with unfamiliar or uncomfortable sounds. As he puts it, this does not necessarily imply agreement or acceptance, but offers an opportunity to understand other forms of existence.

Originally conceived as an installation that challenged visitors to adopt unfamiliar physical positions in order to listen, the two compositions retain something of that deliberate discomfort. They ask us to reconsider what deserves our attention, and why. Rather than offering an idealised portrait of rural Japan, *Attuning To / Resonating With (Aomori)* reveals a landscape of overlapping, sometimes conflicting voices, where the boundaries between noise, nature and human activity remain persistently unsettled.

To further attune myself I discuss the production process with **[Nicola Di Croce](https://nicoladicroce.cargo.site/)**.

**The recordings for Attuning To / Resonating With (Aomori) were made in a region where traditional activities such as fishing coexist with nuclear and wind energy infrastructure. What struck you most about the sonic relationships between these different environments during your time in Aomori? Were there particular sounds or encounters that challenged your expectations, or changed the way you approached the project?**

Over the past fifteen years I have developed many research projects, both artistic and academic, in marginalized rural areas of Southern Italy. Many of these areas share growing rates of depopulation, which contribute to an alarming contraction in essential services (schools and healthcare in particular). They are also often subject to speculative forms of energy extraction and management, in which the promise of local development and short-term profits for private actors obscures territorial impacts that a shrinking population struggles – and will increasingly struggle – to counter, while bearing the consequences (think of oil extraction in Basilicata and the impairment of the region’s aquifers).

The project developed in Aomori Prefecture (“Energies in the rural”, curated by Leandro Pisano and Yukiko Shikata) started from these considerations, building an imaginary bridge between Southern Italy and marginalized areas of Japan, and focusing on both the similarities and the profound differences between rural areas so far apart. Arriving in Aomori, I therefore tried to understand in what ways the territory I was investigating felt “familiar” compared with the mountainous, inland areas of southern Italy, and to what extent it instead offered different and unexpected scenarios. I soon realized that what struck me most concerned not only the sonic dimension but, more broadly, the cultural one. Unlike Italy, which used nuclear energy only between 1963 and 1990, Japan has had active nuclear power plants since 1966, and their presence in Aomori Prefecture is set to grow in the coming years.

In the interviews I conducted on site, I was struck above all by people’s degree of “commitment”: their acceptance of this type of energy production (especially as compared to the Italian context), their acceptance of risk and, more generally, the great trust they place in the central government’s decisions. It was also very interesting to find that interviewees who work inside these plants think of energy as a silent matter: a “non- sound”. Yet the silence outside the nuclear plants contrasts sharply with the soundscape inside them, where the sounds of the equipment create a very noisy working environment, which I had the chance to record during the residency.

Surprisingly, in the interviews the association between “sound” and “energy” did not refer only to wind turbines or nuclear production and management but, more abstractly, to the sound of ocean waves: a presence that every inhabitant of Aomori inevitably encounters in daily life, and that reveals a very deep relationship between people and the natural environment. The sound of waves exemplifies well what interviewees understand as the sound of energy in rural settings: not necessarily a powerful sound, but a weak, constant one, intimately tied to the force of nature – a sound that helps one to relax and concentrate.

**The project began as an installation with several listening points, inviting visitors to engage with different aspects of Aomori’s sonic environment. The album, however, presents the material as two extended compositions, “Dialogue I” and “Dialogue II”. How did you approach this transformation from a spatial experience into a linear one? And what role did editing and composition play in shaping the relationships between the original recordings?**

The installation comprises five distinct sound-diffusion elements placed in the exhibition space (the west wing of the semicircular gallery of the Aomori Contemporary Art Center). They were designed to disorient visitors, that is, to subvert the usual, often passive, way of settling into listening in a given space.

Two of the five devices are pairs of simple speakers playing the two most articulated compositions (“Dialogue I” and “Dialogue II”). One pair is placed under a table, so visitors have to crouch down to hear the composition: the audio is set at a relatively low volume and is barely perceptible when standing in front of the table. The other pair sits on two small plinths, between which a mat invites visitors to sit and listen to the second composition. In both cases, listening is mediated by a spatial arrangement that is “uncomfortable” for a human being, and it therefore seeks to establish a negotiation with the listener, starting from the bodily position needed to achieve the best listening conditions.

Two other devices follow a similar logic but attempt an even more ambitious relationship with visitors. Here, microphone stands arranged in a semicircle and fitted with classic ice-cream microphones seem to invite people to come closer and speak, evoking the typical image of a rally in which a speaker, surrounded by amplification devices, addresses a large audience. In the first device, the microphones are placed higher than the average standing reach of a visitor; to approach them, one has to climb two steps, at the top of which the ideal height is reached. In the second, the stands are again arranged in a semicircle but tilted downwards, inviting visitors to lower themselves and lean on a parallelepiped that can also serve as a seat. In both cases, once at the optimal height to address the microphones, it becomes clear that they are not set up to amplify the voice of the person in front of them, but to play back sounds. The microphones are in fact used as speakers, through an inversion of the electrical signal that also reverses their symbolic value. From each microphone one can listen, again at a very low volume, to some of the sounds recorded during the residency – sounds of the ocean or the rice fields, recordings of nuclear facilities or Buddhist temples, etc. – which were then used in the two compositions described above.

The last device completes the picture: a simple pole with a subwoofer mounted on top, a speaker suited to reproduce low frequencies that is usually placed on the floor, given how these frequencies propagate. Here too, an ad hoc composition (“Antenna”), made from the recordings containing the lowest frequencies (above all from nuclear research laboratories and wind power plants), exploits the potential of this particular playback system and subverts both the usual placement of a subwoofer and the expectation about where low frequencies come from and how they spread in space.

As for the compositions on the album, the editing of the two versions of “Dialogue I” and “Dialogue II” is minimal. Specifically, I integrated some elements of the subwoofer composition to make the frequency range of the two tracks more varied and complete.

**In your writing on sonic coexistence, you’ve argued that disturbing or uncomfortable sounds can open up new possibilities for understanding relationships between humans, other species and their environments. This seems to challenge the conventional idea of soundscape preservation as something primarily concerned with reducing noise or** **protecting pleasant acoustic environments. How do you negotiate this tension in your artistic practice? Can listening to sounds we might instinctively reject actually change our relationship with the places and communities that produce them?**

If we think about it, soundscape preservation often reflects a very anthropocentric approach. Its aim is to preserve an environment that we (humans) consider worthy of continuing to exist – when, again from a human standpoint, it has specific qualities and when, ultimately, we intend to keep extracting value from it, even if only the value our attention economy requires. In my view, it is not a matter of “preserving” a soundscape, and nature more broadly, but of granting it a voice, of giving it the possibility to self-determine. The only way an ecosystem can self-determine is for us to dispose ourselves differently to listening to it, both metaphorically and practically.

I am convinced that listening differently, welcoming sounds we initially find unhomely, disturbing, or annoying, can increase our opportunities to engage with “otherness”. I believe that the growing attention given to the more-than-human world, in order to perform a real political impact (think of legal innovations such as the attribution of environmental personhood to non-human entities and entire ecosystems, and more broadly the growing “Rights of Nature” movement), must be accompanied by direct engagement with the entities, ecosystems, non-human animals and materialities that characterize our contemporary world, in all its contradictions. I think of this engagement as an action that deep listening can facilitate: a listening that entails a change of (sensory and cultural) posture towards the sonic environment we live in or move through.

The term that, I believe, best sums up this action is attunement. Attunement is about an opening to something unfamiliar; it is a practice of patience. For example, attuning to the way a language is spoken by someone from another country takes time and attention. This process of exposure and adaptation – especially to what humans can find challenging or unsettling – does not necessarily imply agreement or acceptance. Instead, it offers an opportunity to get closer and to gain a deeper understanding, both intellectually and intuitively, of the standpoints and the rights of more-than-human bodies and ecosystems – and not least their legal rights.

**Your work moves between sound art, architectural research and urban planning. You’ve also investigated everything from the changing street cries of Palermo’s markets to the sonic consequences of urban policies in Montreal and Venice. How do these different practices inform one another? Do you see projects such as Attuning To / Resonating With (Aomori) primarily as opportunities to raise awareness and encourage different ways of listening, or do you believe sound-based artistic research can also contribute to concrete political and environmental change?**

In the project developed in Aomori, the research methods I have adopted in the initial research phase drew on a well-established repertoire in the social sciences (such as semi-structured interviews and participatory workshops), while the artistic approach I have later undertook – which falls within the framework of sound art – has acted as a complementary practice for exploring the rural contexts under study.

This combination of scientific research methods and artistic practice falls within what has been called, in recent years, research-creation. Research-creation is an interdisciplinary approach applied in fields such as the arts, design and media studies, which aims to integrate and promote the production of knowledge through the joint practice of creative exploration and scientific inquiry. Within this paradigm, artistic creation emerges as a mode of inquiry: creative projects are developed and carried out to inform and help develop new theoretical, conceptual or critical frameworks. The artwork itself becomes a form of research, in which new insights (including scientific and academic ones) are reached through the creative process. For example, an artwork may be shaped by the results of academic research, or may help present those results through different and potentially more accessible media (such as visual or sonic ones). Likewise, a creative process can generate valuable results for scientists: a participatory art project could be of great interest to a social scientist studying community interactions within a group of users of a public space. The insights produced by the creative process can then be further analyzed with scientific methods and, finally, translated into an academic format. This approach mobilizes the potential of artistic practice to generate forms of knowledge that conventional academic methodologies do not always capture, especially in the social sciences and in urban and regional planning.

I believe that adopting a research-creation approach is itself an important cultural, aesthetic and political shift. Following this approach, *Attuning To / Resonating With (Aomori)* is the first chapter of an ongoing series of projects and works under the umbrella title *Attuning To / Resonating With*. These are site-specific works that I am developing through residencies and workshops, each time involving a group of participants in identifying “problematic” sound sources: sources that often receive little attention and pass unheard, yet testify to the “social” and “political” role of energy and production facilities, from the micro scale of the building to the territorial macro scale of water treatment plants and military production sites. Once attuned to these sources, the groups are asked to create choirs that imitate them with their own voices, following a score in which each source joins the choir to the extent that its members are able to welcome that “voice” among the others. These performative moments, the result of group work, are recorded and filmed, with the idea of collecting a series of them to be organized into an installation. But I’m still working on that.

( **Gianmarco Del Re** )

## Carl Stumpf

The name Carl Friedrich Stumpf (1848–1936) is historically associated with one of the most important philosophical trends in the early twentieth century, phenomenology. Stumpf supervised Husserl’s habilitation thesis in Halle in 1887 and the latter’s seminal work on phenomenology, Logical Investigations (1900–1901), is dedicated to him in recognition of his friendship and his philosophical contribution to this book. Stumpf is also known as the founder of the Berlin Institute of Psychology, which gave rise to Gestalt psychology, another important current during the early twentieth century and whose main adherents were among others, his students W. Köhler, K. Koffka, W. Wertheimer and K. Lewin. Founder of the Phonogram Archive in Berlin, now under the protection of the UNESCO, he is also considered one of the forefathers of comparative musicology and a pioneer in ethnomusicology. He held positions in the philosophy departments at the universities of Göttingen, Würzburg, Prague, Munich and Halle, before obtaining a professorship at the University of Berlin, where he was also rector in 1907–1908. His two main sources of inspiration in philosophy are Franz Brentano, of whom he was the first student in Würzburg, and Hermann Lotze, who supervised his 1869 doctoral thesis on Plato and his habilitation thesis on mathematical axioms (1870). The philosophical work he left us is as original and as diversified as his academic and institutional achievements. Besides many treatises in the fields of acoustics and musicology, his important contributions to the development of the “new psychology” and to the philosophy of the mind in general should also be noted. His friend William James said of him in his Principles of Psychology (1890: vol. II 282 [ch. XX]) that he was “the most philosophical and profound of all writers; and I owe him much”. His studies in the field of descriptive psychology and phenomenology (known as the science of phenomena) for example, are of particular interest to current research in the fields of philosophy of mind and cognitive sciences.

## 1. Biographical Sketch

Stumpf’s intellectual biography is rich and complex due to his long university career that lasted for more than 50 years, his academic achievements, and his philosophical work. To complete this biographical sketch, the reader is invited to consult Stumpf’s autobiography (published in 1924) and the Sprungs’ biography, published in German under the title Carl Stumpf – Eine Biografie (H. Sprung with L. Sprung 2006).

- 1848 Carl Friedrich Stumpf was born on April 21, 1848 in Wiesentheid in Franconia, Germany.
- 1859–1863 Attended the Gymnasium in Bamberg, studied music and composed several pieces.
- 1864–1865 Attended the Gymnasium in Aschaffenburg where he studied Plato with Hocheder.
- 1865 Entered the University of Würzburg and during his first year studied aesthetics and law
- 1866 Met Franz Brentano on July 14, 1866 during the disputatio of his habilitation and then decided to study philosophy with Brentano. From 1867 to 1870 he attended Brentano’s lectures on the history of philosophy, metaphysics, Comte and positivism and logic.
- 1867–1868 Because Brentano had not been habilitated to supervise dissertations, it was recommended that Stumpf study with Hermann Lotze in Göttingen. He attended Lotze’s lectures on psychology, history of philosophy since Kant, philosophy of nature, and practical philosophy. He also attended lectures from the physiologist G. Meissner and the physician W. Weber.
- 1868 Graduated on August 13, 1868 with a dissertation on Plato and then returned to Würzburg to study with Brentano.
- 1869–1870 Entered the ecclesiastical seminary in Würzburg and resigned in July 1870 due to the influence of Brentano and Lotze.
- 1870 Returned to Göttingen to prepare his habilitation on mathematical axioms under the supervision of Lotze and successfully defended it in October 1870.
- 1870–1873 Lectured at the University of Göttingen where he founded the Eskimo society along with his friend Felix Klein. He also met G. Fechner and probably G. Frege, who studied in Göttingen during this period.
- 1873 Published an important treatise on the origin of space perception ( Über den psychologischen Ursprung der Raumvorstellung) , and dedicated it to Lotze.
- 1873–1879 Was appointed to his first professorship at the University of Würzburg at the age of 25 to replace Brentano, who moved to Vienna in 1874.
- 1878 Married Hermine Biedermann (1849–1930).
- 1879–1884 Moved to Prague and was joined there by his friend Anton Marty in 1880. He developed professional contacts with Mach and maintained a close relationship with Ewald Hering.
- 1882 Was visited by William James in Prague and this encounter led to the beginning of a lasting friendship between both philosophers.
- 1883 Published the first volume of Tonpsychologie .
- 1884–1889 Replaced H. Ulrici at the University of Halle and became a colleague of Georg Cantor and J. E. Erdmann.
- 1887 Husserl submitted his habilitation thesis on the origin of the concept of number under Stumpf’s supervision.
- 1889–1894 Arrived in Munich in 1889 as the successor to K. Prantl.
- 1890 Published the second volume of Tonpsychologie. He also worked with H. Ebbinghaus, H. von Helmholtz, and G. E. Müller, among others, on the prestigious journal Zeitschrift für Psychologie und Physiologie der Sinnesorgane , of which Stumpf was one of the founding editors.
- 1891 Involved in a controversy with W. Wundt and his students on the use of experiments and on Fechner’s law.
- 1894 Joined the philosophy faculty in Berlin after a long period of hesitation; marked the beginning of a new period in his intellectual life.
- 1896 Presided along with T. Lipps the third International Congress of Psychology in Munich.
- 1898 Joined the Academy of sciences in Berlin. Founded the journal Beiträge zur Akustik und Musikwissenschaft , which contains many treatises written by Stumpf and his students.
- 1900 Founded the Institute of Psychology in Berlin, which gave rise to Gestalt Psychology; started the Phonogramm-Archiv in Berlin on the basis of some phonographic recordings of a Siamese company performing in Berlin; in the same year along with F. Kemsies he started the Berlin Gesellschaft für Kinderpsychologie .
- 1900–1901 Husserl’s groundwork Logical Investigations was published and dedicated to Stumpf.
- 1904 Asked by the Board of Education to investigate the well-known case of “clever Hans” and in 1907 the results of this investigation were published by Stumpf and his assistant O. Pfungst in the book Clever Hans (The Horse of Mr. von Osten): A Contribution to Experimental Animal and Human Psychology .
- 1906–1907 Published three important treatises, which were extensively discussed by philosophers and psychologists: “Erscheinungen und psychische Funktionen” (1906b), “Zur Einteilung der Wissenschaften” (1906a) and “Über Gefühlsempfindungen” (1906c).
- 1907–1909 Accepted the honorific position of rector of the University of Berlin; pronounced his first address “Die Wiedergeburt der Philosophie” [“Renaissance of Philosophy”] (1907) on the state of philosophy in Germany since Lotze.
- 1908 Robert Musil, the author of The Man without Qualities , wrote a dissertation on Mach under the supervision of Stumpf.
- 1909 Wolfgang Köhler received his PhD with a dissertation under the supervision of Stumpf, which was published under the title “Akustische Untersuchungen I”. Trip to Cambridge to celebrate the 100 th anniversary of the birth of Charles Darwin.
- 1911 Published Die Anfänge der Musik in which he summarized the results of his research on ethnomusicology.
- 1912–1913 Established a station for anthropoids in Tenerife by the Academy of Sciences; as a member of the Academy, Stumpf recommended his student W. Köhler as director of this station. Köhler began his investigations in 1913 and published the results in his classic book Intelligenzprüfungen an Anthropoiden [The Mentality of Apes] (1917 [1925]).
- 1921 Was appointed professor emeritus in Berlin and continued to teach philosophy in Berlin until the summer 1923.
- 1922 W. Köhler succeeded Stumpf as director of the Institute of Psychology in Berlin.
- 1922–1923 With his assistant E. M. von Hornbostel, Stumpf edited four volumes of the classical Sammelbände für vergleichende Musikwissenschaft. The fourth volume contains a study on popular music in Romania by the well-known composer Béla Bartók.
- 1923 Festschrift in honor of Stumpf’s 75th anniversary in the Gestaltist journal Psychologische Forschung ; this volume includes contributions by his students A. Gelb, G. J. von Allesch, W. Köhler, K. Koffka, M. Wertheimer, and K. Lewin, among others.
- 1926 Published the results of extensive research on the nature of vowels and the sounds of speech in Die Sprachlaute; experimentell-phonetische Untersuchungen .
- 1927/1928 Published a short biography on his friend W. James, based on their correspondence: William James nach seinen Briefen .
- 1928 Published Gefühl und Gefühlsempfindung , an important collection of papers on emotions and feelings.
- 1928 Celebrated his 80 th anniversary for which an allocution was given by his friend and colleague Max Planck.
- 1936 Carl Stumpf died on December 25 in Berlin at the age of 88.
- 1939–1940 With the recommendation of Max Planck, his son Felix Stumpf published the two volumes of his monumental work Erkenntnislehre .
## 2. Historical Background

The two most important names associated with the young Stumpf’s philosophical formation are those of Franz Brentano and Hermann Lotze. His debt to Brentano is well documented in his autobiography and in the three biographies, which Stumpf (1918, 1919a, 1922) devoted to him after his death in 1917. But opinions diverged regarding Stumpf’s later position to Brentano’s philosophical program. Some claim that Stumpf is a truly orthodox Brentanian (Schuhmann 1996) while others argue that Stumpf gradually distanced himself from Brentano’s thinking and moved closer to that of Lotze (Ewen 2008, Milkov 2015). The truth must lie somewhere in the middle if we are to judge the matter in light of Stumpf’s many testimonies in his biographical articles and in his substantial correspondence with Brentano where he unequivocally acknowledges his debt to Brentano.

Stumpf’s debt to Lotze’s philosophy is certainly significant but it is not very well documented. Most studies on the relationship between Stumpf and Lotze emphasize Lotze’s theory of local signs (see Woodward 1978; Fisette 2006, 2012; Centi 2011) and the problem of the origins of space perception, which is in fact the central theme of Stumpf’s Raumbuch (1873; Kaiser-El-Safti 1994; Pradelle 2015). In this book, dedicated to Lotze, Stumpf offers a summary of the debates between philosophers, scientists, and psychologists on the origins of space perception since Fechner. In the preface to this book, Stumpf explains that his starting point is the controversy between nativism and empiricism triggered by Helmholtz in his Handbuch (Helmholtz 1910: vol. 3, § 25) while his inspiration lies in Lotze Medizinischer Psychologie (1852). Lotze’s influence on the young Stumpf’s thought is not limited to his doctrine of local signs as Stumpf repeatedly emphasized (Rollinger 2008c; Milkov 2015; Fisette 2009b). Beyond the question of influence, Stumpf assigns a central role to Lotze’s thought in the history of philosophy and associates him with a renaissance of philosophy in the mid-nineteenth century (Stumpf 1907).

From his two mentors Brentano and Lotze, Stumpf inherited a marked interest in the history of philosophy. This interest was not strictly historiographical: his point of departure was Brentano’s theory of the four phases in the history of philosophy, and he worked out his own philosophy of history, which constitutes the basis of his diagnosis on the state of philosophy in the nineteenth century, which is inseparable from the way he conceived of philosophy. In his first address as the rector of the university of Berlin delivered in 1907 under the title “Renaissance of Philosophy”, exactly a hundred years after Fichte’s “Address to the German Nation” at the same university, Stumpf applied this philosophy of history to the nineteenth century and asked whether philosophy at this time belonged to an ascending stage of history and whether it tended towards a renaissance of philosophy. He identified two factors which marked the development of philosophy during this period: the empty space left by the decline of speculative philosophy of German idealism during the first half of the nineteenth century, and the remarkable development of psychology and of the physiology of senses during the second half of this century, due to the works of physiologists and physicists such as Fechner, Weber, Hering, and Helmholtz. These two factors corresponded to two divergent philosophical orientations at the time when Stumpf was undertaking his studies in philosophy. The first was the Kantian tradition in its different ramifications, including Neo-Kantianism; the second corresponds to what he called Erfahrungsphilosophie or philosophy of experience, which began with Fechner and above all with Lotze’s works on psychology and more particularly on the problem of space perception. Although it does not represent a homogeneous tradition, the philosophy of experience refers to common features of several schools and currents of thought which attempted to bring philosophy closer to natural sciences, and more particularly to the “new psychology”, which was neglected and relegated to the background by the other tradition. Corresponding to these two orientations are two different ways of doing philosophy: the philosophy of experience starts from below, and like any empirical science, uses the inductive method. They differ from an a priori and speculative approach to philosophy which favors an autocratic regime entirely disconnected from the empirical.

As B. Russell pointed out in his Essay on the Foundations of Geometry (1897), Stumpf’s main criticism against Kant and a priori philosophy concerns the dichotomy between form and matter, more precisely the postulate of a priori forms of thought and sensibility. This criticism was already clearly formulated in his Raumbuch , where he examined the nativism-empiricism controversy on space perception, prepared some years earlier by Helmholtz in the third book of his Handbuch . This controversy is at the origin of an important division in the middle of the nineteenth century within the new psychology proponents, between empiricism advocated mainly by Helmholtz and Wundt; and nativism which, according to Helmholtz, characterizes the works of Ewald Hering in physiology, the latter of which in fact exercised an influence on the Brentano school and to a certain extent on Gestalt psychology. Instead of using Helmholtz’s terminology, as did most historians, Stumpf preferred the term phenomenology to designate the study of phenomenal experience, which occupied center stage in the field of physiology and psychology. In his Raumbuch Stumpf takes a stand in favor of a moderate form of nativism, according to which space is a unitary sense, its content is perceptible in an immediate and direct way, and it is inseparable from sensory qualities such as color and sound. Consequently, space and color constitute one and the same content, of which they are partial contents or attributes. They are in a relation of logical dependence with the phenomena of which they form a part. Hence, extension and color form a concrete whole which can only be separated through abstraction. From this point of view, the concept of space, as any concept, draws upon its origin in sense perception and is, to use the Scholastic expression, an abstracta cum fundamento in re .

## 3. Philosophy of Mind

Philosophy of mind or what is called descriptive psychology represents one of the main axes of Stumpf’s program in philosophy. His treatises in this domain are quite diversified, ranging from animal and developmental psychology to acoustic psychology and Gestalt psychology. Other than his Raumbuch , the book that made Stumpf renowned in psychology is Tonpsychologie [Tone Psychology] (published in two volumes in 1883, 1890) which was widely received in Germany and England (see reviews by Natorp [1886, 1891], Meinong [1885, 1890], and Sully [1884, 1891]). In this book, as in most of his treatises on psychology, Stumpf’s approach is similar to that of Brentano’s descriptive psychology. It differs from experimental and physiological psychology in that it conceptually analyses and describes what physiological psychology explains through the descriptive apparatus of the natural sciences such as biology or physiology. Between these two branches of psychology there is a form of division of labor wherein the first analyses and describes what the other explains. However, descriptive psychology has a methodological priority over experimental psychology in that the analysis and description of the explanandum is a prerequisite to its explanation. The two main tasks assigned to descriptive psychology are the analysis and the classification of mental states (also called acts or mental functions). In his influential study entitled “Erscheinungen und psychische Funktionen” [“Phenomena and Mental Functions”] (1906b), Stumpf shows how phenomena are closely linked in that they form a real unity, which can only be separated by abstraction. He conceives of phenomena as unitary wholes and not as aggregates, and claims that they are perceived as concrete and unitary wholes. As such, phenomena are the contents of sensations that are characterized by certain properties or attributes, for example extension, intensity, brightness, etc., and these contents of sensations are first-order phenomena as opposed to second-order phenomena like “mnemonic images” and phenomena such as color or sound, to the extent that they “are merely represented”. Although Stumpf rarely uses the concept of intentionality, one might say that mental functions are distinct from physical phenomena in that they are related to their objects by intentional relations.

Psychical functions have a specific structure that is characterized by the distinction between the content of a function and its relation to an object. This relationship is characterized by the notion of specific content, to which Stumpf refers with the concept of Gebilde (product), and by the quality and matter of an act. In an act of judgment, for example, the quality of an act consists in an affirmation or a negation, and it is characterized linguistically by the copula “is” or its negation. The “matter” ( Materie ) of a judgment is what remains when one disregards the affirmation and negation, i.e., the mere complex of presentations (subject and predicate without the copula). In addition to its quality and matter, the judgment conveys a specific “formation” or product ( Gebilde ) that Stumpf sometimes calls a state of affairs. They are “correlates” of thought and distinguish themselves from the individual act, of which they are the content, through their objective character. All other functions, from the simplest to the most complex, have their specific content. For example, the act of abstraction, which is responsible for the formation of concepts, has a concept as its specific content. In the field of more complex functions such as emotion, desire, and will, Stumpf maintains that we must also presuppose specific contents which he calls values.

Descriptive psychology’s second task is the classification of acts or psychical functions. This classification is based on the distinction between two classes of acts: intellectual and emotional functions. All functions that fall under either of these two classes have relationships ranging from the simplest to the most complex, so that functions of the second class presuppose, and are based on, lower level functions of the first class. This class of intellectual functions subsumes all acts ranging from sense perception to judgment. Sense perception in this classification has a particular status because it gives direct access to first-order phenomena and as such it is the function of consciousness (attention) through which something is noticed or apprehended. It serves as the foundation of all functions in that it provides them with their sensory material. Between perception and judgment, there is a series of intermediate acts: the act of presentation, which has as content second order phenomena, the act of abstraction and what Stumpf calls the acts of synthesis, whose specific contents are sets ( Inbegriffe ).

From the class of intellectual functions, Stumpf sets apart the class of feelings or emotional functions. Stumpf’s works in the field of emotions led to a debate with Brentano and were the subject of many discussions, particularly by the American psychologist E. B. Titchener (Titchener 1908, 1917, 1929; Reisenzein & Schönpflug 1992; Fisette 2013). At issue was whether the nature of pleasure provided by an object such as a work of art, for instance, is intentional, as was the case in Brentano’s theory wherein it is closely related to the class of emotions, or phenomenal as in Husserl and the sensualist theories of James and Mach. Stumpf claims that there is a specific difference between sense-feelings (bodily pleasure, pain, etc.) which are sensory qualities like sound and color, and emotions (joy, sadness, anger, disgust, etc.) which are intentional states directed towards states of affairs. Between emotional and intellectual functions, there is the same relation of foundation as that between judgment and perception, since judgment, or more precisely states of affairs, are presupposed by emotional functions which, although more complex, are nevertheless structured in the same way. In addition to emotions, this class of feelings subsumes the acts of desire and will, upon which the field of ethics is based. Between emotions and the will, there is a hierarchy comparable to that of the class of intellectual states, with the difference being however that the phenomenal basis of the class of emotional acts is nothing other than sense-feelings (pleasure and displeasure). Emotions belong to the subclass of passive feelings while desire and will belong to the subclass of active feelings. Feelings are passive in that they have something existent as an object (that is any object of a true judgment) while active feelings are related to a duty (object of a voluntary act). Values are the specific content of the class of active feelings (desire and will) while the contents of an emotion are values. Emotions are evaluative states concerning the content of a judgment and the evaluative element of emotions lies in the positive or negative stand taken with respect to the judged state of affairs. The difference between these two classes of acts lies therefore in their quality, meaning their negative or positive stand ( Stellungsnahme ) regarding their object: affirmation and negation in the case of judgment, love and hate in the case of the entire class of feelings. The relation of foundation between emotions and judgments or beliefs presupposes, on the one hand, a causal relation between states of belief and valuation (or stand), and on the other hand, an intentional relation between the content of belief and the emotion. From this point of view, jealousy, to use Stumpf’s example, would be a negative stand and a valuation of the state of affairs that a given person possesses and which another person wants or covets for herself, but which she does not possess; and this state is caused by the belief or judgment (true) that this state of affairs exists ( besteht ).

## 4. The Classification of Sciences

The starting point of Stumpf’s classification is the cardinal distinction made in Brentano’s Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint (1874) between two classes of phenomena, physical phenomena and mental phenomena, or what Stumpf calls sensory phenomena and psychical functions (Rollinger 2008b).
