articleBody:
A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

Many adolescents care deeply.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our [recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure](https://doi.org/10.1177/01650254261485170), an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

## 1. Compassion has to survive peer dynamics

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

At first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: Compassion unfolds within relationships.

During adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

This means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

When educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on [teaching empathy or kindness](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/how_educators_are_using_kindness_to_transform_schools). Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as important. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

In other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

## 2. Compassion involves social risk

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

Consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention quickly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

The question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

This perspective does not excuse harmful behavior or passivity. But it does encourage us to understand helping as a social act rather than a purely moral one.

If we want young people to act compassionately, we need environments where compassionate action is socially supported instead of socially costly.

## 3. Compassion requires emotional regulation

Perhaps the most surprising finding from our study is that recognizing suffering alone did not consistently predict helping.

Many students understood that someone was struggling. The difference was what happened after that recognition occurred.

One of the strongest predictors of compassionate action is distress tolerance, the ability to remain engaged in the presence of emotional discomfort. This matters because witnessing another person’s suffering is often uncomfortable. We may feel sadness, anxiety, uncertainty, helplessness, or fear of saying the wrong thing. Adolescents experience these emotions, too.

Imagine a teenager whose friend is crying. The challenge is not simply recognizing that the friend is upset; it’s navigating the delicate space between overidentifying with another person’s suffering and distancing oneself from it. Too much emotional absorption can lead to overwhelm and withdrawal. Too much distance can lead to disengagement. Compassion requires something different: remaining connected to another person’s experience while maintaining enough emotional balance to respond effectively.

People sometimes assume that compassion and empathy are the same thing. They are not. [Empathy](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/empathy/definition#what-is-empathy) allows us to resonate with another person’s experience. [Compassion](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/compassion/definition#what-is-compassion) involves channeling that awareness into a desire to alleviate suffering. Doing so requires emotional regulation. Without it, concern can become overwhelm, uncertainty, or avoidance. Instead of moving toward suffering, we move away from it.

Our findings suggest that compassionate action depends not only on recognizing another person’s distress, but also on the ability to stay present with that distress without becoming consumed by it. In this sense, emotional regulation is not separate from compassion; it helps make compassion possible.

For parents and educators, this finding has important practical implications. Teaching young people how to navigate difficult emotions may strengthen their capacity for compassionate action. Skills such as mindfulness, emotional awareness, reflection, and distress tolerance are not simply tools for managing stress. They may also be the very capacities that help adolescents transform caring into action by staying engaged when helping feels uncertain, vulnerable, or emotionally difficult.

## 4. Compassion needs motivation

Even when adolescents care and have the emotional skills to stay engaged, one additional factor matters: motivation.

In our study, intrinsic prosocial motivation was one of the strongest predictors of helping. Simply put, adolescents who genuinely wanted to help others were more likely to translate concern into action.

This may sound self-evident, but it carries important implications.

Adults often try to encourage helping through external incentives, praise, rewards, or behavioral expectations. While these approaches can influence behavior, our findings suggest that compassionate action is especially powerful when it emerges from internal values and genuine concern for others.

Young people are constantly asking themselves what kind of person they want to be. When helping becomes connected to identity, meaning, and purpose, compassionate action appears more likely to follow.

This suggests that fostering compassion is about more than encouraging kind behavior. It is also about helping young people develop a sense of responsibility toward others and a meaningful connection to shared humanity.

## What gets in the way of compassion?

Taken together, these findings challenge a common assumption.

There is a tendency to treat moments of inaction as moments of moral failure. We see a young person remain silent, fail to intervene, or walk past another person’s suffering, and we assume we understand what happened.

Yet our research suggests that these moments are often more complicated than they appear.

They unfold within social worlds shaped by belonging, friendship, identity, uncertainty, vulnerability, and the deeply human desire to remain connected to others. They are influenced by relationships, social risks, emotional capacities, and personal motivations.

What looks like indifference from a distance may sometimes reflect a struggle between compassion and the realities that make compassionate action difficult.

This perspective shifts the conversation from a question of character to a question of conditions.

Rather than asking whether adolescents are compassionate, we might ask: What conditions help compassion become action?

## Helping caring become action

The encouraging message from this research is that the factors influencing compassionate action are not fixed traits.

Relationships can be strengthened.

School climates can be improved.

Emotional regulation skills can be taught.

Prosocial values can be nurtured.

When we think about compassion this way, the goal becomes larger than helping young people recognize suffering. The goal is helping them develop the capacities that allow caring to become action.

Perhaps this is what adolescence reveals so clearly. The distance between caring and acting is rarely empty space. It is filled with questions about belonging, uncertainty, responsibility, and risk.

Young people are learning to navigate that space every day.

Our responsibility as the adults who support them is not simply to teach them to care. It is to create the relationships, communities, and opportunities that help them act on the care they already possess.

title: Kognition: Was ist Intelligenz?
subtitle: Vier Experten aus Tierkognition, Neurobiologie, Psychologie und KI-Forschung beleuchten diese Frage aus unterschiedlichen Blickwinkeln.
feedText: Im Stadtpark drückt eine Krähe mit ihrem Schnabel auf den Knopf eines Wasserspenders. Ein dünner Strahl schießt hervor. Eine zweite Krähe tritt heran und trinkt. Dann wechseln die Tiere die Rollen. Währenddessen spazieren Menschen vorbei, ohne stehen zu bleiben. Auf sie wirkt die Szene wohl nicht ungewöhnlich.
body:
# Was ist Intelligenz? Menschliches Denken, künstliche Intelligenz - Spektrum der Wissenschaft

## Was ist Intelligenz? Menschliches Denken, künstliche Intelligenz

Im Stadtpark drückt eine Krähe mit ihrem Schnabel auf den Knopf eines Wasserspenders. Ein dünner Strahl schießt hervor. Eine zweite Krähe tritt heran und trinkt. Dann wechseln die Tiere die Rollen. Währenddessen spazieren Menschen vorbei, ohne stehen zu bleiben. Auf sie wirkt die Szene wohl nicht ungewöhnlich. Die Krähen haben offenbar beobachtet, wie Menschen den Automaten bedienen. Doch was spiegelt das Verhalten der Vögel eigentlich wider? Die spontane Antwort lautet: Das ist selbstverständlich intelligentes Verhalten. Schwieriger wird es allerdings, zu erklären, was damit eigentlich gemeint ist. Denn der Begriff »Intelligenz« entzieht sich bis heute überraschend hartnäckig einer klaren Definition. Können Krähen abstrakt denken? Verstehen sie Ursache und Wirkung? Oder wiederholen sie lediglich ein bewährtes Verhalten? Und wäre auch das schon intelligent? Die Szene lässt sich je nach wissenschaftlichem Hintergrund unterschiedlich deuten. Manche Fachleute definieren Intelligenz über die Fähigkeit zur Problemlösung. Andere interessieren sich für die dahinterliegenden neuronalen Prozesse. Wieder andere knüpfen Intelligenz an das Nutzen von Symbolen wie etwa Schrift oder Zahlen. Und seit Maschinen Schachweltmeister besiegen, Bilder erschaffen und Texte verfassen, stellt sich zudem die Frage, ob Intelligenz überhaupt ein biologisches Gehirn voraussetzt. Die folgenden vier Gespräche nähern sich dem Begriff aus jeweils unterschiedlichen Perspektiven – und suchen Antworten auf eine scheinbar einfache Frage: Was ist Intelligenz? Tierkognition: Intelligenz befähigt zur Lösung von Problemen Julia Fischer ist Professorin für Primatenkognition an der Georg-August-Universität Göttingen und leitet die Abteilung Kognitive Ethologie am Deutschen Primatenzentrum. Für sie hängt Intelligenz davon ab, welche Probleme ein Lebewesen in seinem ökologischen Kontext lösen muss.

A self [is a forest](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/09/pando/). A self [is a ship](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/08/plutarch-the-ship-of-theseus-ted-ed/). A self [is an illusion](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/21/iris-murdoch-unselfing/), and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is [a sum of selves](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/04/10/parts/), contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

[Kahlil Gibran](https://themarginalian.org/tag/kahlil-gibran) (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about [the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/04/04/youth-and-age-kahlil-gibran/), takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic [The Madman](http://www.amazon.com/Madman-His-Parables-Poems/dp/0486419118/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/madman-his-parables-and-poems/oclc/242642&referer=brief_results) | [free ebook](http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5616)).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated [the Japanese concept of ma](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/07/ma/).)

Kahlil Gibran

articleBody:
Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public in what became the largest IPO in American history. Given my sustained criticism of Anthropic’s beliefs and actions, many people have asked me for my opinion on this event.

The good news for the curious among you is that I captured my thoughts in an op-ed for *The New York Times*, which they published Thursday, the same day that Anthropic went public. It was titled “[Don’t Play Anthropic’s Game](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/opinion/anthropic-ipo-ai-regulation.html),” and it opens as follows:

“By the close of the stock market today, Anthropic will have become a central pillar of the American economy. This is deeply concerning to me, because it’s unclear how many of the retail and institutional investors handing over their money to Anthropic realize that they are, in some sense, funding a doomsday cult that also happens to build enterprise software.”

My use of “doomsday cult” isn’t facetious; it underscores a critical reality. As many have reported ([including myself](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/05/opinion/ai-silicon-valley.html)), the leaders of Anthropic have long believed that AI is destined to transform the human species, either delivering a utopia or killing us all. They see themselves, with their highly rational minds, trained on long hours during the 2000s debating these issues on blogs like *Less Wrong* and *Overcoming Bias*, as the select few who must rise up to guide humanity through this next evolution.

This may sound like hyperbole, but it’s not. [It’s exactly what they believe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jt508VjX2H8).

Some ask, “Why is this a problem? If any company is going to advance AI, shouldn’t it be one that cares about bad outcomes?”

As I elaborate in my op-ed, the situation is not so simple. Anthropic’s belief that transformational AI is imminent has made it reckless. Anthropic now releases models faster than they can build safeguards because they believe the fate of the human race depends on getting to superintelligent AI first. (Case in point: earlier this year, they announced they were relaxing rules that required them to slow down development if models became hard to control. Their reason? If they applied such rules “unilaterally,” other – presumably less righteous – parties might get ahead of them in the race.)

Indeed, Anthropic stated a key rationale for their IPO is to raise the money needed to accelerate investments in so-called “recursive self-improvement,” where AI systems upgrade themselves. This is, of course, a terrible idea, as it creates models that are even less safe and harder to understand. Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its S-1 filing, but sees no alternative if they’re to continue as humanity’s shepherd through this revolution.

It’s unclear to what degree they even care about profits or building a durable business. As I summarize in my op-ed:

“It’s a business plan that starts with a lot of red ink and then abruptly ends with superintelligence arriving and rendering money superfluous.”

To be clear: generative AI is an incredibly important technological revolution. It brings with it great promises and real risks. But the right way to navigate these innovations can’t possibly be to let a small number of people in Silicon Valley, who have been worshipping AI as a millenarian agent since well before LLMs entered the scene, gather as much money as possible to fund their self-proclaimed role as prophets who will lead the rest of us to their idiosyncratic vision of a better future.

#### In Other News

For more on the question of whether Amodei and company are right in their beliefs that we’re on a trajectory toward superintelligence, check out [my recent technical article](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-superintelligence-debate) for the *IEEE Spectrum*, which lays out an engineering case against the feasibility of AI superintelligence. (You should also consider signing up for the Spectrum’s always insightful [AI Alert newsletter](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-alert-signup).)

title: When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery

articleBody:
The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the [Vancouver Art Gallery](https://www.vanartgallery.bc.ca/art-of-wellbeing/), and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend [PaRx](https://www.parkprescriptions.ca/), Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access.

Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

*Credit: Vancouver Art Gallery*

## An artful approach to treatment

The process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

The prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

After the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

This is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs. The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

Carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She says the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

“For them to understand that so many people have come together to create this opportunity, I think that in and of itself is special,” Fry says. “They say, ‘Wow, my community cares.’ The possibility that this exists, it’s available, it’s free—there’s something about that... that’s noteworthy.”

Fry is one of the professionals who gives these kinds of prescriptions to her clients. It’s another tool available to promote well-being.

“Of course, I’m never telling them to go. We talk about this as a prescription, but I always present it as ‘here’s an opportunity to meet some of your goals, and here’s what the opportunity looks like,’” she says.

As yet, no one has declined her prescription.

“They’re surprised that something so seemingly simplistic as slowing down and really looking, really living in front of the art or in nature is actually an intervention,” Fry says. “People in our culture are set up to think that growth has got to be painful, growth has got to be difficult, growth has got to be expensive, growth is going to take a long time. When I bring forward an intervention of going to a location, and your job as a client of mine is to appreciate, the first reaction is surprise. It opens up an entire conversation—‘I can just appreciate my life and not always be grinding to make it better.’ It’s a special process for me to witness.”

## Awe and nature in community

The goal is to do more than increase the number of people who have exposure to art, though that might be a side effect. The formal prescription to nature through art is designed to reduce stress, anxiety, and social isolation. The ability to bring a guest, as well as the opportunity to experience art with other patrons, is key.

“There are other people there; these aren’t private viewings. But of course, sometimes people don’t feel connected to others in a room. Sometimes they do; sometimes it’s enough to feel that they’re part of a community. But others really benefit from being able to have a shared experience where they can reflect in real time and reflect afterwards,” Fry says.

Paula Toledo is the mental health advisor and lead well-being consultant at Vancouver Art Gallery, leading the [Richardson Family Art of Wellbeing Lab](https://www.vanartgallery.bc.ca/art-of-wellbeing/). The lab aims to connect the community to art as a means to improve mental and physical well-being, drawing on a collaboration of researchers, scientists, physicians, and Indigenous Elders and healers.

Toledo came to this work through the personal experience of losing her husband and her mother within months, while also caring for her newborn child. That grief and her recovery changed the course of her life and her career in wellness.

“When we encounter something so vast that it transcends our current understanding of the world, it can be very mysterious,” Toledo says:

> Sometimes it can be a very positive experience, but other times, like in cases of grief, it can also make you stop and wonder about the mystery behind it. I was in awe and I remember that exact moment where I thought, “Well, if that could happen, then the opposite must also be true.” That’s what the research supports: When we experience awe, it can lead to wonder, which is this mental state of openness and curiosity. Every day I woke up with that sense of curiosity that this might be the day that I turn the corner and collide with good fortune. That experience was so transformative that it led me to actually seek out resources.

Toledo’s health care provider connected her with a social worker who prescribed movement and art in the form of yoga and music classes.

I started to feel more energized and connected to my own self-determination,” she says. “If we look at the research on why social prescribing is so impactful, it’s because it really does encourage self-determination. I started to feel more connected to my community, more connected to my children, connecting to their own wonder, and it became this upward spiral towards healing and towards rebuilding my life.”

## Art by prescription

Monica Harrison is one of the many prescription holders who has learned to lean into the peace and beauty of slowing down through the program. She is an educational assistant who works with students with support needs and advocates for their inclusion in schools. She experienced health issues that required her to be on leave from work and that triggered depression and anxiety.

“I’m neurodivergent, so I’m autistic and I have ADHD. I’ve had anxiety my whole life, and I’ve learned a lot of coping mechanisms that help me to control that. But with undiagnosed conditions that have been going on, it has awoken a lot of anxiety, and it makes it hard to manage my mood,” she says.

Harrison met Toledo, who introduced her to the prescription program. What started with Harrison’s immersion in art has resulted in her increasing use of the program in other locations, both indoors and out.

Harrison, who enjoys nature photography, says she was introduced to Carr’s paintings in elementary school, and she fell in love with the local subject matter. Now as an adult, that connection to art has opened new opportunities.

“When we visited the gallery, I was able to discuss paintings and identify what I was feeling. It really allowed me to label what I was feeling more accurately and then think about it. Just through her artwork, it really made me feel nurturing and protection,” she says.

Through other exhibitions at the gallery, Harrison says she found surprise and joy and “a lot of beautiful sensory feelings to my mind and my body and my soul”:

> Chronic illnesses [have] made my life very small, with a lot of losses that come with the territory, such as giving up things that I once enjoyed like working, walking in nature, seeing friends, traveling. I found the prescription to be very flexible. You can do it whenever you’re able to. It can give you something specific to try out. You can do it on your own. You can do it with friends and family, and I think it’s a great thing for people with chronic illness. And it can also give those people a practical way to learn how nature connects to positive mental health. It can be something they can build on through a positive experience with their prescription... and add to their toolkit.

Fry says she hears two recurring themes from prescription holders: Experiencing art feels immersive, and the process of visiting the gallery—from the prescription as an invitation to the encouragement to engage in “slow looking”—is a special event that makes them feel cared for.

“It’s something different. It’s something novel. It’s something fresh,” she says, whereas doing the same gratitude practices over and over can get repetitive. “It’s a lot more powerful when we add novel opportunities or events or experiences to our practice. For every person that I’ve prescribed this to, it’s been new to them, so it hits that mark really nicely,” she says.

## A new, slow way of seeing

Art, nature, music, dance, and other social prescriptions have decades of demonstrated success. Toledo points to social prescribing in the U.K. as an example where community connectors or social workers serve as entry points for patients to discover what activities might be meaningful to them. For some, that might mean a return to an activity they enjoyed in years past, like Toledo’s own reengagement with music during her grief.

The social prescription movement continues to gain ground, with providers taking notice at a growing pace. It requires community, collaboration, and a foundation of care that looks at health through a wide lens. In the United States, organizations like Social Prescribing USA are championing the effort as a medical intervention.

For Rao, the impact extends far beyond people’s visits to the gallery.

“What we’re looking at is a way of seeing,” Rao says. “That way of seeing then applies to anything.”

articleBody:
When Siddhartha Gautama gave his first teaching after enlightenment, it was to five friends in the deer park at Sarnath, not far from Varanasi in the Ganges Valley. Wanting to transmit to them the essence of his breakthrough, he crystallized his insights into what would become known as the four noble truths. These include the truth of the way out of suffering, known as the noble eightfold path: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

The eightfold path offers a way to touch awakening as Gautama did. These insights were not the result of thinking or study, nor were they a creed or philosophical doctrine. They were the fruit of Gautama’s own direct experience and meditative realization, and they conveyed a path that traced a “middle way” between the two extremes of asceticism and indulgence. It was a way, he believed, that could lead anyone to realize understanding, liberation, and peace.

#### “You don’t hurry to get the dishes done quickly so you can get on with something else. You encounter the miracle of life that includes dishes.”

As a species we’re still struggling to find a middle way, to steer a wise course through the extremes of fanaticism, greed, nihilism, rage, and despair. The ancient wisdom of the eightfold path offers eight matrixes that are powerfully relevant today as a guide to help us navigate these extremes and bring a meaningful direction to our daily lives, actions, and relationships.

All elements of the eightfold path inter-are. You cannot extract any of them from the context of the path. So, for example, if you take mindfulness out of the ethical context of the path, it is no longer right mindfulness. All eight elements are interrelated and interdependent. They enhance each other. When practiced deeply, each element of the path contains the other seven within it, and they complement each other to create a complete path to liberation.

My teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, taught that right mindfulness is at the heart of the eightfold path. So, with the energy of right mindfulness as the foundation, we’re able to develop right concentration. This gives rise to insight or “right view,” which Thich Nhat Hanh described as the “insight of interbeing.” It is this deep view of the world that guides us to an ethical and beneficial life through right thinking, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort. So, when you generate the energy of mindfulness, you are naturally concentrated on the object of your mindfulness, whether it’s your breathing, your body, the sunset, or the presence of the person in front of you.

Photo © Noumae | Dreamstime.com

The energies of mindfulness and concentration naturally give rise to insight, right view. You touch the insight of interbeing between your breath and the earth, or between your body and your ancestors and descendants, or between your heart and the sun in the sky. You realize that you inter-are with the person in front of you.
Already, this insight of interbeing helps us touch peace, joy, and freedom.

Now, with the energy of mindfulness, concentration, and insight, your thinking will naturally be right thinking.

It will be free from discrimination and separation, and on the basis of that thinking, your speech will be right speech and your action right action.

Cultivating right diligence (or effort) in that moment, you’ll be able to see and calm any unwholesome seeds that may get triggered in your consciousness, such as anger or despair, and identify and activate positive seeds, such as gratitude and compassion. With all those energies alive in you, the way you spend your time, energy, and labor—your livelihood—will be “right.” It will be beneficial for you and everyone around you.

Of course, if there’s “right,” there must also be “wrong.” The Buddha’s teaching does assert that there’s a right and wrong way to go about things. There’s a distinction, for example, between “right mindfulness” and “wrong mindfulness,” between “right concentration” and “wrong concentration,” between “right speech” and “wrong speech.” There’s a way of practicing mindfulness, concentration, and the others that goes in the direction of healing and well-being, and there’s a way that goes in the direction of harm and ill-being.

This is where ethics comes into every aspect of the eightfold path. The wrong path *does* exist—it’s the “ignoble” path of wrong view, wrong thinking, wrong speech, and wrong action that leads to suffering for ourselves, for others, and for the planet. It’s the reason why we’re in the state we’re in. And it’s why we need to find another way of being.

You may wonder, how can there be a wrong way to practice mindfulness? Surely *all* mindfulness is beneficial? In 2014, Thich Nhat Hanh’s last year of teaching, he spoke about the importance of not diluting or appropriating mindfulness as it spreads in the West and reaches new audiences and settings. He explained that the first way to distinguish “right” from “wrong” mindfulness is to realize that right mindfulness is not an instrument or tool but *a way*, a path. It cannot be used as a means to an end.

Yet many of us do speak of mindfulness as a tool. We say that with mindfulness we can heal, with mindfulness we can reconcile, with mindfulness we can make more money, and, in applying mindfulness in the military, with mindfulness we can kill the enemy more effectively. To appropriate mindfulness in this way is to instrumentalize it. Used as a means to an end, whether for profit, success, or even for apparently “beneficial” ends, mindfulness loses its true, authentic spirit. In fact, if you extract any of the eight elements out of the wider ethical context of the path, it is no longer “right.”

The image of “path” or “way” is essential to Buddhist spirituality, and yet it may be challenging for those of us educated in Western capitalist countries. We prefer there to be a goal, a destination, a clear program. We may be seeking a powerful, final moment of “grace” or “attainment.” But as Thich Nhat Hanh used to ask us teasingly,
“Why haven’t you ever asked if the Buddha kept practicing after enlightenment?”

The eightfold path is not so much linear as circular, which is why it’s often seen more as an eight-spoked wheel than a list. The Western-educated mind may struggle with this. We want to know where to start and where we end up. We want to know which element is more important.

The eight-spoke dharma wheel symbolizes the eightfold path. Photo: godongphoto / shutterstock.com

But in his later years of teaching, Thich Nhat Hanh revised his translation of the eightfold path to be not merely “the path leading to happiness,” but “the path of happiness.” He taught that in the true spirit of the insight of interbeing, every step along the path leading to happiness *must be happiness itself*. If we suffer along the way, we’ve lost the game already.

This is strong medicine for the Western tendency to sacrifice means for an end, and for the deep energy of running and striving in our culture. And it’s good news. The eightfold path is not a path of thorns or sacrifice. There’s no need to set our jaw or grit our teeth. There’s an art and poetry to the path of spiritual practice. With every step along our journey we can arrive at our destination. With every step, we can touch happiness, peace, and freedom.

It’s true that at any given moment, one aspect of the path may come more to the fore than another. There may be times we spend a few weeks or months developing right concentration and stillness. Or other times when we focus more on transforming habits of speech, or redirecting our livelihood to be more in line with our aspiration. These things take time to nurture and ripen, and cannot happen all at once.

On the other hand, there may be some settings, as simple as washing the dishes, in which we can actively realize all eight elements at once, and touch joy and freedom right in the heart of our daily life. Every aspect of the path can be realized right in the heart of the present moment: you don’t need to practice for ten days or ten years in order to have insight.

Suppose at some point today you need to wash the dishes. While standing at the sink, you generate the energy of mindfulness—mindfulness of your body and breathing, of your feet on the ground and hands in the water. On an out-breath you may release tension in your body, shoulders, and face, and become fully present for yourself, the dishes, and the wonder of life right in this moment.

You don’t hurry to get the dishes done quickly so you can get on with something else. You encounter the miracle of life that includes dishes. Within a few moments, you begin to develop concentration, and looking deeply into the water, the soap, the sponge, and the dish, insight may naturally arise. Can you see the galaxy in the spoon? Can you see the mountains in the plate? Can you see your grandparents’ hands in your own?

With this kind of insight, your thinking will be right thinking. You won’t think, “Why is it always me who has to do the dishes?” As you enjoy every aspect of washing the dishes and cleaning up, our thinking, speech, and action will carry the insight of interbeing, compassion, and nondiscrimination.

With these energies in you, you’ll be able to handle reactions or frustrations as they arise and generate gratitude, peace, and freedom. In that moment, you won’t discriminate between “work” and “life.” Every part of life belongs to the miracle of being alive. And in that moment, you penetrate the matrix of the eightfold path, you realize the Buddha’s insight in your own life, and you touch peace, freedom, joy, and happiness right in the heart of the present moment.

articleBody:
# A Jazz Walk Incoming — Roden Newsletter Archive

### RodenIssue #120November 22, 2026

## A Jazz Walk Incoming

### Twenty-one days of chasing jazz and Shōwa in Kyūshū

Roden Readers —

Fall! Finally! Jacket weather! Sweaters! Snow on Fuji! Oh, my!

What has been going on this past month? A whole lotta hermiting. I’ve been on a decidedly teenager-like (or Mishima-like, if you prefer; the man almost never rose before noon) schedule, which my body clock seems to love, working late into the night and passing out around two or three and then waking up around ten or eleven, pounding a big ol’ smoothie, and then working like mad from noon to six, breaking for a nice dinner with friends, and then diving back under until my futon calls. This is an ideal schedule for me. Because I am insane. I basically never shifted back from Europe time to Japan time in October. Also, a smoothie + slow, delicious dinner turns out to be a great eating schedule? I feel light and energetic. Am I an adult? I’m not sure. I do push-ups and walk 10,000 steps a day. Such is the glamorous life of being self-employed at forty-six years old while the world speedruns its own unique flavor of insanity in the background. Is the singularity here yet?

#### #SHŌWA! COLOSSUS!

My big announcement here is a new pop-up newsletter / “tour” starting in two days (on Wednesday the 25th). It’s called: SHŌWA㍼COLOSSUS.

Sign up here (as with all my pop-ups, you have to enthusiastically opt in):.

For twenty-one+ days I’ll be on the road visiting some of the last remaining classic jazz kissas of Kyūshū. As usual, I’ll be sending daily dispatches and more. As usual, I have no idea what we’ll discover. And as usual, I am forever grateful to my SPECIAL PROJECTS members who make projects like this possible. All funding and support for these tours (which are complicated, expensive, slightly crazy affairs) comes directly from memberships and book sales.

If you don’t mind sharing the Ridgeline link, or the Instagram post, please do. These tours are one of the few chances to grow my audience without having to be a full-time social media bobblehead. I appreciate it!

#### #Holiday Presents?

Thank you to everyone who has grabbed a notebook! They’re almost sold out. We have about fifty sets left. If I make some more, it won’t be until next year.

Things Become Other Things, the hardcover black-and-white Random House edition, is available for a paltry $18 shipped from the Evil™ Amazon® (and probably about $25 book-in-hand from your local bookshop, which you should go to, say hello to the people working there, smile at a few customers, smell the smells of literal tons of paper lined up on the walls; and if they don’t have a copy and you request one, a thousand baby kittens are instantly born into loving families).

Here’s what’s available in the fancy SPECIAL PROJECTS shop:

- Kissa by Kissa 6th ed., unsigned
- Things Become Other Things, fine art 2nd ed., signed
- OTHER THING, first ed., signed
- ⬤ — a made-in-Japan lay-flat notebook (I should have signed these)
Just a reminder, SPECIAL PROJECTS members get big discounts on everything in the SP Shop. And shipping for an order with multiple items is a significantly better deal than single items (just the way DHL works; the first kilogram is the most expensive). Orders ship next business day from my warehouse in Osaka, and arrive almost everywhere around the world in (usually) 2-3 days. It’s very efficient! These all make good presents.

We just — finally! — sold the last Tomato Farmer’s print. Thank you to everyone who bought one over the years. One of my goals for next year is to do more printing (working with local high-end photo shops doing C-prints?). Maybe even do a show at some point? I have a huge back catalogue of shots (many now with negatives) and should probably do something with some of them.

Otherwise, I’ve been working on a new book and writing near-daily dispatches (fifty-nine so far) to SPECIAL PROJECTS members about the meta-progress of it. The manuscript’s coming along (I hate it or am OK with it depending on the day), but I significantly underestimated the prep for SHŌWA㍼COLOSSUS. My plan was to complete this draft before leaving, but that’s not happening. So my new plan is to have it done by the end of the year, which is … probably possible?! We’ll continue to believe irrational things, since that’s gotten us this far.

#### #Recent Inspirations

As usual, I try to fill my downtime with interesting films, books, art, exercise, and conversations, and try to minimize the dooming, the scrolling, the Netflix “documentaries.”

My device of choice for reading is: physical books. But for when digital reading can’t be avoided, I now reach for an iPad Mini devoid of anything fun or interesting. You can strip-mine these devices pretty thoroughly, leaving behind just Readwise Reader and Readwise Books. I was using the old Mini with a matte screen protector on it, and it was fine. I upgraded to the new OLED Mini with Nano Texture, but quite frankly, for lying on your side in bed with the brightness low, I don’t see much of a difference. If you can pick up a used last-gen Mini, it’s a great reader.

Why did I stop using my Boox? (Which I used for a couple years.) I just … didn’t like the software that much? And didn’t trust it that much? And hated being logged into my Google account on a device I didn’t fully trust? And the Mini is overall a smoother software experience? And if you delete everything superfluous on the Mini, it’s pretty distraction-free? And it syncs better with your laptop? And I’ve come to feel like (brace yourself) e-ink is (gasp) overrated? (It’s great for very specific circumstances?) That a great LCD/OLED panel with a matte texture, and black background with light text is fine for almost all reading scenarios?

Hence: iPad Mini.

Speaking of which, Readwise Books — Readwise’s book app — recently soft-launched. It’s REALLY good. Like: a beautifully engineered application. I think it’s by far the best digital reading app we’ve ever had. They’ve spent years working on the business contracts to become a full-fledged digital bookstore, too. It’s US-only for now, but it’s looking to expand soon. The focus on reading stats and whatnot can be a bit off-putting (many people have privately complained about that aspect to me), but you can turn them off! Don’t miss out on the best e-reading experience around. TBOT is, of course, available on the platform.

I miss Longform.org. It was a great resource for finding something good to read. So I built a SPECIAL PROJECTS members-only RSS feed called “Dinnertime” that aggregates the long-form pieces coming from sixty or so of the top magazines, journals, and newspapers. I plug that into Readwise Reader’s RSS processor and I am never in want of a great long-form piece.

Tony (2026) was surprisingly … excellent? Fun? I don’t know why I had such low expectations. (Maybe the bad reviews?) It’s probably best to think of it as a coming-of-age story about a statutory rapist drug addict and an obnoxious literary freak in 1970s Rhode Island. Forget the Bourdain angle. It’s a very “crisp” film, with little flab (106 mins), something I’m increasingly sensitive to. You can imagine this having been pitched as a series and we are all so much better for it being a film. You can do a lot in ninety mins if you’re smart. In a moment of weakness (this is why it’s always good to have a list of things to watch; so you don’t fall prey to The Algorithm) I watched about thirty minutes of The Altruists and … it’s a good example of the inverse of Tony. (I will not be finishing it, and if I ever hear the phrase “sub-optimal” again, or anyone talking about Harry Potter sex fan-fiction I will have to remove my ears.)

A Prophet (Un prophète) (2009) is a great example of a non-English film getting lost in the shuffle (for me, anyway). Try to watch it knowing as little as possible. One of the best film’s I’ve seen this year. Kudos to actor Tahar Rahim and director Jacques Audiard for making something special.

A friend of mine was shocked the other day when I told him I send notes of thanks to actors, directors, writers, musicians, artists — basically anyone putting themselves out there in a way that inspires — as if the sending of these messages was somehow gauche or lame. No! Always Send The Note Of Gratitude! You cannot imagine how thankful folks are — no matter how “famous” they may be. A good note is short, asks NOTHING in return, and simply expresses thanks as gracefully as possible.

I read an advance copy of My Eliot by Donald Antrim. It comes out in January. It’s one of the strangest, funniest things I’ve read in ages. It is so — SO — bizarre. I had never read Antrim before. He’s a funny cat, a writer of great talent who applies those talents in odd ways. My Eliot is a perfect “anti-AI” novel simply by dint of its outlandishness.

Gene Smith’s Sink (amzn | bkshp) by Sam Stephenson was amazing. I knew of Smith’s photography but didn’t know of this book. It covers the singularly bizarre life of Smith in his 6th Ave loft, recording thousands of hours of the greatest jazz musicians who ever lived. I can’t recommend this book enough. Stephenson spent two decades researching Smith and you feel the work behind every page. Gene was famous in Japan for helping expose the mercury poisoning that happened at Minamata.

After finishing Gene Smith’s Sink I was legally obligated to watch the Johnny Depp film Minamata (2020), where he portrays Smith aside a star-studded Japanese cast. It was better than expected! Although, someone get that man a non-zoom lens.

OK, diving back into packing. I hit the road in about thirty-six hours and still have lingering equipment todos. Subscribe to SHŌWA㍼COLOSSUS. See you out there.

Thanks, C

title: The Hidden Spiegeltent in Chicago, Illinois

articleBody:
Spiegeltents were made to travel. These round wooden dance halls, lined with mirrors and stained glass, went from fair to fair. They went up fast and came down fast. The one on Randolph Street is not going anywhere. It was built indoors, on the 14th floor of a Loop building.

The building opened in 1926. Rapp & Rapp designed it, with the Oriental Theatre movie palace on the lower floors. The theater is now the James M. Nederlander Theatre. The whole building stands on the site of the Iroquois Theatre, where a fire in 1903 became one of the deadliest in American history.

High above the theater, the architects put a large hall for Masonic meetings. It sat empty for decades. Later it was turned into offices, and a dropped ceiling hid the room completely. When the building was converted into the Cambria Hotel, workers took that ceiling down and found the old hall again, steel bow trusses and all.

In 2019 the tent came over from Belgium in pieces, about 4,000 of them. Belgian tent builders put it together inside the hall, the traditional way, with no nails. It is about 72 feet across. From the hall, it looks like a small circus parked under factory trusses. Inside, there is carved wood, stained glass, velvet and mirrors everywhere. The mirrors are not just for looks. They let guests see around the posts that hold up the roof.

Since October 2026, the tent has been the home of Kermess by Circensia, which kept it right at the center of the room.

articleBody:
Do you hear all this noise? It's frightening.

The sky is pink, and orange, and yellow all washed-out by the grey of the clouds.

A group of people is going by, they are laughing, they are living.

And I wonder how.

I'm trying to understand, how can I go by? How can I laugh? How can I live?

Why aren't they walking alone?

The room is getting dark, the colors have faded.

I can't hear the people anymore, but they are still walking around my brain.

They are going by, they are laughing, they are living.

Getting my head through the window, I am looking at the trees. Looking right in their eyes.

"I'm sorry", I tell them.

You didn't deserve this.

"You are precious", I tell them.

And I wonder why I don't hear it coming from everywhere.

Why is there only this scary noise?

The noise of life going on, of people going by.

As if it was all ok. As if all around us wasn't screaming.

But the noise is too loud, too loud to listen with our ears.

I wonder if people can listen with their hearts.

I wonder if people can look at trees right in their eyes.

Just like they can go by,

Just like they can laugh,

Just like they can live.

I hope they can look at trees right in their eyes.

And tell them they are sorry.

Stop going by.

Stop laughing.

Stop living if just for a moment.

And tell them they are sorry.

I hope people can be alone and look at themselves.

At the sky full of pink, and orange, and yellow.

Hear all this scary noise they are making. Hear it with their hearts.

Then maybe they can all be silent, we can all be silent.

Be silent while all around it's getting dark.
And wait the night out.

Wait alongside the trees, the rivers, the critters running under our feet.

Tell them all they are precious,

That we never meant it and that we are sorry.

Maybe then I can go by.

Maybe then I can laugh.

Maybe then I can live.

## Keep tabs on Parliament.

### What we’re doing

Finding out what your representatives in Ottawa are up to can be tough.We’re trying to make it easy.

Find your MP by entering your postal code above. See what your representatives are saying, and what laws they’re proposing. Poke around.

### What they’re talking about

The latest House transcript is from Friday, November 27th, when the word of the day was moved. The House sits again on Monday. These are the topics that were discussed.

This summary is computer-generated. Usually it’s accurate, but every now and then it’ll contain inaccuracies or total fabrications.

Building Canada Strong Act Report stage of Bill C-39. The bill proposes measures to accelerate major projects and strengthen the economy, including changes to environmental assessments, labour rules, and federal powers. Opposition members criticize its potential effects on Indigenous rights, environmental protections, workers’ right to strike, and parliamentary oversight; Conservatives also seek project-approval deadlines and limits on ministerial powers. Liberals argue it can support economic growth while protecting the environment. 12700 words, 2 hours in 2 segments: 12.

Statements by Members

Christmas volunteers and celebrationsSaint-Léonard 140th anniversaryRené Dépatie rememberedLicensing foreign-trained doctorsBeauport social economy organizationsMen's mental health and purposeNew Ontario Liberal leaderSupport for Canadian cadet programsEmployment insurance and maternal equalityStudent leaders and post-secondary prioritiesHuman trafficking and online predatorsFord Oakville plant investmentSole-source government contractsFood insecurity in Saguenay—Lac-Saint-JeanAlleged Liberal insider benefitsViolence against Inuit women

Question Period

The Conservatives oppose the costly Alto train and accuse the government of rewarding insiders and obscuring the Prime Minister’s wife’s role. They criticize spending and affordability, cuts to national parks, weak honey import testing, and failures in immigration management and public safety. The Liberals defend major projects, including high-speed rail and Bill C-39, as ways to create jobs and strengthen economic sovereignty. They promote investments in Canadian tech companies, clean energy and forestry, while emphasizing affordability, fiscal management and support for food security. They also highlight efforts to uphold the Charter, protect borders, manage immigration and sustain public health care. The Bloc defend Quebec’s authority to legislate on secularism and the notwithstanding clause, demanding respect for the National Assembly and Quebec’s distinct character. They also call for transparency about the Prime Minister’s wife’s oceans role and oppose Bill C-39, citing threats to Indigenous rights and the environment. The NDP demand federal action to uphold the Canada Health Act and prevent Alberta’s Bill 11 from enabling two-tier health care, while seeking assurances that Albertans will retain dental-care coverage.

Canada Student Financial Assistance Act First reading of Bill C-299. The bill expands access to federal student financial assistance for Canadians pursuing qualifying training in aviation, marine and road transportation careers. 200 words.

Ability of Member to Represent Constituents Kevin Lamoureux argues that a constituent’s workplace reprisals after meeting an MP do not establish a breach of parliamentary privilege, since the MP’s duties were not obstructed. 600 words.

Spectrum Policy Framework for Canada Act Third reading of Bill C-268. The bill requires verification of carriers’ coverage data, regular updates to Canada’s spectrum policy framework and periodic reporting. Members support modernizing spectrum rules to improve rural connectivity, public safety and economic opportunities, while recognizing that better data alone will not ensure network expansion. 1600 words, 10 minutes.

Was this summary helpful and accurate?

### Recently debated bills

C-268 Spectrum Policy Framework for CanadaC-39 Building Canada StrongC-28 Canadian Space LaunchC-255 Amend the Criminal Code (mischief — religious property)C-31 Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 2C-221 Amend the Corrections and Conditional Release Act (disclosure of information to victims)

# A free multi-CDN, jsDelivr style - James Stone

## A free multi-CDN, jsDelivr style

28 Nov 26 post 1674 words #webdev #cdn #dns jsDelivr does something I have always found neat: it does not use one CDN, it uses several, and for every user it picks whichever one is fastest for them.fastest for them right now.right now, based on RUM. I wanted to see how close I could get to that on free tiers only. Plus the vanity of it is kinda nice. How many people can say their site is served from ~660340+ Cloudflare, 210+ Gcore and 114 Fastly340+ Cloudflare, 210+ Gcore and 114 Fastly, as at Nov 2026 data centers globally.

The experiment lives at cdn.jamesst.one, which now serves a copy of this site, and you can watch where it is routing at rum.jamesst.one.

### How a normal CDN works

A plain server has one IP address in one place, so every visitor’s packets travel all the way to it. A CDN instead announces the same IP address from hundreds of locations,from hundreds of locations at once (this is called anycast: one address, many machines, and the network decides which one you reach), and internet routing (BGP) delivers each visitor to the nearest one. That location serves a cached copy, and only goes back to the origin on a cache miss. For example, 151.101.1.242, one of Fastly’s addresses this site uses, answers in 0.6 to 2 ms from Globalping probes in Copenhagen, Singapore and Melbourne alike. No single machine can be that close to all three.

The above diagram is actually a simplification, because before that, a client first has to look up the IP address to connect to, i.e. DNS. A multi-CDN hooks into the DNS reply and picks which CDN is best, then that CDN’s anycast picks which specific data center based on network routing rules.

### How it fits together

The CDN is chosen in DNS. When your resolver asks for cdn.jamesst.one, the answer is a CNAME to one of three CDNs, and which one depends on where you are. Or, more accurately, the network you are on.

- DNS:Gcore Managed DNS. Its free plan supports “dynamic” records: a set of answers with metadata (countries, continents, networks) and pickers that choose one per query.
- The CDNs: Fastly, Gcore CDN and Cloudflare Pages. All three pull from the same origin and add the same response headers, plus a Server-Timing: cdn;desc="fastly" style header so every measurement knows who served it.
- rumd:rumd, the RUM daemon, as in Real User Monitoring: a small Go service that collects measurements, scores each CDN per country, continent and network, and recommends a routing policy.
- dnsctl: applies that recommendation to Gcore, but only once it has been stable for a few checks and a minimum interval has passed, so DNS does not flap.

## Alfred Schutz

Alfred Schutz (b. 1899, d. 1959), more than any other phenomenologist, attempted to relate the thought of Edmund Husserl to the social world and the social sciences. His 1932 Der Sinnhafte Aufbau der sozialen Welt supplied philosophical foundations for Max Weber’s sociology and the social sciences. When Schutz fled Hitler’s Anschluss of Austria and immigrated to the United States in 1939, he developed his thought further in relationship to the social sciences, American pragmatism, logical empiricism, and to various other fields of endeavor such as music and literature. His work has been developed in different directions and has generated wide-ranging applications in humanistic and social-scientific research.
