## 1. Life and Influence

Vienna-born Alfred Schutz joined the artillery division of the Austrian army during World War I and served on the Italian front before returning to pursue studies at the University of Vienna. There Schutz studied law, social science, and business with renowned figures such as Hans Kelsen and Ludwig von Mises, but his most significant educational experience occurred while he was a member of the Mises Circle, one of many Viennese circles, of which the “Schlick Circle” was the most famous. In the interdisciplinary Mises Circle, Schutz formed friendships that would continue throughout the cataclysmic decades of the 1930s and 1940s and that included colleagues such as economists Gottfried von Haberler, Friedrich A. von Hayek, Fritz Machlup, and Oskar Morgenstern; philosopher Felix Kaufmann; and political scientist Eric Voegelin. While continuing to pursue his academic interests, in 1927 Schutz was named executive officer of Reitler and Company, a leading Viennese banking firm with international business relations, and thus he commenced a life-long pattern that led Edmund Husserl to describe him as a young man “who spends his days at the bank and is a phenomenologist by night” (C-Gurwitsch: xv).

From the beginning, Schutz admired the methodological writings of Max Weber, who had lectured in Vienna in the summer of 1918 and whose work was immensely popular among Viennese intellectuals. However, Schutz felt that Weber’s work rested on tacit, unexamined presuppositions resulting from his lack of interest in fundamental epistemological problems that had no direct bearing on special sociological problems. In 1925–1927, Schutz turned to Henri Bergson’s philosophy of consciousness and inner time to clarify notions such as meaning, action, and intersubjectivity, and his results have been collected in manuscripts published as Life Forms and Meaning Structure (LFMS). Dissatisfied, though, with his analyses of temporality to the extent that he never published them and prompted by comments of Felix Kaufmann, he discovered the relevance of the phenomenology of the consciousness of inner time of Edmund Husserl (1859–1938). He then in 1932 went on to produce his major life’s work, The Phenomenology of the Social World (1932 [1967]), an achievement for which Husserl praised him as “an earnest and profound phenomenologist” (Barber 2004: 42). He spent the rest of the 1930s authoring essays showing how his phenomenology of the social world could come to terms with the economic thought of Mises and Hayek. Also, before any direct encounter with American pragmatism, he developed a manuscript on personality in the social world that stressed the pragmatic elements of the everyday social world (Schutz 1936 &1937 [CP6: 199–309]).

Schutz’s career, academic and business, was thoroughly convulsed when Adolf Hitler implemented the annexation ( Anschluss ) of Austria by Germany on March 13, 1938, especially since he, on a business trip in Paris, was separated for three months from his own family, whose emigration to Paris he finally arranged. As an international lawyer and businessperson, he was able to assist numerous intellectuals to escape Austria, but the westward movement of the Nazi juggernaut eventually compelled him to immigrate with his family to the United States on July 14, 1939.

In the United States, he continued assisting emigrants from Austria and working with Reitler and Company in reestablishing its business, and he supported the United States war effort by reporting on German and Austrian economic matters for the Board of Economic Warfare. He also cooperated with Marvin Farber in founding the International Phenomenological Society , whose initial turf-battles he often mediated, and in instituting and editing Philosophy and Phenomenological Research . In 1943, Schutz began teaching sociology and philosophy courses as a member of The Graduate Faculty of The New School for Social Research, and his responsibilities included presenting papers in the school-wide General Seminar, supervising dissertations, and serving as chair of the Philosophy Department from 1952–1956. While in the United States, Schutz published a collection of articles on a wide variety of topics, explaining and criticizing Husserl’s thought; examining the works of American philosophers such as William James or George Santanyana; engaging continental philosophers such as Max Scheler or Jean-Paul Sartre; developing his own philosophical positions on the social sciences, temporality, language, multiple realities, responsibility, and symbolism; addressing socio-political questions dealing with strangers, homecomers, well-informed citizens, and equality; and treating themes in literature and music.

In spite of his many activities, he managed to carry on an extensive philosophical correspondence with Farber, Aron Gurwitsch, Machlup, Voegelin, and Maurice Natanson. However, to date, only the correspondences with Gurwitsch (C-Gurwitsch) and with Voegelin (C-Voegelin) have been published. In the former, one finds debates on the noetic/noematic starting point of phenomenology, the existence of the ego, the different direction phenomenology takes when undertaken in reference to the social sciences as opposed to physics and mathematics, the topic of intersubjectivity versus the field of consciousness, and the significance of starting with a theory of action rather than perception. Voegelin and Schutz differed on interpretations of Husserl, ethics, and the seeming relativism of Schutz’s theory of relevances (values and interests).

Schutz’s graduate students continued Schutz’s tradition in philosophy and sociology. Natanson, for example, emphasized the tension between individual, existential dimensions of everyday-life experiences and the social, anonymizing aspects of such experience. Thomas Luckmann, who served as co-author for the posthumous publication of Schutz’s The Structures of the Life-World (two volumes, 1973 & 1983; SL), developed the sociology of knowledge implications of Schutz’s thought and stressed the differences between science and the life-world as well as the importance of language, symbolism, and the moral order of society. In the years after Schutz’s death in 1959, his works have been posthumously published and his thought expanded in several directions. Peter Berger and Thomas Luckmann wrote The Social Construction of Reality (1966), which focused on how subjective human processes construct the objective societal structures that human subjectivity is shaped by, interprets, and reacts to. That book was among the most widely read books on social science in the twentieth century.

## 2. The Phenomenology of the Social World

In his principal work, Schutz’s introduction engaged his principal interlocutor, Max Weber. Schutz praised Weber’s views on value-freedom in social science and the autonomy of science vis-à-vis other activities (e.g., politics), and he commended Weber’s ideal-type methodology and his methodological individualism. Alexis Gros (2022) has provided a subtle analysis of how Schutz developed his own notion of this methodological individualism as a weak, partial, hermeneutical (and non-ontological) individualism that is not atomistic, reductionist, or subjectivist, but which is compatible with moderate ontological holism. In addition, Schutz applauded Weber’s refusal to reduce the social sciences to the natural sciences, while nevertheless providing for their ideal-typical results to be testable for adequacy. However, Schutz also supplemented Weber, pointing out how interpretation was involved at even the basic level at which one selects an experience out of one’s stream of experience, thereby giving meaning to it. One further highlights the meaning of an action to an actor by taking account of the project guiding the extended temporal process of the action and of all the sub-acts leading to the project’s realization.

These initial criticisms of Weber required Schutz to develop his own theory of meaning and action, beginning with Husserl’s study of the consciousness of internal time, in particular consciousness’s capacity to capture reflectively and distinguish lived experiences, which at first appear as undefined phases melting into each other. Schutz had appropriated this notion of flowing consciousness, or duration , from Bergson, on whom he had relied in the manuscripts later published in 1982 as Life Forms and Meaning Structure (LFMS, reprinted in CP6). Those manuscripts, for analytic purposes, split the ego, indivisible in its lived experience, into ideal-typical constructs of various life forms, that included the “I” as living in duration, remembering, acting, thinking, and relating to a “Thou”. Though Schutz never made explicit his reasons for not publishing those earlier manuscripts, Helmut Wagner (Wagner & Srubar 1984: 40–41, 101–104, 127) speculated that he was ill at ease since one could only have access to duration through acts of memory, which, of course, constituted a life-form entirely separate from duration itself. As a result of this methodology relying on distinct ideal-types, duration began to appear as an inaccessible Ding-an-sich . Husserl’s account of the consciousness of inner time remedied just this problem by carefully describing how the stream of duration was changed at every moment into a remembered having-just-been-thus , as the primal impression passed into primary remembrance, or retention. The continuum extending backward from the now of the primal impression through its retentions formed a “specious” present, to which reflective acts of secondary remembrance, that is, recollection or reproduction, turned, differentiating one experience from another. In sum, Husserl’s phenomenological description of experience uncovered the process of retention that bridged the duration/(reflective) memory gap that had bedeviled Schutz’s earlier efforts insofar as he had relied on an ideal-typical methodology that had isolated present duration from later memory.

Schutz, though, turned this Husserlian account of temporality in the direction of an action theory, demarcating levels of passive experience (e.g., bodily reflexes), spontaneous activity without a guiding project (e.g., acts of noticing environmental stimuli), and deliberately planned and projected activity, known technically as “action” (e.g., writing a book). In planning an action to be realized in the future, one relies on reflective acts of “projection”, like those found in reflective memory, only now oriented in a future as opposed to a past direction. Through such reflectivity, one imagines a project as completed in future perfect tense, that is, what will have been realized after one’s acting. Such a project, also of central importance for Martin Heidegger and the pragmatist tradition, establishes the “in-order-to motive” of one’s action. By contrast, one’s “because motives” consist in the environmental, historical factors that influenced the (now past) decision to embark upon the project and that can only be discovered by investigating in the “pluperfect tense”, that is, exploring those past factors that preceded that past decision.

Schutz’s distinctions here are relevant to contemporary debates about whether freedom is compatible with determinism since from the perspective of the lived in-order-to motive, one experiences oneself as free and morally responsible, but from the perspective of examining one’s because motives after completing one’s action, one correlates, as an observer of oneself, the choice of the project with its historical determinants. Of course, Schutz, working within the parameters of Husserl’s non-naturalistic account of consciousness, would have conceived such determinants not as empirico-mechanical causes but rather as influences discoverable through a backward-oriented interpretive process, associating earlier events with the later ones they seem to have motivated. Schutz’s position comes closest to the roughly compatibilist outlooks of P.F. Strawson and Thomas Nagel, who distinguish between the participant and observer attitudes prior to theoretical discussions and who align the participant attitude with freedom and the observer attitude with determinism. Schutz, however, contributes the unique insight that these attitudes take place within distinctive temporal frameworks, oriented toward the future or the past.

Schutz’s account of the temporal framework of motivation permitted criticism of Weber’s view that one could orient one’s action to the past behavior of others, since, while such behavior might have served as the because motive of one’s action, one could not aim via an in-order-to motive at affecting another’s already completed action. Similarly, failure to appreciate how temporality and motivation are intertwined often leads to misinterpretations of action, as when one assumes that the outcome of an act may have been its motive without considering the actor’s in-order-to motive, which due to unforeseen events may have had to have been adjusted in such a way as to lead to results, even contrary to those intended. Due to Schutz’s recognition that our well-designed projects may enter into a temporal process in interaction with other actors and produce unintended consequences, it is clear that he allowed for spontaneous social orders that some in the Austrian Economic School thought to be impossible within his framework, given his emphasis on planning future actions (Storr 2010a: 174). Likewise, one can mistakenly interpret an economic action after the fact as less than rational without taking sufficient account of the limited information that was available to the actor at the time of deciding to act and that could have rendered that decision at that time to be perfectly rational. Moreover, the fact that one’s own temporal stream of consciousness never completely coincides with that of another, whose sequence of events and intensity of experience inevitably differs from one’s own, places limits on one’s understanding of another. Consequently, the objective meanings of language, defined in dictionaries as invariant regardless of users, also bear subjective connotations for language users due to their unique histories of linguistic experience, even though for practical purposes of communication they are unable to focus on such differences. For instance, one would have to consider in depth Goethe’s works in their entirety to understand what he meant by “demonic” (Schutz 1932 [1967: 124]). Schutz’s basic point in these analyses involves getting behind constituted meanings to the temporal processes by which actors build up the meaning of their own actions—a meaningful build-up accentuated by the German title of his Phenomenology of the Social World ( Der sinnhafte Aufbau der sozialen Welt ).

The example of “demonic” in Goethe also points to Schutz’s view that everyday actors give meaning to their experiences, beginning at the fundamental level when they single out one experience from another, by apprehending experiences and objects through typifications. Typifications, such as classifications, categories, and patterns of action, systematically related to each other, socially transmitted, often unreflectively absorbed, and correlated to systems of ranked relevances (or values and interests)—pertain to one’s “stock of knowledge”. For instance, auto mechanics organize their worlds meaningfully in terms of typifications, such as “carburetors”, “lug nuts”, or “serpentine belts” and through typical behavioral patterns such as “diagnosing problems” or “wielding wrenches”—all at the service of some governing, socially acquired, relevance—here the in-order-to motive of repairing a dysfunctional automobile. Physicists and farmers, by contrast, operate with different interrelated systems of typifications and relevances, as do inhabitants of divergent life-worlds.

In addition to this account of consciousness, motivation, action, and meaning, Schutz examined the structure of the social world, including Consociates who share the same time and spatial access to each other’s bodies, Contemporaries with whom one shares only the same time, and Predecessors and Successors with whom one does not share the same time and to whose lived bodies one lacks access (Schutz 1932 [1967: 139–214]). Consociates, present to each other physically, partake of each other’s inner time, that is, the on-rolling life of the other, grasp the building up of the other’s experience, and live in a We-relationship that entails “growing older together”. While Consociates revise their types of each other immediately, one must proceed more inferentially with Contemporaries, Predecessors, and Successors, constructing ideal types based on letters or reports and running greater risks of misunderstanding, depending on the degree of anonymity of the person to be understood. One could say, then, that Weber’s method of ideal type construction, illustrated in his sociological account of the Protestant at the origins of capitalism, is not really that foreign to the everyday life-world in which actors beyond the Consociate level continually relate to each other via such type-constructions. Human actors in everyday life already adopt toward each other the attitudes of social scientists.

Schutz (1932 [1967: 44]) conceived his work as developing a “phenomenological psychology” of “inner experience” and focusing on the invariant features of the life-world toward which theoreticians, including social scientists, turn reflectively. According to him, social scientists develop constructs, ideal types, of the meaning-contexts of life-world actors, and they test these types to determine if they are causally adequate, that is, conforming to past experience, and meaning adequate, or, consistent with whatever else is known about the actor. Responding to Mises’s critique that Weber’s ideal-types are too historically specific, Schutz suggested that the later Weber’s ideal types in Economy and Society attain a generality comparable to that of Mises’ own economic theory, which itself could be interpreted as presenting ideal-typical descriptions of the behavior of economic agents. The later Weber’s types depict the invariant subjective experiences of anyone who acts within the economic framework as defined by the principle of marginal utility, that is, choosing to maximize satisfaction.

Several critics have charged that Schutz’s focus on a phenomenological psychology grounded in individual consciousness leaves him with an account of the life-world that is “abridged in a culturalistic fashion” and that is not able to take adequate accounts of institutional orders, personality structures, and the exercise of power (Habermas 1981 [1987: 2:138], see also 126–132). Schutz’s supposed subjectivist account is said to be “uncritical of society”, its objective reality, and the control that such objective reality exercises over subjectivity (Bauman 1976: 65, see 56–70; Bourdieu 1980 [1990: 25–26]). In defense of Schutz, Jochen Dreher and Daniela López (2015) argue that these critics have overlooked Schutz’s ideas of the imposed relevances, the pervasive intrusions in experience from social and ontological structures through which such structures reveal themselves and exercise power, such as the laws with which one is forced to comply or the inevitability of one’s own death. Everyday actors find themselves continually compelled to come to terms with such relevances (Barber 2024). In addition, the recent Phänomenologie und Kritische Theorie (Gros, Dreher, & Rosa [eds] 2026), containing essays from phenomenologists in the Schutzian tradition and Frankfurt School critical theorists (in the Habermas tradition), examines the critical potential of Schutzian phenomenology to affect such structures.

## 3. Extensions

### 3.1 The Bergson Writings

Schutz’s manuscripts on Bergson, produced from 1925 to 1927 and finally published in English in 1982 as Life Forms and Meaning Structure (LFMS), illuminate his subsequent works, with which they share the general purpose of “the grounding of the social sciences in the Thou experience” (LFMS [CP6: 40]). In reaction to positivistic approaches of the Schlick Circle (in which Felix Kaufmann participated) that reduced experience to what the method of natural scientific observation found acceptable, Schutz sought to give an account of the life-form of pre-scientific experience preceding conceptual-categorical comprehension, the “highest and most powerful life-form” (LFMS [CP6: 59]). Of course, by moving in this direction, he encountered the problem, faced by Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Wilfrid Sellars, John McDowell, Robert Brandom, and others, namely, how it is possible to access the pre-conceptual without conceptualizing it. Hence, he acknowledged that his work is “in conflict with its material” since it “is forced to resort to conceptual formulations” (LFMS [CP6: 76]). This problem parallels the problem of reaching the life-form of the present unfolding of experience (duration) since one can only speak of it by arresting its flow, distinguishing its moments, and thus remembering what has lapsed—but then one is in the new life-form of memory. Although this gap between present duration and memory prompted his turn to Husserlian phenomenology, the problematic itself highlighted for him the pervasiveness and hiddenness of interpretive activity as one moves between interpretive frameworks—a principal theme of all his later work. He took notice of this theme when he frequently pointed out how one’s reconstitution of a past experience in memory varied according to the interests of the present from which one remembered the past. Indeed, a favorite example from Bergson’s work involved an actor reflecting upon a prior process of choosing and interpreting it as if it had been a choice between two clearly defined possibilities, whereas in fact the process often oscillated between several options, retaining, reproducing, comparing, and modifying them in succession (Schutz 1932 [1967: 66–69]). In general, Schutz concurred with Bergson on such notions as attention to life, planes of consciousness, the body as the intersection of outer and inner temporality, music as the model of duration, and multiple types of ordering, but rejected his bio-evolutionary theory, vitalism, and the idea of a supra-personal elán.

### 3.2 The Social Sciences

Although Schutz defended Weber against Mises, he agreed with many basic premises of Mises and the Austrian School of Economics that succeeded Mises and that focused on the subjective preferences of the purchaser conferring value on objects instead of explaining value as the result of objective processes such as production costs or labor time invested. He also shared Mises’s suppositions about value-freedom in economic science, the need to describe rather than evaluate preferences, and the instrumental task of science, namely, of showing how to achieve ends rather than assessing their value. Since Mises considered all acting economic insofar as any consumer choice involved maximizing satisfaction in the widest sense, he opposed the narrow type of the Homo economicus , modeled on the businessperson driven solely by economic motives at the expense of all others. While Schutz posited the life-world with its wide diversity of motivations at the base of economic theory, he conceived that theory as adopting a reflective, scientific perspective governed by the principle of marginal utility, namely, that ideal types ought to be constructed as if all actors “had oriented their life-plans to realize the greatest utility with minimal cost” (1943 [CP2: 87]). Besides thus resuscitating a version of Homo economicus , Schutz insisted that economists study purposive-rational actions, which, in Weber’s sense, involved a reflective comparison of alternative projects before adopting one as one’s in-order-to motive. In addition, he classified the sense of uneasiness that Mises described as prompting the search for satisfaction under the category of because motives; one first adopts a rationally determined economic project and in retrospect discovers such a preceding, (because)-motivating dissatisfaction. To understand the difference between conceiving all action as economic and conceiving economic action as one type of action within an more encompassing life-world, one might compare Mises with Schutz with reference to a problem raised within contemporary discussions of collective action, namely, how traditional non-economic values (e.g., those of politics or ethics) ought to intersect the market. Mises would contend that, when actors decide whether to purchase or not (e.g., as a protest against polluting companies), they simply register their values economically as they do in every other economic commitment they make—all values then become economic values. Schutz, by contrast, would call for a process negotiating the boundaries between different life-world value domains, such as those of economic or politics (Schutz 1932 [1967: 242–246]; Schutz 1930, 1934, 1936 [CP4: 84–105]).The Austrian School of Economics continues to utilize Schutz’s work as foundational, though recent members of the school have explored basing their work on Gadamerian and Ricoeurian hermeneutical approaches (López 2016; Storr 2010a).

In “Concept and Theory Formation in the Social Sciences”, Schutz (1953 [CP1: 48–66]) addressed the broader issue of the relationship between philosophy and the social sciences. In that essay, he responded to Ernest Nagel’s positivistic view that the social sciences should make use of natural scientific methods, identifying evidence with sensory observable data and criticizing the Weberian method of “understanding” as appealing to uncontrollable and unverifiable introspection. Schutz agreed with Nagel on several counts, namely that social scientists needed to validate theoretical beliefs, that lack of predictability in the social sciences did not disqualify their scientific character, and that Weber would have been wrong if his method of “subjective interpretation” implied empathy with unobservable, introspective states. The problem was, though, that the natural scientific approach to the social sciences, insofar as it separated verifiable observable behavior from unverifiable inner states (purposes, emotions), seemed to play on the map drawn by Descartes who divorced body from mind and allowed only statements about the former to be scientifically verifiable. Further, the natural scientific approach depended on a basic presupposition since without first examining the object of social science—social reality, in Schutz’s terms—one would be simply presupposing that the methods of the natural sciences were appropriate to its study. Therefore, Schutz attempted first to clarify social reality, described in depth by his own phenomenology of the social world, and to indicate how actors sustain that reality by understanding quite successfully each other’s in-order-to motives in typical terms (e.g., going to school, making a purchase, marrying). Such mutual understanding takes place without somehow or other either penetrating the other’s private, inner sanctum, or reducing the other to the status of animal organism responding to stimuli. Given this account of social reality, in which actors give meaning to their world, as opposed to physical reality whose objects (e.g., electrons, quarks) do not interpret their world, Schutz argued that the appropriate social-scientific method involved developing constructs of everyday actor’s constructs. Social scientific constructs, ideal types in Weber’s sense, aimed at reaching not some introspectively given inner occurrences but the meaning of the actor as opposed to that of the social scientist. In addition, while Schutz conceived statistical and other formulations of social scientific laws as a legitimate kind of intellectual shorthand, they always presuppose the meaningful activity of the individual social actor, the “forgotten man” of the social sciences (1960 [CP2: 6–7]). To ensure the kind of validation that Nagel sought, mistakenly though, by restricting himself to sensory observable data, Schutz proposed that social scientists displace their everyday practical interests in favor of a guiding interest in accurate scientific description, observe the postulates of logical consistency and adequacy to the whatever experiences are described, and test their findings in the intersubjective community of scientists.

In order to elucidate the meaning of rational action, Schutz hypothesized what a rational actor would have to know, even though such completely rational actions might never be realized in everyday life. Such an actor would have to know: an end’s relationship with other ends, the consequences and by-products of realizing an end, the means suitable for the end, the interaction of such means with other ends and means, and the accessibility of those means. In addition, the rational actor would need to understand: her interactors’ understanding of all the previous factors, the interpretation of her act by others, the reactions of other people and their motivation, and the useful categories she had already discovered in the social world. Although social scientists might use such models of completely rational action to assess the rationality of everyday actors, Schutz cautioned social scientists that if their task were to describe life-world actors, they also needed to be wary of replacing the viewpoint of everyday actors with a fictional, non-existing world constructed by scientific observers (1943 [CP2: 64–88]). In fact, a central point of discussion in the published correspondence between Schutz and Talcott Parsons concerned the subjective viewpoint of the actor, whose sub-acts, for example, could not be adequately understood without comprehending the actor’s overarching project, whose temporal span is at first accessible only to that actor (C-Parsons). Finally, it should be noted that Schutz (1944, 1945a, 1946 [CP2: 91–134]) produced three pieces of applied research in which he constructed ideal types of the Stranger, the Homecomer, and The Well-Informed Citizen, taking account of what their experiences meant to them instead of what social scientists or others, disregarding their point of view, might think they meant.

The Schutz/Parsons correspondence has given birth to debates about whether social science ought to focus on the meaning of individual actors (subjectivism) or institutional structures (objectivism) (Schwinn 1993). Insofar as Schutz’s account of the structure of the social world builds out from face-to-face relationships to include links with individual Contemporaries, Predecessors, and Successors, it might seem to focus at most on dyads or small groups and to neglect social institutions, as Habermas and Bourdieu have charged (Bourdieu 1989: 18–19). Recent research in phenomenology in the Schutzian style might seem to be confirming that criticism insofar as it has focused on “small life-worlds” (B. Luckmann 1970; M. Pfadenhauer 2023). However, one might take Schutz’s acknowledgment of the legitimacy of social scientific research, which, in addition to constructing types of individual actors, also deals with curves, mathematical functions, and institutions such as bank systems or currency, as indicating his appreciation of the importance of encompassing social structures (1943 [CP2: 84]). Taking another tack, Martin Endress (2005) has charged Bourdieu with not sufficiently acknowledging his own usage of phenomenology, the resources it offers for self-reflectivity, and the continued value of making a place for subjectivity in social scientific analyses.

In addition, the reduction of the themes of this entire conversation to only two possibilities: individuals and small groups or larger groups and institutions, has been problematized through the many viewpoints expressed in The Palgrave Handbook of Macrophenomenology and Social Theory (Belvedere & Gros [eds] 2023). The authors of this collection consider, among other things, the possibility of a Schutzian macro-phenomenology in terms of how institutions and large groups are experienced, for instance, as lying anonymously on the horizons of what is materially perceived. In this approach, classes, for instance, are appresented via symbolic references (clothing, language, etc.), and social groups pertain, as ideal rather than material objects, to the world of Contemporaries beyond the face-to-face relationship.

### 3.3 Other Philosophies

Although references to philosophers in the pragmatist tradition, such as John Dewey and George Herbert Mead, are scattered through Schutz’s writings, it was to William James (Schutz 1941 [CP3: 1–14]) that he devoted his first full-length essay after arriving in the United States. Briefly alluding to the methodological differences between Husserl and James, he emphasized two points where the “great masters” converged: the stream of thought and the theory of fringes. Both thinkers stressed that personal consciousness involves no multiplicity of elements needing to be reunited, but rather a unity from which one separates out components, and both examined the modifications that reflection introduces into the lived stream, converting an “I” into a “Me” or uncovering the workings of intentionality. Further, Husserl’s idea that the kernel of meaning distinguishing an object stood out against the unthematized network of relationships that makes up its horizon paralleled James’s belief that topics have their “fringes”. Such fringes connect a topic with other experiences, such that, for instance, one does not hear merely “thunder”, but “thunder-breaking-in-upon-silence-and-contrasting-with-it”. Similarly, the Jamesian idea about grasping as a unity what must be learned through a multi-stepped process, such as the Pythagorean theorem, could be translated into the Husserlian terminology regarding the monothetical grasping of polythetic processes. Likewise, James’s discussion of focusing on an object within a broader topic resembled Husserl’s view that one could discern a noema, that is, a perspectival aspect, through which a thing, constituted of many such aspects, presented itself.

Another American philosopher to whom Schutz (1952 [CP2: 201–225]) dedicated an entire essay was George Santayana, whose Dominations and Powers he reviewed. While most of the essay was expository, Schutz praised Santayana’s effort to base politics on a philosophical anthropology and his insights into the enslaving potential of technology. However, Schutz, no doubt convinced by Mises’s positive assessment of economic activity, resisted Santayana’s reduction of it to domination. Likewise, as a phenomenologist opposed to Santayana’s naturalistic founding of spirit on the physical order of nature, Schutz dissented from a conviction derived from this naturalism, namely, that democracy could solve its problems only by returning to the “generative order” of agriculture.

Besides these interchanges with American philosophers, Schutz interpreted the work of Max Scheler (Schutz 1956b [CP3: 133–144], 1957 & 1958 [CP3: 145–178]) and engaged thoroughly his treatment of intersubjectivity (1942 [CP1: 150–179]), a topic that Schutz insisted was to be treated within the natural attitude, in which one never doubted the existence of others. Schutz agreed with Scheler’s belief that the “We” is given prior to the “I”—a position that the latter defended on the basis of the psychology of children and cultures less accustomed to self-reflection. Schutz supported this priority, however, on the grounds that while living in one’s acts in the natural attitude and living also in the other’s present experience as it unfolds, one at first does not clearly distinguish one’s own thoughts from others’. Nevertheless, as soon as one reflects on one’s own stream of consciousness—and children and cultures may develop this capacity for self-reflection later—one becomes aware that one’s experiences are one’s own. Schutz found plausible Scheler’s belief in the inner (indubitable) perception of the other’s existence, if “inner perception” refers to objects of psychic or mental life and if one situates the experience of the other as taking place within the vivid simultaneity of the “We”, as Schutz believed possible. However much one dwelling in that vivid simultaneity might be unable to doubt the other’s existence, one could still be mistaken about specific thoughts of the others, since by belonging to the other’s stream of consciousness these thoughts share the dubitability characterizing outer perceptions, likewise transcendent to one’s stream of experience.

Another figure, more or less within the phenomenological tradition, whose views on intersubjectivity Schutz (1948a [CP1: 180–203]) examined and criticized, was Jean-Paul Sartre, particularly the Sartre of Being and Nothingness . In “Sartre’s Theory of the Alter Ego”, Schutz elucidated Sartre’s attempt to develop an extra-empirical, real communication with the other that avoids the extremes of an empiricist intersubjectivity beginning with the other’s body and an idealist reduction of the other to a series of presentations. After explaining Sartre’s differences regarding intersubjectivity with Husserl, Hegel, and Heidegger, Schutz laid out Sartre’s existential account of how the other is given as a subject through the “Look” and how one can in turn objectify the other by returning the gaze. Although Sartre had intended to describe how one’s body is given to the other, he instead portrayed how the other’s body is given to oneself, assuming that such descriptions were reversible. Schutz, who did not believe that the problem of intersubjectivity could be addressed adequately within the transcendental sphere, applauded Sartre’s rejection of Husserl’s transcendental approach to intersubjectivity. The main problem, though, with Sartre’s doctrine was that its starting point in a mutual looking, by which each subject reduces the other to an object, precluded any possibility of a relationship between the I-subject and other-subject. Further, Schutz wondered how Sartre would know that the other’s body was given to other in the same way that one’s own body was given to oneself since the other’s subjectivity escaped one’s “I”. Moreover, Schutz acknowledged that the other’s interests might not coincide with one’s own, but he failed to see how this fact entailed that either the other or oneself reduce each other to a utensil. Instead, he pointed to the “mutual tuning-in” to be found in making music together and in language as proof that subjects interact as “co-performing subjectivities” and that mutual interaction in freedom better describes intersubjectivity than Sartre’s practical solipsism.

### 3.4 Applications

Schutz (1945b [CP1: 207–259]) published an essay, “On Multiple Realities”, that extended the theory of The Phenomenology of the Social World and anticipated later essays. While he reiterated earlier views about levels of activity (e.g., passive behavior, spontaneous action, and long-term planned action), Bergsonian tensions of consciousness, and the structure of the social world, he brought to the fore his pragmatic understanding of everyday life, especially through the idea of “working” ( Wirken ), which involves involving bodily movements gearing into the world to practically transform it, as opposed to the covert performances of mere thinking. In manuscripts in the 1930s and after The Phenomenology of the Social World , Schutz had already turned in this pragmatic direction. In “On Multiple Realities”, he amplified on this “world of working” by demonstrating how there we operate with a unified self in lived action, but when we reflect or enter another “province of meaning,” the unified self dissolves into different, partial, role-taking selves. Schutz also included in his understanding of everyday life Mead’s idea of the “manipulatory sphere” to include worlds within “potential reach” in nearby space or present time, within restorable reach (from the past) through locomotion to past sites or memory (of past events), or within attainable (in the future) reach in space or time. This “world of working” constitutes the paramount reality, organized in its interests in the face of the fundamental anxiety that derives, as it did for Heidegger, from the inescapability of one’s own death. Following Husserl’s views on how consciousness can modify its stances toward reality and de-ontologizing James’s sub-universes of reality, Schutz developed the notion of various finite provinces of meaning. One enters any of these provinces, such as those of phantasms, dreams, the theater, religious experience, or theoretical contemplation, by undergoing different types of epoché , analogous to the phenomenological prototype, as when one slips into a daydream, falls asleep, watches theater curtains open, commences a ritual, or assumes the scientist’s role. Each province contains its distinctive logical, temporal, corporal, and social dimensions, and the movement between the provinces only becomes paradoxical (e.g., asking how phenomenologists are able to communicate their private findings publicly or how one can communicate indirectly with others about the contents of one’s dreams) if one conceives the provinces as ontological static realms to which one would have to transmigrate as a soul passing to another world. Rather the provinces are permeable, and one can move between several of them in a single hour, and, also, one adopts the attitudes of scientist or religious believer within the world of working as if it were being seen through by another viewpoint, all the while that working’s bodily communicative activities subtend these other provinces. Som ething remains paradoxical, though, about describing one’s dreams or theorizing about religious experience since to give an account one must absent oneself from the province of which one seeks to give an account. Kierkegaard’s notion of indirect communication and various postmodern critiques of theory address themselves to just such paradoxes.

The essay on multiple realities underpins Schutz’s theory of signs and symbols in “Symbol, Reality, and Society” (1955 [CP1: 287–349]). Synthesizing the notion of potential reach from the earlier essay with Husserl’s concept of appresentation , namely the idea that one element of a pair refers to another not directly given in experience, as the front of a house appresents its backside, Schutz describes how agents overcome whatever transcends them. Hence, they leave marks to bring within reach what they leave behind and will need to recover later (e.g., breaking a twig to remind oneself to turn when one returns); or they follow indications , that is, regular connections that they do not produce but that are found (e.g., smoke indicating a distant but not yet visible fire), and in this way they bring within their knowledge what lies beyond it. Signs , however, appresent in an intersubjective setting the meanings of one person to another, but an insuperable transcendence remains insofar as each one’s stream of consciousness and therefore meanings are never identical with another’s. Finally, through symbols , developed within groups, something given within everyday reality appresents a reality belonging to a entirely different province of meaning, such as an ultimate transcendence (e.g., the stone where Jacob dreamed of a ladder to heaven memorializes God, accessible within the religious province of meaning) or a vast object not able to be encompassed (e.g., the flag standing for a whole nation).

Schutz (1950 [CP1: 260–286]) dealt with the theme of language in other contexts, comparing Husserl’s distinction between pre-predicative (pre-propositional) and predicative levels with Kurt Goldstein’s separation, based on studies of brain lesions, of a concrete attitude relying on automatic speech associations from an abstract attitude forming propositions and utilizing rational language. Husserl’s pre-predicative/predicative differentiation plays a key role in Schutz’s essay “Type and Eidos in Husserl’s Late Philosophy”, in which he (1959b [CP3: 92–115]) shows a gradual development from empirical types passively constituted within the pre-predicative sphere to presumptive universals spontaneously formed in the predicative sphere. At the predicative level, scientific reflection further transforms nonessential types (e.g., that whales are fish) into essential ones (whales are mammals), and philosophy goes further by seeking to determine eidetic universals. At the end of this essay, Schutz speculates about whether the Husserlian method of freely varying examples to determine the essential features that survive through such variations is not constrained by both ontological structures (e.g., sounds are not colors) and the socially shaped, natural-attitude experience of types. In his essay “Tiresias, or our Knowledge of Future Events”, produced contemporaneously with the essay on types, Schutz (1959a [CP2: 277–293]) explains how knowledge based on natural attitude types functions in contrast to the mythical Tiresias’ knowledge of the future, which is private and detached from his present or past experience. These types, based on past experiences or socially transmitted, aim at future occurrences not in their uniqueness but with an emptiness that future events will fill in, such that only in retrospect, after an event occurs, is one able to determine how much that event was expected or unexpected. Finally, there are future events lying beyond one’s influence that one expects only to conform with past experience, and there are indeterminate projects that provide direction—not too tightly, though—as one gives shape to what is within one’s power.

Schutz, himself a trained pianist, integrated his phenomenology with his understanding of music (1951 [CP2: 159–178]). Music, differing from language in being non-representative, lends itself to phenomenological analysis in the meaning it carries beyond its mere physical nature as sound waves and in its character as an ideal object that must be constituted through its unfolding stages, i.e., polythetically. Further music is bound to inner temporality, and its themes, even though their note sequences are the same, vary according to context, require reflection for their recognition, and emerge through an interplay between musical elements and the listener’s attention and interest. Schutz (1951 [CP2: 177]) found music instructive regarding social relationships insofar as, prior to any communication, parties to musical performances establish a non-linguistic, non-conceptual “mutual tuning in relationship”. This “tuning-in”, this sharing of another’s flux of experience in inner time already described in his Phenomenology , is very clearly exhibited whenever a listener to a musical performance participates in quasi-simultaneity in the composer’s stream of consciousness or when co-performers orient themselves to each other, the composer, and their audience. Hence, Schutz disagreed with Maurice Halbwachs who posited musical notation as the basis of social relationships between performers, when in fact it is merely a technical device accidental to their relationship. In another essay, Schutz (1956a [CP2: 179–200]) depicted Mozart as a social scientist, presenting a succession of situations that different characters interpret, and Schutz showed how orchestral representations of characters and their moods in melody made possible a simultaneity of fluxes of inner time that the non-operatic, non-musical dramatist can only unfold successively. Without self-consciously philosophizing, Mozart conveyed in music and better than most philosophers in their own medium, how human beings meet each other as a “We”.

Fred Kersten (1976) discovered in Schutz’s musical writings important philosophical insights. For instance, music and inner time unfold polythetically and cannot be grasped monothetically; that is, one must live through the unfolding of a symphony or musical inner experience, and any conceptual summary of their contents inevitably fails to do justice to their meaning. However, since all conceptualization consists in a monothetical grasping of polythetic stages, Schutz’s work points to the fact that certain dimensions of consciousness elude conceptualization; and he thus demarcates the limits of rationalization, just as he had pointed out how certain provinces of meaning (e.g., dreams) evade theoretical comprehension or duration eludes memory. According to Kersten, Schutz has seen clearly that the passive associations of listening (e.g., recognizing the appearance of symphonic themes) differ from those of sight (e.g., apprehending an object like a house), with the result that listening does not identify numerically distinct items but produces an illusion of identification. Schutz’s conclusion that sameness in music involves not numerical unity but recurrent likeness challenges the fundamental Husserlian thesis that the synthesis of spatially distinct objects through passive identification lies at the basis of the constitution of the world is universal.

Schutz was also a master of literature, a careful student of the works of Goethe (Schutz 1948b [CP6: 311–405]), and the author of an article that analyzed Miguel de Cervantes’s Don Quixote through the prism of the theory of multiple realities (Schutz 1954 [CP2: 135–158]). Cervantes repeatedly brings Quixote’s “world of chivalry”—an order of reality with its arguments for its own reality, its system of knowledge, modes of social reinforcement, and views about space, time, and causality—into conflict with the worlds of drama, common sense, and science. Although Quixote can construct a defense of his own chivalrous world from within the province of meaning of phantasy that he inhabits, the fact that this phantasied world contains within it an enclave of dreams (at the cave of Montesinos) ends up undermining itself by raising the possibility that it itself is but a dream. Quixote’s final withdrawal of the accent of reality from his private province of meaning reveals for Schutz the importance of the paramount reality of everyday life and the importance of someone like Sancho Panza who “remains deeply rooted in the heritage of common sense” (Schutz 1954 [CP2: 158]).

Schutz also brought his phenomenology to bear on political issues such as citizenship or racial equality. His essay “The Well-Informed Citizen” (1946 [CP2: 120–134]), dealing not only with citizenship but also the sociology of knowledge under the rubric of the social distribution of knowledge, constructs ideal types of the expert, the man on the street, and the well-informed citizen (to whom it falls to determine which experts are competent). Schutz delineates various zones of relevances, extending from those within reach to those absolutely irrelevant; comments on the constant changeability of relevance configurations; and differentiates between relevances intrinsic to a theme, which one chooses, and those imposed. Paradoxically, as modernity’s rationalization processes heighten anonymity, modern technology also brings everyone within reach of each other, as the nuclear arms race demonstrates. Schutz suggests as a solution to problems of this type that citizens become broadly informed rather than succumb to the narrow dogmatism of the man on the street or the short-sighted specialization of experts. In becoming well-informed, one depends on knowledge socially derived through the consultation of eyewitnesses, insiders, analysts, and commentators, depending on their access to facts and governing relevances, much as Alvin Goldman’s social epistemology (Goldman 1999: 87) involves appraising the ’veritistic’ value of assorted agents’ claims and practices. Schutz, usually the value-free describer of social reality, in his conclusion endorses a normative notion of democracy in which it is a duty and a privilege, frequently not available in non-democratic societies, for well-informed citizens to express and defend opinions that often conflict with the uninformed opinions of the man in the street.

Schutz composed “Equality and the Meaning Structure of the Social World” (Schutz 1957b [CP2: 226–273]) at the time of the legal decision of Brown v. Board of Education that ended racially segregated education in the United States. With typical dispassion, Schutz explains how the meaning of the term “equality” depends on the domain of relevances to which it pertains (e.g., economic equality, equality of civil rights, etc.) and on the in-group or out-group utilizing it—and here he conceives interpretation in terms of groups rather than individuals. He spends most of the essay contrasting subjective and objective interpretations of group membership, equality, and equality of opportunity, construing “subjective” and “objective” in terms of in-group and out-group interpretations. As regards group membership, he illustrates that the mere categorization of another as a member of a group need not be discriminatory but depends upon an appropriate evaluation of the category from the viewpoint of the afflicted individual. In-groups and out-groups differ in whether they understand equality merely as “formal”, i.e., as nondiscrimination, or “real”, calling for special rights and services. Similarly, groups think of equality of opportunity from an out-group perspective as “the career open to all” without appreciating how in-group members might subjectively experience insuperable obstacles in trying to avail themselves of opportunities supposedly objectively equal. In this essay, Schutz is concerned not to present a final definition of equality, but to highlight the differences between in-group and out-group understandings that serve as the preconditions of any discussion about it.

Some recently published texts (1999) that Schutz authored during an ethics institute in 1956 make possible an even richer awareness of his views on politics. In these documents, he recognizes the complex, unforeseen consequences resulting from social change, urges active engagement with others as crucial for developing social and civil judgment, and examines the barriers to sound civil judgment created by government, political parties, pressure organizations, mass media, and educational, familial, religious, and professional institutions. At one point, he even criticizes views that limit democracy to mere majoritarian rule insofar as they neglect the importance of the single individual’s ability “to make his personal opinion be heard and appreciated”, preferably in smaller publics, such as families, schools, local communities (Schutz 1999: 271). One could take Schutz’s thoughts here to converge with political theories favoring what is today known as deliber ative democracy. Moreover, his normative judgment against implementations of democracy that increase the anonymity of citizens suggests that a parallel normative, even ethical, framework, may be informing his many theoretic endeavors to retrieve from anonymity the neglected subjective viewpoint of actors, whether strangers, homecomers, victims of discrimination, or the “forgotten man” of social sciences.

### 3.5 Phenomenology

Schutz’s philosophical concentration on the social world had its repercussions upon his understanding of phenomenology, which appeared in his critique near the end of his career of Husserl’s account (also referred to as a “transcendental constitution”) of how the other person comes to appearance in consciousness. In “The Problem of Transcendental Intersubjectivity in Husserl”, Schutz (1957a [CP3: 51–91]) begins his criticism at the point at which Husserl in his Fifth Cartesian Mediation prepared the ground for the other’s appearance in consciousness by the methodology of screening off everything that referred to other minds. Husserl had begun his Cartesian Meditations by reflectively abstaining from believing in the existence of what appeared in experience to ensure that he might gain a maximal freedom from injecting unexamined, dogmatic suppositions into the discussion. But since this first epoché , or phenomenological reduction, still left meanings that referred to lived intersubjective relationships and that might be carrying unscrutinized presuppositions about the relationships with others whose constitution he was trying to explicate, this screening-off methodology, or second epoché , became necessary. For Husserl, one’s actual or potential experiences of correlates that were not properly of the ego could be said to belong the sphere of ownness he was striving to reach, but one had to seek to exclude any reference to those correlates themselves, as products of the sense-determining of other subjectivities. For Schutz, however, insofar as these experiences, which belonged to one’s sphere of ownness, had their origin in the intersubjective world of everyday life, it seemed that the higher-level phenomenological reflection, initiated by the second epoché , could not help presupposing those correlates, which referred to the sense-determining of other subjectivities. It was as though Husserl was striving for a theoretical detachment that the origins of his theory in everyday life would not allow. In addition, for Schutz the very consciousness of another inevitably instituted a relationship with him or her. Husserl’s argument in the Fifth Meditation continued by affirming that a non-ratiocinative “pairing” occurred through which one transferred the sense “another living body” to the other’s body, like one’s own and paired with it. One could then go on to verify that the other’s body was like one’s own if it continued manifesting behavior congruent with what one would expect from a living body. Schutz challenged this sense-transfer, however, since one’s experience of the other always involved experiencing the other’s body from the outside and never from the inside as one would experience one’s own body—thereby blocking the sense-transfer to a body that really could not be given like one’s own. Furthermore, the verification through behavior which was taken to be congruent with that expected of a lived body would have to draw on social-world presuppositions of how bodies ought to behave and would have to depend on what was already supposed to have been excluded. Finally, he questioned whether the philosopher, refraining from belief in the existence of the world or others and entering into a certain reflective solitude, could ever experience the transcendental community of which Husserl spoke, since one would be able to experience only the world constituted for oneself and not for all other transcendental egos. Intersubjectivity, Schutz concluded, was a matter of everyday life to be simply described and not to be constituted within the transcendental sphere of a self-reflective consciousness giving an account of how the other comes to appearance. Just as Schutz had argued that the social world dictated the methods for its own social scientific investigation, so here it seemed to prescribe to phenomenology the approach appropriate to its description. Schutz’s criticisms of Husserl have not, however, gone unquestioned (Kersten 2010; Barber 2013)

In the last thirteen years of his life, Schutz was preparing a comprehensive phenomenology of the natural attitude, and one manuscript, edited by Richard Zaner, was posthumously published as Reflections on the Problem of Relevance (Schutz 1970b), and another, co-authored by Thomas Luckmann, appeared as The Structures of the Life World (SL). The former book distinguishes different sets of interests, or relevances: topical (which focus attention on a theme), interpretive (through which subjects are led to confer meanings on experiences or through which objects are able to solicit subject’s attention to them), and motivational (in-order-to and because motives). Such relevances often involve a subject, with more or less systematized relevances, interacting with the world, and from this interaction between subject and world, it becomes evident what is “of relevance” to an actor. Such relevances, interdependent on each other and conjoined with one’s system of typifications, constitute one’s stock of knowledge, which Schutz examines in terms of its genesis and structure. He further explores relevances in terms of what is of value one due to one’s biographical situation, including one’s types and relevances; one’s body; and the ontological constraints of space and time that, for instance, prevent one from being at certain places at certain times or compel one to wait (for salt to dissolve in water).

The Structures of the Life-World represents a complex and thorough restatement of many of the themes Schutz addressed throughout his life. After a more general account of the life-world and its relation to the sciences, the book takes up its various stratifications, such as provinces of meaning, temporal and spatial zones of reach, and social structures. Schutz and Luckmann then comment on the components of one’s stock of knowledge, including learned and innate elements and relevances and typifications, and they the trace genesis of such a stock. The authors further study the social conditioning of one’s subjective stock of knowledge and inquire about the social stock of knowledge of a group and the different possible combinations of knowledge distribution (generalized and specialized). They consider how subjective knowledge becomes embodied, in turn, in a social stock of knowledge. In addition, the authors pursue such issues as the structures of consciousness and action, the choosing of projects, rational action, and forms of social action, whether such action be unilateral or reciprocal, immediate or mediate. A final section analyzes the boundaries of experience, different degrees of transcendencies (from simply bringing a perceptual object within reach to the experience of death), and the mechanisms for crossing boundaries (e.g., symbols).

## 4. The Schutzian Tradition

In the immediate aftermath of Schutz’s life, a number of scholars developed his thought in different directions. While John O’Neill (1974) fused Schutz’s perspective with that of Merleau-Ponty by focusing on the lived, communicative body, Richard Grathoff (1989) investigated the experience of normality within the bounded and situated context of a milieu. Ilja Srubar (1988, 2007, 2019) explored the pragmatic dimensions of Schutz’s thought and several of its symbolic, economic, and political implications, and Hans-Georg Soeffner (1992 [1997]), along with Jochen Dreher (2003), articulated the importance of Schutz’s work for understanding symbolism. Following Schutz, Lester Embree (2015) has worked out a typology of the cultural sciences after the fashion of Wissenschaftslehre , while Fred Kersten (1976) provided insightful commentary on Schutz’s theory of music and Maurice Natanson (1986, 1998) fashioned theories of literature and anonymization based on Schutz’s corpus. Several other scholars worldwide have dedicated themselves to Schutz’s work and to the development of his insights, and Germany, Japan, and the United States are home to archives containing Schutz’s work and correspondence.

A major decades-long division emerged among Schutz’s successors that Thomas Eberle (1993) documents in his essay, “Schütz’s Analysis of the Lebenswelt : Sociology or Protosociology?” In that essay, Eberle demonstrates how Thomas Luckmann, on the one hand, emphasized subtle epistemological distinctions between Schutz’s phenomenology, as an eidetic phenomenological approach (a protosociology), and empirical sociology. On the other hand, a counter-position took shape among a group of thinkers who represent a “phenomenological sociology” that focused on the processes by which everyday actors themselves (and not sociologists) build their own worlds of meaning, the understanding of which could be imperiled by abstract theoretical and methodological concerns. This second group took its starting point in the “ethnomethodology” of Harold Garfinkel (1967), who took up the Schutzian side of the Schutz/Parsons debate and who was followed by George Psathas (1989), who himself drew on Erwin Goffman (1959), and, beyond ethnomethodology, also originated the field of conversation analysis (Psathas 1995).

Challenges, however, have been raised to both these trends. On the one hand, Garfinkel (1967) and Knoblauch (2020) object to Luckmann’s protosociological interpretation of the Schutzian tradition since it seems to espouse as its foundation a phenomenological “egology”, that is, a view of a pure ego as isolated from social conditioning and yet serving as the starting point from which the world is to be deduced. Perhaps, though, Schutz conceived individual consciousness as a stratum analytically distinguishable within, but never appearing apart from, the entirety of the social world; hence Schutz described his phenomenology of the social world as a meaningful Aufbau , alike, but different from, Rudolf Carnap’s (logical) Aufbau . Additionally, critics (Göttlich 2008; Knoblauch 2020) have questioned how it can be claimed that the Schutzian/Luckmannian structures of the social world are universal and eidetic, when the social conditioning and relativization of all cognition is so widely recognized by the very social sciences that those structures were intended to found. One must be wary, though, of succumbing to the genetic fallacy that might argue that the origins of a thought undermine its validity. Moreover, Husserl (1950, 2001), although he acknowledged the social/genetic conditions of claims to truth, did not think that such conditioning ruled out the validity attainable when intentionally-oriented propositions are fulfilled.

On the other hand, questions have been raised of the phenomenological sociological track of the Schutz tradition. The recent practices of social scientists in the style of Schutz have engaged in forms of ethnography, which, while recognizing the need to understand everyday actors adequately as the ethnomethodologists required, does not preclude social scientists from aiming at the same time at social scientific validity. For instance, ethnographers such as Anne Honer and Ronald Hitzler (2015) recommend that researchers become participants in the activities of those they investigate to ensure adequacy of understanding, even as they strive to maintain their role as social scientists. Such observer-participants become, according to Michaela Pfadenhauer and Tilo Grenz (2015), strangers and wanderers between the worlds of social science and everyday life. This rift and reconciliation regarding the values of adequacy of understanding and validity represent a tension that Lester Embree (2015) highlighted in his The Schutzian Theory of the Cultural Sciences .

Beyond these debates in the Schutzian tradition, what is impressive is the manifold areas in which Schutz’s framework has been fruitfully applied. This can been by considering the three major collections published to commemorate the passing of Thomas Luckmann and celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of The Social Construction of Reality: Social Constructivism as Paradigm? , Lebenswelttheorie und Gesellschaftsanalyse , and Mathesis Universalis . While these volumes focus on Luckmann’s work, including The Structures of the Life-World , several of the essays make manifest the many domains in which Schutz’s thought has been expanded by treating: the objective dimensions of societal institutions in contrast to interpretations that construed Schutz’s perspective as depending only on subjective processes and overlooking the operation of institutional power (Eberle 2019, Knoblauch 2019, Mijić 2018, Srubar 2019); the possibility of a “communicative” construction of reality (Knoblauch 2019); the Schutzian paradigm’s preservation of agents’ potential to resist societal control in contrast to Bourdieu’s account of habitus (Dreher 2019); the role of the body in We-relationships (Meyer 2018); the capacity of the Schutzian framework to account for resilience in the face of trauma (Endress 2021); inequality as an imposed relevance (López 2021); space and bodiliness as pertinent to the life-world as a protosociology (Mijić 2018, Dörfler & Rothfuss 2021, Steets 2021); degrees of freedom within Schutz’s relevance theory (Göttlich 2021); linkages between Schutz’s phenomenology and recent representatives of the Frankfurt School, such as Hartmut Rosa (Gros 2021, Wannenmacher 2021); and the role of the life-world as a mathesis universalis , that is, the ground-structure of all human experience that makes possible any comparison between cultures without reliance on the specific features of any one culture (Dreher 2021, Meyer 2021, Sebald 2009).

Apart from papers appearing in these volumes commemorating Luckmann, several authors have deepened the understanding of Schutz’s work and opened new vistas. For instance, sociologists Hubert Knoblauch (2013) and Carlos Belvedere (2017) have shown the relevance of Schutz’s framework to communication theory and questions of social ontology, respectively. Michael Staudigl and George Berguno (2014) have edited a collection of essays on the connection between the Schutzian approach and various hermeneutic traditions. Staudigl (2017) and Michael Barber (2017, 2024) have highlighted the connections between Schutz’s philosophy of multiple realities and such topics as religious/spiritual experience and humor. A collection of essays has explored the value of Schutz’s paradigm for music, literature, and the arts (Barber & Dreher 2014). Authors have also been envisioning the potential of Schutz’s theory of the social world and multiple realities for coming to terms with the digitalization and mediatization of everyday life (Zhang 2023, Bența 2018). In addition, there has been discussion about whether Schutz’s emphasis on planned action precludes recognizing the importance of innovation and creativity, as might appear in musical improvisation (Figueroa-Dreher 2008, Knoblauch 2020). For Schutz, however, passive-synthetically acquired typifications are remarkably flexible and elastic when applied to novel objects and situations, and this fact indicates an openness to inventiveness (Wehrle 2022); however, there are those (Straßheim 2016) who illustrate how habitual reliance on typifications can contribute to rigidity, reification, and closed worldviews. Thomas Eberle (1999) has contributed important methodological observations regarding Schutz’s successors; and he has argued against the standard view that social scientific research oscillates between the poles of quantitative and qualitative methodologies. Instead, Eberle has drawn a boundary between scientistic approaches that deny the need for any interpretation and those investigative strategies that integrate both quantitative and interpretive methods. After all, quantitative procedures require interpretation in the very formulation of their questions, and many interpretative strategies find themselves compelled to take account of quantitative findings. Also some (Embree 2015, Knoblauch 2020) have proposed that Schutz’s theory can be conceived more broadly as a meta-level “science theory” or “social theory”.

What becomes obvious is that the tradition of philosophy and the philosophy of the social sciences that Alfred Schutz initiated have continued developing vigorously for over sixty years, generating competing perspectives on the philosophy of the social sciences, giving birth to a vast field of applications across a multiplicity of disciplines, and stimulating internal philosophical and social scientific controversies. The tradition after Alfred Schutz’s lifetime remains very much alive.

# Let's Play with Hardcaml! - Metasepi

## Let's Play with Hardcaml!

Posted on November 28, 2026 / Tags: takibi, fpga, ocaml, hardcaml

### Table of contents

I prepared a five-minute lightning talk for the 8th Homebrew CPU Meetup on November 28, 2026. The slides are below.

Open slides in a new tab · Download PDF · View Markdown source

This talk is a gentle introduction to Hardcaml, an RTL design library embedded in OCaml. Rather than discussing advanced verification techniques, I wanted to share the fun of building digital circuits in an interactive programming environment.

We start with a simple 5-bit counter and do everything inside utop, an OCaml REPL:

- Describe a digital circuit using ordinary OCaml functions.
- Generate Verilog from the circuit.
- Simulate the circuit cycle by cycle using an ordinary OCaml for loop.
- Display the recorded waveforms directly in the terminal.
No FPGA, external Verilog simulator, or even a separate OCaml project is needed to try this example. I tested the installation steps and the REPL session in a Docker environment, so you can follow along with the slides.

And what happens if we keep playing with Hardcaml?

With the help of AI coding agents, I ended up building a dual-core RISC-V SoC that boots Linux 6.18 with SMP on a Colorlight i9 FPGA board.

I hope this talk encourages more people to give Hardcaml a try and enjoy building their own digital circuits.

# The human voice

This is a post from Robin Sloan’s lab blog & notebook. You can visit the blog’s homepage, or learn more about me.

## The human voice

November 20, 2026

I encourage you to open Levent Alpöge’s PDF note announcing his proof of the Rie­mann Hypoth­esis with the help of AI — because although the work was AI-assisted, this note is so clearly and beau­ti­fully human. It’s fabulous.

I have noticed the steady creep of AI-generated text into the pub­li­ca­tions of the big AI com­pa­nies themselves, and while it tends not to be on the level of “egregious slop”, it does lend every­thing a … smoothness. I note also that these pub­li­ca­tions are very rarely signed; they come from The Blob. Who wrote this?Who wrote this? I know it’s cus­tomary for big com­pa­nies to speak Blob-like, but/and I still find it jarring.

Coun­ter­point Alpöge: his note is not only better than a smooth, AI-generated summation, it’s also better than an aca­d­emic paper, because his passion — his appre­ci­a­tion of sur­prise and beauty — is so clear on the page. It seems almost to rise off the screen, a 3D layer of sparkling energy.

Tell you what, you can use all the AI you want in your project, if you write about it like this, in your real human voice.

P.S. And then there’s this, the absolute sig­na­ture of our new era: “The Rie­mann Hypoth­esis is proven, but not yet understood.”
